News.title: Cops hunt man, 40, and blue van after dad, 56, attacked & ‘murdered’ in ‘violent’ street brawl – as 10 arrested
News.content:
FATAL BRAWL Cops hunt man, 40, and blue van after dad, 56, attacked & ‘murdered’ in ‘violent’ street brawl – as 10 arrested

A MAN and a blue van are wanted by police after a dad was attacked and allegedly murdered in a violent street brawl.

Athony Paul Jones, 40, is wanted in connection with the chaos that took place in Pontnewynydd, Wales at around 7.15pm on August 6 which has led to the arrests of ten men.



Police rushed to the scene following reports of a violent brawl on Mill Street in Gwent.

Anthony “Tony” Jones, 56, was found badly injured before dying a few days later in hospital.



His family are being supported by specialist officers.

A further three men were also taken to hospital, with two said to be critically injured.



Since the father, from Brecon, passed away a murder investigation has been launched.

A manhunt is underway for Athony Paul Jones from Blaenavon, Torfaen, as cops believe he can assist with the investigation.



Cops are also searching for a blue Ford Transit van, with the registration MA23 FLC, which was reportedly involved in the disorder.

Ten men, aged 31, 33, 34, 39, 40, 40, 45, 59, 61 and 73, have also been arrested in connection with the violence, and three men aged 39, 45 and 61 have since been released on bail.

Seven men remain in custody as police continue their enquiries.

Senior investigating officer, Detective Superintendent Laura Bartley said: “We recognise that reports of this nature will cause concern in our communities, but our officers are working around the clock and conducting enquiries as part of this live investigation.

“We’re trying to establish the movements of those involved both before and after the disorder and are asking motorists who were driving along Hospital Road, Mill Road and the surrounding areas between 6pm and 9pm on Thursday to check their dashcam footage.



“Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the victim.”

Anyone with information on Anthony Paul Jones, or the blue Ford Transit van’s whereabouts, has been urged to submit information via the Major Incident Public Portal or contact police quoting log reference 2600255536.

You can also call on 101 or direct message them on Facebook or X social media pages.

Alternatively, you can call Crimestoppers, anonymously, with information on 0800 555 111 or visit online.

News.title: Woman in her 20s dies after car ploughs into parked street cleaner in late-night crash – as ‘uninsured’ driver arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FATAL CRASH Woman in her 20s dies after car ploughs into parked street cleaner in late-night crash – as ‘uninsured’ driver arrested

A WOMAN in her 20s who was a passenger in a Smart car was killed in a after the vehicle struck a street cleaning vehicle.

Tragically she was pronounced dead at the scene after the horror crash shortly before midnight on Wednesday last week.

Cops arrested the driver, a man in his 20s, on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving over the prescribed limit.

He was also arrested on suspicion of failing to provide a specimen for analysis and causing death by driving while uninsured.





Cops are appealing for witnesses after the fatal smash in Epsom, Surrey, at around 11.40pm, to come forward.

Ththe victim’s next of kin have been informed.

Christ Church Road was closed for several hours while officers carried out their initial enquiries.

The road reopened shortly after 9.45am.



Cops are now urging anyone who was in the area between 11.35pm and 11.40pm to come forward.

Officers are particularly keen to hear from anyone who saw the black Smart car in the moments before the crash.

They are also appealing for anyone with CCTV, dashcam or helmet cam footage which may have captured all or part of the incident.

Anyone with information is urged to contact police.

News.title: Royal Navy drones secretly sent data to China through ‘heartbeat communications’ after years of Beijing spying fears
News.content:
SPY drones used by British special forces have been secretly sending data to China amid concerns over espionage from Beijing.

Cameras in the drones used by elite Navy forces contain components which were made in China and have reportedly been transmitting information back to Beijing.



The K3 Scout surveillance drones have been part of the Royal Marines’ £12million fleet since March.

After finding the breach, the Ministry of Defence has reportedly been forced to remove all internet connectivity from the cameras, the Telegraph reports.



The drones were from major British defence contractor Kraken Technology Group which sourced the cameras from a third party.

The third party is said to have given assurances about the equipment’s security.

After the breach was discovered, an investigation revealed that cameras were sending “heartbeat communications” to an IP address in China.

This data confirms the devices were online and functioning as they should be.

The MoD said no systems were compromised or transmitted externally.

A source said the drones had been part of the UK’s future defence package offered to help secure movement in the Strait of Hormuz.



They added that preparations had already been conducted on the drones and the find was a “major failure to check origins of components and we have lost confidence in the platform.”

A spokesperson for the MoD said: “The first duty of government is national security, and we take the security of our equipment, networks and data extremely seriously.

“A routine cyber vulnerability assessment identified an issue affecting a Kraken Unmanned Surface Vessel sub-system used by the Royal Navy.

“A thorough investigation found no evidence of MOD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.

“Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment.”



This comes as the Labour Party tries to maintain relations with the Chinese Communist Party despite the looming threat the country poses.

Last month, a huge Chinese embassy was given the green light after a High Court challenge against the planning permission was dismissed.

The vast complex at Royal Mint Court, near the Tower of London, was approved despite concerns it could lead to terror attacks and the suppression of protests.

The Sun previously revealed that staff at British defence firms were told not to take phones to Wes Streeting’s first speech as Shadow Defence Secretary over fears of Chinese spying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Streeting spoke at an arms fair packed with Chinese firms – including an electronic warfare specialist that lists signals “cracking” as a flagship service.



Workers at Britain’s List X defence firms – which hold secret government contracts – were advised to leave phones, tablets and other devices outside the exhibition hall where Streeting delivered his keynote address.

News.title: Married doctor who Lucy Letby was ‘infatuated’ with could be identified if Lucy Letby has retrial, says Tory MP
News.content:
LUCY Letby campaigner David Davis MP says the anonymity order given to a doctor she was infatuated with is likely to be reviewed in the wake of his death.

The MP said it could take place at any future retrial.



The Sun on Sunday revealed how the medic, who was granted anonymity and referred to in court as Doctor A, died last month.

Mr Davis said: “I don’t think this changes much, I assume that the anonymity orders will be reviewed in the event of a retrial.”



At trial, prosecutors alleged Lucy would create “crisis situations” to gain his sympathy.

Her supporters later turned on him because he said in court that she might have “manipulated” him.



The married registrar – known as Doctor A – previously gave evidence against Letby during her trial for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others.

It is understood the medic – who was in his 50s – had been ill before passing away last month.

Prosecutors alleged Letby was infatuated with the physician and would create “crisis situations” by attacking infants to ensure he would be bleeped to attend.

Although the pair exchanged 1,300 messages and enjoyed day trips to London, Letby denied a romance and insisted they were simply “trusted friends”.



The 2024 Thirlwall Inquiry later found the doctor had been “misled” and “maybe manipulated” into giving Letby information about the babies she had attacked.

Letby continues to claim her innocence while serving a whole-life sentence at Bronzefield Prison.

News.title: Cops hunt firebomb maniacs after week-long arson rampage through Scots towns
News.content:
DETECTIVES have launched a manhunt after four cars were firebombed less than two miles apart.

Thugs torched the motors in two Lanarkshire towns in a nine-day wrecking spree.



In the first attack, a vehicle on Hamilton’s Sneddon Terrace was set on fire at around 2.20am on July 24.

Two other motors were targeted in nearby Reid Street at around 3.40am six days later.



The maniacs left a Mini and a black estate car burnt out.

Shocking footage showed both vehicles ablaze as fire crews arrived to put out the flames.

Pictures later revealed the charred wrecks of the cars with the estate’s bonnet lying mangled.

Meanwhile, officers are hunting two masked suspects over another car attack in Ivy Place, Blantyre, at 11.40pm on August 2.

Police said the suspects were dressed head-to-toe in black. They were spotted pushing a bicycle around the time of the blaze.

Last night, Police Scotland confirmed inquiries into all three attacks remained ongoing.



It is understood the force is treating the Hamilton attacks as linked while keeping an open mind on the incident in Blantyre.

No one was injured in any of the blazes.

Detective Constable Stuart Adams said: “I am appealing to anyone who was in the area to think if they noticed anything suspicious or unusual.

“I would also appeal to any motorists with dash-cam to check their footage for any images which could assist our investigation.

“Any information could prove relevant.”

News.title: Brit teen, 16, dead and two siblings badly injured after ‘terrible accident’ on luxury Caribbean family holiday
News.content:
A BRITISH teenager has died in a “terrible accident” on a family holiday which also left her two siblings badly injured.

Abbie Lainton, 16, from Swindon, died while on vacation in the Dominican Republic with her heartbroken friends and school paying tribute.



Family friend Becky Jamieson described Abbie as a “beautiful” young girl who was loved by everyone who knew her.

She said in an emotional statement that Abbie lost her life on July 30, with her sister Carley and brother Bradley also being left badly injured.



It remains unclear how the siblings got into danger.

Becky continued: “Abbie had her whole life ahead of her. She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results.



“She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her.

“For Abbie, forever 16, forever loved and never forgotten.”

A GoFundMe page, which was set up to help Abbie’s family, has already received more than £5,000 in donations.

Abbie’s former school Tanwood School for Performing Arts, also honoured her in a statement.



A spokesperson said: “Abbie joined Tanwood as a dinky dot and was part of an exceptional group of dancers who formed strong friendships which spilled over to the audience when they performed together.

“She always performed with a huge smile, and those beautiful feet.

“We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time.

“You will always be in our hearts.”

Abbie joined Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club at a later date where she excelled and took part in competitions around the world.



The club invited people to come together and remember Abbie as well as celebrate her life and share memories.

A spokesperson for the club said: “There are simply no words that feel enough.

“Abbie was a much-loved member of our Swindon Lightning family.

“Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years.

“She brought so much light to our gym, and her loss has left us all heartbroken.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our thoughts, love and deepest condolences are with Abbie’s family and loved ones during this unimaginable time.”

Anyone wanting to contribute to the appeal can click here.

News.title: Islamist terrorists who plotted to blow up 10 planes must not be eligible for early release from prison
News.content:
Too dangerous

IT could have been the worst mass murder in criminal history.

A gang of Islamist terrorists plotted to blow ten passenger jets out of the sky with liquid explosives smuggled through Heathrow disguised in hand luggage as drinks, shampoo and toothpaste.



Had the plot succeeded, up to 10,000 innocent people could have been killed — three times the death toll of the 9/11 attacks on New York’s Twin Towers.

Britain was spared that unimaginable slaughter thanks to the bravery, skill and ingenuity of MI5 and the police, who smashed the conspiracy just days before the planned attacks.



But three of the men convicted of conspiracy to murder — Waheed Zaman, Ibrahim Savant and Arafat Waheed Khan — could soon be eligible for parole after serving 20 years of their life terms.

These were not misguided young men caught up in some minor offence.



They were convicted of planning mass murder on an appalling scale.

All three recorded “martyrdom” videos, intended to be released by al-Qaeda after the attacks.

The British public has had enough of violent criminals being released early while victims and their families are left to live with the consequences.

The Parole Board must not allow pressure to ease prison overcrowding to cloud their cold-headed judgment when considering these cases.



Some prisoners are just too dangerous to release.

These terrorists should be among them.

Off to prison

BRITAIN’S overcrowded prisons are at breaking point — yet 10,000 foreign lags are taking up scarce places.

Most of them would have been booted out long ago if their home countries had agreed to take them back.

Instead, the Government has been forced to free thousands of offenders early to stop the system collapsing.



So Nigel Farage’s idea to ship foreign convicts to serve their sentences 5,500 miles away in the grim jails of El Salvador is worth exploring.

It would end the sickening spectacle of violent crooks being freed halfway through their sentence.

And make foreign visitors think twice about bringing criminal activities to Britain.

Back to work

FRESH back from holiday, Andy Burnham will embark on a cost of living tour tomorrow — and recycle an idea first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago.

He will re-announce plans to end “subscription traps” which deliberately make it tricky for people to stop recurring charges after ordering online.

Perhaps when he’s delivered his latest “easy win”, the PM might find time to turn his mind to more pressing issues.

Like the economy, illegal migration, hospital waiting lists and rebuilding our hollowed-out Armed Forces.

News.title: Andy Burnham kicks off cost-of-living tour with reheated Labour pledge to crack down on subscription traps
News.content:
ANDY Burnham will kick off his cost-of- living tour tomorrow with a reheated pledge first announced by Labour in 2023.

The PM is promising to end so-called subscription traps that lure customers into costly and hard-to-cancel online plans for the likes of streaming services.



Back from his holiday, Mr Burnham will accuse Westminster of “telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life” for too long.

But the crackdown on subscription traps was first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago and started in April before his resignation.



It will force companies to give customers clearer information when subscriptions are automatically renewed at a higher cost, and impose a 14-day cooling-off period allowing them to cancel after a trial.

Like Sir Keir — who was seen playing football yesterday in an Arsenal strip — Mr Burnham claims this will save an average £14 a month for every unwanted subscription, ending an estimated total of £1.6billion a year being wasted.



The only difference in the cut-and-paste policy appears to be the PM bringing forward the date from spring next year to January.

Mr Burnham is also announcing plans to end rip-off discounts whereby sellers deliberately raise their prices before slashing them to give the impression of a bargain.

He will launch a consultation to see whether such practices should be banned by law.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Burnham has already run out of ideas.



“Labour’s tax hikes have sent costs soaring for hardworking families and destroyed jobs.

“Consultations and reheated measures won’t make up for that.”

News.title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
News.content:
A domestic violence victim has told BBC Breakfast how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.

The woman, whom the BBC is calling Lucy, said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.

She contacted the BBC after hearing about the sentencing of Kyran Smith, who sexually assaulted a woman in her bed at a Travelodge in Maidenhead in 2022.

Speaking about Lucy's case, Travelodge said that while incidents like this were "very rare", customer safety and security was, and remained, a priority with staff undergoing recent training.

Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted".

"He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.

The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said.

"I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.

She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.

After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive".

"I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."

She said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."

Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.

News.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
News.content:
Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.

The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much lower prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.

It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

It is already unlawful to use false "was" prices for items on sale, but it is not on the list of the Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) list of banned practices.

Practices on the list, such as operating pyramid schemes or displaying a quality assurance mark without authorisation, are automatically considered illegal without consumer harm having to be proved.

The Liberal Democrats urged Burnham to "go further" to protect consumers, with Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper calling for "strengthened protections against rogue traders" and action to tackle supermarket "shrinkflation" â the practice of products being made smaller yet being sold for the same price.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a Â£2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

News.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
News.content:
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.

The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday.

While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north.

Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year.

It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.

Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.

News.title: Brief relief ahead of fifth heatwave - as more areas could move into drought
News.content:
Much of the country will feel some relief from the heat early in the week before temperatures spike again.

On Monday, the air will feel a little fresher compared to the weekend with maximum temperatures in northern areas of the UK around 18 to 24C.

Further south, while cooler than Sunday, it will still be a very warm day with temperatures between 22 to 27C.

By Tuesday, warmer air will start to move back in across the UK with the highest temperatures across central southern England, the Midlands and east Wales.

Yellow heat-health alerts remain in force for much of England until 21:00 BST on Tuesday, though they are likely to be extended or upgraded as the heatwave nears.

Highs are likely to be around 27 to 30C.

Wednesday will see temperatures widely across England and Wales head into the high twenties and low thirties.

The peak of the extreme heat is set to arrive on Thursday, with temperatures reaching 36C (97F) in south-east England, and up to 35C likely across central and eastern England.

This would mark the fourth consecutive month where 35C has been reached in the UK â a new record.

Many locations will exceed their heatwave threshold of 25 to 28C â dependent on location â for the first day.

Some of the warmth will spread further north into northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures into the low to mid-20s Celsius.

As heat builds throughout the week, overnight temperatures will stay relatively high bringing some uncomfortable nights for sleeping.

Minimum temperatures may not go lower than 16 to 18C across England and Wales.

There's also a possibility of a 'tropical night' â where temperatures remain above 20C all night â in south-east England.

News.title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
News.content:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear â plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to Â£50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was Â£101.94 with a pinafore, and Â£83.95 without â but this year it will cost families an average of Â£53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.

News.title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS.

Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill.

The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished.

The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety.

The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal â where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths.

A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal â one of the biggest in NHS history â involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008.

Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.

Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.

Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.

News.title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
News.content:
The first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.

Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.

The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".

The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".

News.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she's freezing her eggs
News.content:
New York Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has revealed she has decided to freeze her eggs and has shared her first steps in the process on social media.

The 36-year-old posted the clips on Sunday, hours before telling ABC News This Week she had not "ruled out the possibility" of running for president.

In the clips, Ocasio-Cortez shows herself taking an injection and talks through tips she has learnt, before answering questions about costs, clinical procedures, storage and how fertility care works under what she calls the US's "broken" medical system.

In an interview on ABC News she said she wanted to "normalise" conversations about the process.

She said it was important "especially in this political environment".

"This administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy," she said. "I think it's important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes," she added.

In an earlier post on Instagram she said she wanted to share the information even though there was a "political risk" in doing so.

When asked if she would run for president in the 2028 elections after being shown polling reflecting her popularity as a potential candidate, Ocasio-Cortez chuckled and tried to sidestep a direct answer.

"I'm focused on winning the mid-terms, I'm running for Congress right now," she said.

But when pushed as to whether she was open to it and whether it was a realistic prospect, she said: "I haven't ruled out the possibility and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."

"We have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans," she said.

After she was asked about a possible Senate run against minority leader Chuck Schumer, the US Senate's top Democrat, Ocasio-Cortez replied that "anything was possible".

The midterms are held every two years and fall in the middle of the president's four-year term of office.

They are due to be held in early November. Votes will be cast for all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, and a third of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for grabs.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid Dobby's grave
News.content:
He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

News.title: 'Roll on 2027' as Fleadh 2026 comes to an end
News.content:
The first All Ireland Fleadh in Belfast ended in the early hours of Monday morning with organisers saying they were overwhelmed by the positive response they received from all communities.

It is estimated that there were more than a million people in the city centre during the eight days of the fleadh.

At least 4,000 were still in the grounds of Belfast City Hall at 01:00 BST to hear the closing speeches and final tunes.

Niall McClean, co-chair of the organising committee, told the crowd they were all part of an historic event.

He said: "We've done something that has never, ever happened in this city before. We've brought every single community together â and everybody has absolutely loved it."

McClean added that it has "put a permanent smile on my face. I'm the happiest man in Belfast. Roll on 2027".

"What an incredible week. Everyone I have spoken to has had an amazing time here in Belfast, thousands of people all on a high.

"Belfast has shone, the world has come to our doorstep, bringing the biggest numbers ever seen for a Fleadh Cheoil na hÃireann.

"I'm so proud of our branch and all our members, and what we have achieved together. We dared to dream and those dreams have come true."

To loud applause, he ended by saying: "Well done Belfast, we'll see you next year."

The All Ireland Fleadh returns to the city from 1 to 8 August 2027.

News.title: Parents fear being left behind in screening for rare condition after Jesy Nelson campaign
News.content:
Parents of children with a rare genetic condition say they fear Wales is being left behind as other parts of the UK introduce routine screening for newborns.

After widespread campaigning, including by former Little Mix star Jesy Nelson, testing for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) will happen in England and be trialled in Scotland but not in Wales.

Warren Davies, whose three-year-old daughter Ophelia-May has SMA type 2, external, said it felt like the Welsh government was "playing God because they have the opportunity to effect change and are choosing not to".

The Welsh government said it had followed UK National Screening Committee (NSC) guidance that had not recommended routine newborn screening for SMA.

Newborn screening for SMA is also not in place in Northern Ireland, external.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

Police have seized millions of pounds worth of supercars in a central London crackdown.

More than £8million worth of vehicles – including a Ferrari Monza worth £3.7million - were seized in an operation targeting uninsured drivers, anti-social and dangerous driving across Hyde Park, Kensington and Chelsea.

Officers from the Met, supported by Motor Insurers’ Bureau, seized a total of 90 vehicles between Friday, 7 August and Sunday, 9 August.

open image in gallery Seized vehicles including a Rolls Royce Cullinan and a Rolls-Royce Urus at Wellington Arch ( Met Police )

Cars included a Ferrari Monza SP2, which had only been in the UK for a day, for driving without insurance and not in accordance with a license. The motorist only had a provisional driving license and had been in the car for less than half an hour when he was stopped by Met officers. The supercar was one of only 499 made by the Italian brand, with one model selling at auction for $4,995,000 (£3.7million) earlier this year.

New powers mean officers can seize vehicles involved in antisocial behaviour rather than giving motorists a warning. A total of 15 vehicles were seized under this legislation alone across the weekend.

open image in gallery A car seized in central London ( Met Police )

Special Chief Inspector Geoff Tatman, who led the operation, said: “We regularly hear from local people who are fed up with people driving cars dangerously in the area, or with modifications which make them a nuisance to those who live nearby.

“Through operations like this we’re arresting these drivers and seizing their cars so we can keep our roads safe and send clear message that we won’t put up with their reckless and dangerous behavior.”

The operation featured 120 officers, including 95 from the Met’s Special Constabulary and Vehicle Enforcement Team, backed by Motor Insurers’ Bureau’s expertise in uninsured driving prevention and advanced roadside support.

open image in gallery A seized Ferrari 812 ( Met Police )

Angus Eaton, CEO at Motor Insurers’ Bureau, said: “Operations like these show that the rules apply to all motorists, regardless of the value of the vehicle they chose to drive. We know that while many offenders knowingly violate the law, others that aim to be law-abiding motorists may be caught out by making a genuine insurance mistake.

“We want to help all motorists understand the importance of having the right insurance because the consequences of not having insurance or getting the right cover for their needs are severe and long-lasting.

“We urge all motorists to check they have cover in place and that it’s adequate for them, their vehicle, and their journey types.”

open image in gallery Seized Ferrari Monza ( Met Police )

Met officers said that during this operation, alongside the 90 vehicles seized, stops for suspected insurance offences also enabled officers to detect a range of other criminal activity, including:

A man who was found with 19 bank cards in other people’s names and more than £2,500 in cash, who was arrested on suspicion of handling stolen goods and money laundering

A man who was stopped for driving without insurance and found to have £5,500 in cash, who was arrested on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A, B and C drugs

A man who was arrested for using words and behaviour that would likely cause harassment, alarm, and distress to a member of public

A man who was arrested on suspicion of an immigration offence

open image in gallery A seized Toyota Land Cruiser ( Met Police )

Cllr Caroline Sargent, Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Enforcement at Westminster City Council, said: “People who think it’s acceptable to drive illegally in Westminster are not welcome here. The disruption caused by these reckless drivers and boy racers is often worse during the summer months and, as well as putting people at risk, causes significant nuisance for residents and businesses.

“We welcome the Met Police’s latest round of enforcement and our continued partnership in deterring anti-social driving, as well as the recent High Court injunction, which underlines the council's zero-tolerance approach to this behaviour. Drivers who break the rules risk losing their licence or worse.”

A flight from western Canada to Toronto was cancelled because a young child would not sit down and fasten their seatbelt, leaving other passengers scrambling to find somewhere to stay for the night.

Porter Airlines said Flight PD444 had left the terminal at the Victoria airport in British Columbia and was heading for the runway on Thursday evening when the child, who was standing on the seat, could not be strapped in despite repeated attempts by their parent and the cabin crew.

The crew decided to return to the terminal because the aircraft could not take off safely, said Brad Cicero, a spokesman for the Toronto-based airline. Bringing the plane back to a gate, removing the parent and child, retrieving their luggage, and refiling the paperwork took so long that the flight was set to miss the airport's 12.30am runway closure.

It meant the crew was left with little choice but to ask the remaining passengers to get off. The flight eventually left on Friday afternoon.

"We apologise for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day," Mr Cicero said.

Passengers described a long wait with little information, although one said the child had not been badly behaved, only frightened.

"They just kept hiding under their seat. If they got forced into being strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath," a passenger named Aryeh Kozuch told the CBC.

Another passenger said that the process took far longer than it should have. "It took forever," Hillary Hertzberg told the broadcaster. "The kid eventually got off the plane at 11.30pm, so we had been on the flight for almost an hour at that point."

Ms Hertzberg said she wanted the airline to cover the costs for the passengers. Porter declined to say whether it would compensate the passengers.

Canadian aviation norms require every passenger to be seated with their seatbelt fastened during taxiing, take-off and landing, with no exemption for young children, who must be held or restrained rather than left unsecured.

With comfortable cabins, bar carts and scenic views, sleeper trains have long enticed travellers looking to get some shut-eye on long journeys.

New luxury night carriages have launched this year – costing more than a business-class flight – but those looking for a more accessible ticket can still find options on the continent.

European Sleeper revived the Paris to Berlin night train connection in March this year, with prices beginning from €69.99 (£60) for a one-way ticket in a shared compartment.

open image in gallery Passengers can book tickets across five room types on the Caledonian Sleeper ( Caledonian Sleeper )

Nox, a Berlin-based startup, also aims to offer an affordable alternative to short-haul flights, operating overnight trains in Europe from 2027, with single rooms starting from just €79 (£67).

Not all of the options are quite as affordable, but do offer both transport and a night’s sleep at a price-point below that of a hotel.

While we wait to see if the trains take to the tracks, here is a selection of some more wallet-friendly routes across the continent that are already leaving the station.

Best budget sleeper trains

1. ÖBB Nightjet – European routes

open image in gallery Nightjet connects over 25 European destinations ( Getty Images )

Nightjet, operated by Austrian Railways (ÖBB), connects over 25 cities such as Vienna, Amsterdam and Hamburg on its multi-national train services. Passengers are offered the choice of sleeper cabins, couchettes and seating carriages on its journeys. Several sleeping car categories offer their own shower and toilet, a fully made bed and an a la carte breakfast.

Key routes operate between Vienna and Amsterdam, Graz and Berlin and Zurich and Hamburg with minimum fares starting at €19.90 (£17.30) for a couchette in six-berth, €29.90 (£26) for a couchette in four-berth, €69.90 (£61) for a bed in a double sleeper or €114.90 (£100) for a single-bed sleeper all to yourself.

2. Night Riviera – Paddington to Penzance

open image in gallery Sleeper berths start from £49 in a single cabin ( GWR )

Night Riviera, one of two sleeper trains in the UK, connects overnight passengers travelling from London Paddington to Penzance, Cornwall. The service offers both “airline-style” seats and single and shared cabins. Night Riviera generally departs from London Paddington at 23.45pm six nights a week, arriving in Penzance at 7.50am.

Super off-peak return tickets for the Night Riviera sleeper from London Paddington to Penzance generally cost around £150. Sleeper berths, an additional supplement from £49 in a single cabin, are fitted with plug sockets, sinks, wardrobes and bottom bunks that convert to sofas. All cabin guests can enjoy the use of lounges and showers at Paddington, Penzance, and Truro and a complimentary breakfast in their cabin. There’s also an onboard lounge bar for soft and stiff drinks or a light bite.



3. SJ Night Train – Stockholm to Narvik

open image in gallery Take the SJ Night Train to travel from Sweden to Norway ( Getty Images )

The SJ Night Train (Nattåg 94) is an 18-hour journey departing Stockholm Central in Sweden through arctic landscapes to Narvik, Norway. Aside from regular seats, three different classes of shared or private compartments are available to travellers – an ensuite cabin for two including breakfast, a compartment for three with communal showers and toilets in the corridor and a couchette cabin that sleeps up to six people.

The night train departs daily, usually leaving Stockholm at around 6pm, arriving in Narvik just before 12:40 pm the next day. Beds in a shared sleeping compartment start from around 2,865 Swedish Krona (£233) each way.

4. Caledonian Sleeper – London to Fort William

open image in gallery The Caledonian Sleeper runs every night apart from Saturday ( Caledonian Sleeper )

The iconic Caledonian Sleeper connects London to the Scottish Highlands, with a stop at Birmingham International station as of January 2026. The sleeper train currently runs every night apart from Saturday, with guests being transported from London Euston to some of Scotland’s largest cities, including Aberdeen, Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness, and more rural locations, such as Fort William.

Passengers can book tickets across five room types with access to reclining chairs, bunk and single beds in private rooms or double en-suite rooms. The most basic seating options range in price from £54 to £100. However, a bed on a journey to Fort William in a classic single or twin room can cost between £210 and £405. The train also features a “Club Car” where passengers staying in rooms can order dishes made with Scottish produce or enjoy a late-night drink.



5. VR Finnish Railways – Helsinki to Rovaniemi

open image in gallery VR Finnish Railways offers a scenic sleeper train to Santa’s “official” hometown ( Getty Images )

Looking to lay down in Lapland? VR Finnish Railways offers a direct, scenic sleeper train service from Helsinki to Rovaniemi – Santa’s “official” hometown – via cities such as Tampere and Oulu. The double-decker “Santa Claus Express” night train features basic bunkbed cabins for two people, with shared or private shower and toilet facilities. With journeys up to 12 hours long, prices to stay in private cabins start from €49 (£43) and cabins with showers from €74 (£64.30).

6. InterCity Notte – Italian routes

open image in gallery Trains are transported by ferry across the Strait of Messina to Sicily ( Getty Images )

Trenitalia’s InterCity Notte is another affordable option with sleeper trains connecting the north to the south of Italy. With routes departing Milan and Rome for Palermo, Sicily – the train is transported by ferry across the Strait of Messina – and connections from Turin to Naples, these night trains offer modern coaches with seat, sleeper and couchette categories.

Single, double or triple occupancy sleeper cabins come with air conditioning, a washbasin, power sockets and a continental breakfast. Fares start from €122 (£106) for private sleeper cabins.

Andy Burnham has vowed to tackle “rip-off” subscription traps as part of his blitz of policies to tackle the cost of living crisis and provide “everyday fixes” for rising bills.

The prime minister, who will begin a summer tour of the country on Monday, will accelerate plans to force companies to make it easier to cancel subscriptions and provide more information about costs up-front rather than quietly auto-renewing them at a higher price.

Mr Burnham will travel the country during August where he will ask the public how the government can improve their lives, with officials insisting the PM will be in “listening mode” as he vowed to “pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living”.

The changes to subscriptions, announced in April under Sir Keir Starmer’s government, had been expected to come into force next spring, but Mr Burnham will bring their introduction forward to January.

open image in gallery The PM will begin a summer tour of the country on Monday ( PA Wire )

He will also launch a consultation on adding deceptive discount offers to the Competition and Markets Authority’s list of banned practices.

This would make it easier for the watchdog to punish firms that artificially inflate prices and then immediately offer a “discount” to make a product look much better value than it is.

The prime minister said: “I know people are sick and tired of rip-off discounts and subscription traps. Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life.

“I don’t think that’s right, especially when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives.”

Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, welcomed the proposals, saying subscription traps and deceptive discounts were “a widespread problem”.

Citizens Advice has previously found 26 per cent of UK adults had accidentally taken out a subscription in a single year, with the government saying its action could save households £14 per month.

Further announcements are expected over the summer, with the prime minister describing Monday’s proposals as “just the start”.

The upcoming tour, which is expected to inform his 10-year plan for the country, will also see Mr Burnham focus on improving high streets.

A spokesperson for the prime minister added he would be “getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are”.

But opposition figures have criticised his August plans as a “vanity tour” offering only “tinkering”, and urged him to implement broader tax cuts. Meanwhile, there have also been concerns raised over how Mr Burnham’s cost of living blitz will be funded.

It comes after he announced a swathe of policies to bring down bills in his first week in office, including a 20 per cent business rate cut for pubs, clubs and live music venues, a VAT cut to electricity bills, and bus fares capped to £2 from January.

The business rate cut alone is expected to cost the government around £100m per year – but it is unclear how it will be funded.

Mr Burnham is also facing at least a £4.7bn black hole to fill in Sir Keir’s defence spending plan. But announcing that his first Budget will take place on 28 October, chancellor John Healey vowed it would be “built on fiscal discipline”.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham and chancellor John Healey are trying to bring down the cost of living ( PA Wire )

Last month, the prime minister was warned that he will have to raise taxes or cut spending if he wants to fund his new priorities, in a grim analysis by one of the UK’s leading economic think tanks.

Economists at the National Institute for Economic and Social Research (NIESR) cautioned the prime minister and Mr Healey that “there is no capacity to borrow any more” and that inflation will push up the cost of living much higher than the Bank of England (BoE) is forecasting.

Responding to the latest measures to tackle the cost of living, shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Andy Burnham has already run out of ideas.

“The cost of living didn’t become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government.

“Labour’s tax hikes have sent costs soaring for hardworking families and destroyed jobs. Consultations and reheated measures won’t make up for that.”

Moeen Ali is eager to earn his coaching stripes in the England pathway next year, as he works towards his “ultimate dream” of leading the national side.

The all-rounder retired from international cricket in 2024 and worked as a mentor to the England Lions as part of Andrew Flintoff’s backroom staff in the United Arab Emirates earlier in February.

At the age of 39 he is still in demand domestically, turning out for Yorkshire in the Vitality Blast and Southern Brave in the Hundred this summer, but is already planning for the next chapter.

open image in gallery Moeen Ali (centre) harbours hopes of coaching England one day (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Archive )

The recent decision to put New Zealander Stephen Fleming in charge of the Test team, succeeding his fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum, put the lack of homegrown options firmly back on the agenda in English cricket.

Managing director Rob Key admitted the production line was not moving fast enough and vowed to offer increased opportunities to English coaches in the future. And in Moeen, a three-format international boasting 298 caps and two World Cup winner’s medals, he has a willing candidate.

“I’ve been asked about doing Lions stuff quite often but it’s been pretty difficult while I’m still playing, I think next year I’ll be a lot more available to do that,” he told the Press Association.

“After this winter I’ll be more free to coach. Whether it’s the Lions, the under-19s, whatever they want, it’s something I’m really looking forward to doing.

“I want to gain my experience and put in the hard yards as a coach.”

open image in gallery England’s managing director Rob Key has pledged to hand chances to homegrown coaches (Robbie Stephenson/PA) ( PA Archive )

Moeen, who became the first British Asian to captain England in T20 cricket, has spoken previously about his hopes of having a second act to his England career and makes no apologies for setting his sights high.

“The ultimate dream is to coach England, of course, but I know there is a lot of work to put in before that,” he said.

“When you’re a young player learning to play county cricket the dream is to play for England and it’s the same with coaching. You never know how things turn out.”

Although renowned for his flamboyant strokeplay and attacking spin bowling, Moeen’s coaching philosophy begins with a solid grasp of the basics that have sometimes gone ignored at the top level in recent times.

“With England batters in particular, we can get exposed big time – lots of bowled, lots of lbws,” he said.

“It’s about coaching technique, more than anything. I see a lot of coaches who are hands off and let players do their thing, as long as they are happy. But players like to be told sometimes and they don’t get told enough these days to be honest.”
