OpenAI turned off restrictions that would have prevented its model from “pursuing high risk cyber activity.” Anthropic ran its tests without the standard safety safeguards in models that are generally available to the public. The AI Security Institute also turned off certain tools that could have “reduced the scope” of what the models were capable of.

Researchers typically do this to fully evaluate a model’s capabilities.

“I couldn’t go into ChatGPT or Claude or something like that, and it accidentally breaks into the FBI. That’s not going to happen,” said Adam Meyers, head of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. “So what we’re seeing is these are done in specific test conditions where they’re monitoring to see, ‘Does this thing do something that it’s not expected to do?”

How hackers are using AI

AI isn’t acting autonomously to come up with new attacks, experts say. Instead, it’s helping cyber criminals implement existing techniques much faster while being more efficient and effective.

That can include things like using AI to analyze a company’s website to figure out who to target or deploying an AI agent to handle initial negotiation talks with a cyber extortion victim. AI agents can mimic human conversations through both text and even specific voices. Hackers with little expertise can now leverage AI to pull off advanced schemes.

“They’re using (AI) to enhance the cyberattack methodology, essentially, in all the different stages, but it’s still kind of being run by the human,” said Jud Dressler, head of the risk operations center at cyber insurance firm Resilience.

Bad actors used to hastily scrap together basic scripts – instructions for automating tasks – to achieve their goals, according to Meyers. But now they’re able to churn out higher quality work that looks like it would have taken three times as long to produce.

They’re also using AI for behind-the-scenes work like generating the infrastructure needed to put up malicious websites.

“With AI, they could automate that buildout, and so the cost of rebuilding became very small and that changes the game,” said Rob Lefferts, corporate vice president of threat protection at Microsoft.

The bigger threat

For Etzioni, the recent incidents are a “canary in the coal mine” moment for AI and cybersecurity. And he’s not alone; Nobel prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, known popularly as the “godfather of AI,” recently warned that more rogue AI attacks are likely to come.

The rogue AI reports underscore the importance of implementing strong cybersecurity practices, such as patching vulnerabilities, monitoring AI agents in the workplace and being wary of social engineering and phishing scams, experts say.

But as advanced as AI is becoming, it’s still a program being orchestrated by a human. And those humans are the bigger concern because they’re the ones making the decisions, like conducting espionage or scamming users out of huge sums of cash, says Meyers.

Tech giants are racing to make AI as intelligent as humans, a theoretical milestone known as “artificial general intelligence.” The recent incidents, however, have heightened calls for a slowdown.

More than 1,200 workers at top AI companies, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, recently signed an open letter calling for the government to help pace AI development. The White House met with major AI companies last week to discuss a framework that would allow the government to review certain AI models before they’re released.

Cybersecurity researchers have likely considered the threats of AGI because those in the field tend to be paranoid, said IBM’s Fussell. But we’re still far from a reality in which AI agents are as smart as humans, he says.

“It’s like asking someone, ‘What would it be like to live on a different planet?’” he said. “You can sort of imagine, but it’s so beyond our ability to really make a plan for.”

World.title: How both Iran and Oman have economic claims to the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Iran is waiting for “final approval” on a proposed framework agreement with Oman for shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported yesterday.

Under the agreement, Iranian and Omani routes will remain in use temporarily before traffic is redirected through a central course, according to Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency. Officials in Iran would oversee inbound traffic, while their Omani counterparts would manage outbound traffic, Fars said.

The vital Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed by Iran since the US and Israel began the war back in February. It is the main route for shipping crude from oil-rich countries such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to the rest of the world.

Both Tehran and Muscat have Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) in the strait.

According to the United Nations, a state has “sovereign rights” to explore, exploit, conserve and manage the natural resources of the waters in its EEZ.

However, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), “ships of all States, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea.”

A coastal state should not “hamper the innocent passage of foreign ships through the territorial sea,” it says, except in specific outlined scenarios. It may “take the necessary steps in its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent,” UNCLOS outlines.

CNN’s Aida Karimi and Sana Noor Haq contributed to this reporting.

World.title: Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan, saying no withdrawal until Hamas disarms
World.content:
Israel has rejected the latest US plan to move towards the next stage of peace in Gaza, demanding the full disarmament of Hamas before any Israeli forces withdraw.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the beginning of a cabinet meeting Sunday.

He said the Israeli military would “not withdraw at all until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens.”

“And when I say disarm Hamas, that means heavy weapons, less-heavy weapons, all weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not a fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

“We are now discussing this with the Americans. They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.”

“As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will be established — not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” Netanyahu said.

At the end of July, US President Donald Trump announced what he described as a historic agreement to secure the disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza, months after the president first announced a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Hamas and Israel.

Hamas said it would only go through with the deal if Israel halts strikes in Gaza and pulls troops back to the “yellow line,” as defined by the October ceasefire agreement.

Israeli forces currently occupy more than half of Gaza, in the east and south of the territory.

World.title: UEFA confirms payout to ex-employee under Infantino, amid denials of an affair
World.content:
FIFA chief Gianni Infantino is denying a report that inappropriate conduct was behind a six-figure “departure payment” made to a woman during his years as general secretary at the Union of European Football Associations.

UEFA confirmed the woman’s payout, noting that while it was not out of line at the time, internal regulations have since been “tightened.”

The British newspaper The Telegraph first reported allegations that the woman was paid because of an affair with the beleaguered head of world football.

Infantino “strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue,” a FIFA spokesperson told The Telegraph.

“Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” the statement added. CNN has reached out to FIFA for comment.

Ever since Infantino and FIFA’s controversial plans to sell partial commercial and operational rights to the World Cup were leaked two weeks ago, soccer’s world governing body has come under immense pressure, even after those plans were scrapped.

UEFA, which counts some of the world’s most powerful soccer nations among its members, has threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and publicly declared its loss of confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

This latest chapter in soccer’s civil war was sparked when The Telegraph published an article Friday alleging that “UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Gianni Infantino while he was its general secretary.”

The paper, citing multiple anonymous sources, claimed that Infantino had a “relationship with a junior employee” during his tenure at the helm of UEFA from 2009 to 2016. She was promoted to a “more lucrative managerial role,” and received a “payment” when she left the organization, the paper reported. UEFA also paid for her MBA course, the report added. She was not named in the report.

In a statement to CNN, UEFA confirmed a “departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school.”

“The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time,” the organization added. “Such regulations have been tightened since 2016 and the current staff regulations – which apply to all UEFA employees at whatever level – reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organization.”

On Saturday, FIFA issued a statement condemning efforts to circumvent the organization’s “statutes, democratic procedures and established governance framework.”

“It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President,” FIFA’s statement said. “Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA’s established democratic processes.”

The statement went on to say, “FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, FIFA will challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Senior FIFA officials threw their support behind Infantino after a crisis meeting on Wednesday, but UEFA is still threatening to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups. It doubled down on the threat even after the sell-off plans were jettisoned, saying it needs assurances that nothing like this will happen again.

If that threat came to pass, it would hugely devalue any World Cup since six of the current top 10 teams in both men’s and women’s soccer would not compete in the tournament.

FIFPRO, the players’ union, has also said its confidence in FIFA’s leadership “has now been fundamentally broken.”

However, CONMEBOL, which oversees South American soccer and opposed the plans, has said it won’t back an extraordinary congress to vote on Infantino’s future and will follow the existing timeline for the presidential election, which is set for early next year.

The Confederation of African Football, which is more dependent on the money FIFA distributes than other continental confederations, has backed Infantino.

CNN’s Ben Church, Thomas Schlachter and Kevin Dotson contributed to this report.

World.title: Egypt condemns attack on UAE oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned the targeting of an oil tanker operated by Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) with a missile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, describing the incident as a serious threat to maritime security, navigation and freedom of trade through one of the world’s key waterways.

In a statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry expressed full solidarity with the UAE and firmly rejected acts targeting ships and civilian facilities or threatening maritime safety in the region.

Egypt stressed the need to respect freedom of navigation through international waterways and prevent any actions that could endanger it.

Cairo also renewed its call for de-escalation and urged all parties to prioritize political and diplomatic solutions to help safeguard regional security and stability.

World.title: Egypt, Iraq FMs discuss regional developments, efforts on de-escalation
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty held a phone call Saturday, August 8, 2026, with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein to discuss bilateral relations and regional developments.

The two ministers stressed the importance of building on the growing momentum in Egyptian-Iraqi ties, expanding cooperation across various fields and maintaining coordination on issues of mutual concern.

They exchanged views on developments in the region and future security arrangements, emphasizing the need for joint efforts to reduce tensions, prioritize dialogue and support political and diplomatic solutions to regional crises.

The ministers also underscored the importance of strengthening the trilateral cooperation mechanism between Egypt, Iraq and Jordan as a promising framework for regional integration and for increasing the three countries’ human and economic resources.

They stressed the need to build on the achievements made under the mechanism aimed at supporting the aspirations of the three peoples for greater development and shared prosperity.

World.title: Egypt uncovers ancient cemetery in Daqahliya
World.content:
An Egyptian archaeological mission has uncovered an ancient cemetery and settlement in Daqahliya Governorate, revealing evidence of human occupation in the eastern Nile Delta spanning thousands of years.

The Supreme Council of Antiquities said that excavations at the Kom el Khilgan archaeological site uncovered burials dating from the Predynastic Period through the Greek and Roman eras, as well as a settlement from the Second Intermediate Period.

The oldest finds date to the first half of the fourth millennium BC and include simple oval burial pits containing human remains, handmade pottery and seashells. The number of burials suggests that a sizeable community lived in the area at the time.

Archaeologists also discovered mud-brick buildings, grain silos, ovens and hearths dating from the Second Intermediate Period and continuing into the New Kingdom.

Tombs from the 15th to 17th Dynasties were also found, providing evidence that the area was inhabited during the Hyksos period, when nearby Avaris was their capital. Burial objects included jewelry, amulets, scarabs, bronze tools and weapons, and pottery.

Other discoveries included an early 18th Dynasty mud-brick tomb and Ptolemaic burials, including the remains of a child placed inside two reused amphorae.

Excavations are continuing at the site to uncover further evidence about settlement, daily life and burial practices in the eastern Nile Delta.

World.title: Egypt, Chad expand cooperation in civil aviation
World.content:
The Egyptian-Chadian Business Forum discussed opportunities to boost economic and investment cooperation and broaden partnership between the two countries, alongside specialized talks on civil aviation aimed at developing air connectivity and passenger and cargo transport between Egypt and Chad.

Discussions were held as part of the fourth session of the Egyptian-Chadian Joint Committee, convened in the Chadian capital, N’Djamena, with the participation of a number of ministers, officials, and business community representatives from both sides.

In line with the political leadership’s directives to strengthen Egypt’s relations with African countries and expand areas of cooperation and regional integration, and pursuant to a mandate from Civil Aviation Minister Sameh El-Hefny, Captain Sameh Mohamed Fawzy, head of the Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority (ECAA), and pilot Karim Gamil, adviser to the ECAA chairman and director general of agreements, joined the Egyptian delegation.

They held talks with the Chadian side on ways to develop cooperation in civil aviation and expand passenger and cargo traffic between the two countries.

Discussions included a meeting with Fatime Goukouni Weddeye, Chad’s Minister of Transport, Civil Aviation and National Meteorology, which addressed ways to facilitate operating procedures, overcome challenges facing airlines in both countries, and explore opportunities to increase air traffic between the two sides.

The Egyptian delegation also held talks with the head of the Chadian Civil Aviation Authority and the relevant working team on mechanisms to expand passenger and cargo operations and enhance direct coordination between the two civil aviation authorities to quickly address any operational obstacles.

Talks resulted in an agreement to increase the operational capacity allocated for passenger transport by 100 percent, effectively doubling it, as well as raising air cargo capacity by 125 percent. The measures are aimed at enabling air transport to keep pace with expected growth in travel and trade between the two countries.

The two sides also agreed to maintain technical and operational coordination, exchange expertise and provide technical support in areas of mutual interest in civil aviation, with the aim of enhancing operational efficiency and facilitating the work of airlines.

As part of efforts to support bilateral cooperation, the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on civil aviation, establishing frameworks for cooperation and expertise-sharing while supporting the development of the air transport system and expanding cooperation between institutions and companies operating in the aviation sector in both countries.

These steps underscore the importance of civil aviation as a pillar of regional integration by expanding connectivity networks, facilitating the movement of people and goods, linking markets, and promoting trade and investment. They are also expected to support the shared interests of Egypt and Chad and advance development and integration efforts across Africa.

World.title: After Three Weeks, Three Countries and One Broken Chain of Command, the IB Atlantic IV Is No Longer Liberia’s Alone to Find
World.content:
MONROVIA — For the better part of three weeks, the IB Atlantic IV existed mostly as a rumor with coordinates attached. It was a ship the government said it was watching, a ship whose engine trouble nobody could quite verify, a ship that drifted at 0.3 knots toward a port it wasn’t supposed to be near, flying a flag that asks almost nothing of the vessels that fly it. Liberians read about it in fragments — an anonymous government source here, a rejected letter there, a pursuit off Rivercess that didn’t end so much as move somewhere else.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

That fragment collecting is over. The IB Atlantic IV has been arrested in Ivory Coast, and for the first time since this saga began, the ship everyone was chasing is not the one deciding where it goes next.

It is Ivorian security forces who now decide that. Liberia is left to ask for it back.

A quieter ending than the chase deserved

There is something almost anticlimactic about how it ended. After Armed Forces troops pursued the vessel off Rivercess, after the Coast Guard admitted its boats simply weren’t built for a chase that went this far, after Nigerian partners were brought in to help track a ship Liberia couldn’t catch on its own — the capture came not from a Liberian deck but from a neighboring country’s port authority, acting on a warning Liberia itself had sent to Abidjan and Conakry.

That is not nothing. Liberia’s outreach to Ivory Coast and Guinea worked exactly as regional cooperation is supposed to work. But it also means the country’s own maritime enforcement — the Coast Guard, the National Security Agency, the Armed Forces chief of staff who was, by his own agency’s account, “personally monitoring” the situation for a week — never once had the ship in hand. Now the Liberia Maritime Authority is scrambling to arrange a Sea Shepherd Global escort just to bring the vessel home, the same partnership that has helped Liberian authorities make roughly twenty fishing-vessel arrests since 2017. It is a solution built for a different problem, repurposed now because Liberia has no faster one.

Whether narcotics were aboard the ship remains, as of this writing, unconfirmed. That single unanswered question is the hinge the entire story turns on — and Monrovia will not rest easy until it is answered.

The paper trail that came before the pursuit

To understand why this ship earned three weeks of national anxiety, it helps to go back to July 13, to a letter that, read today, sounds like a rehearsal for everything that followed.

That was the day Mark Egon Kuiah — then a deputy at Roberts International Airport, a man with no formal role in maritime affairs — wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority not as a government official but as “registered agent” for a company called Madris Group of Companies Incorporated. The vessel he was writing about, he said, was in distress at sea, its engine performance compromised by “external obstruction affecting the vessel’s propeller.” It needed a berth. It needed a dive team.

LiMA said no. The agency’s reasoning, delivered plainly to this newspaper, was that the story didn’t add up: the ship hadn’t docked anywhere, was still sitting in Sierra Leonean waters, and yet was already being arranged for a Liberian welcome, as if the paperwork had gotten ahead of the emergency.

Weeks later, Kuiah was swept up in the same dismissal wave that has since widened into Liberia’s broader cocaine purge — a purge that has also ensnared the former commander of the Liberia Immigration Service post at Bo-Waterside and his deputy, both allegedly caught in March carrying suspected narcotics while trying to cross back from Sierra Leone.

The ship in Kuiah’s letter was the IB Atlantic IV.

A ship that told two different stories about itself

What makes the IB Atlantic IV genuinely strange is not that it was suspicious — plenty of vessels off West Africa’s coast are. It’s that the ship told two irreconcilable stories about itself at the same time, and neither matched what its own transponder was broadcasting.

One account, from an anonymous government source, placed it in distress off Sierra Leone, drifting toward Guinea-Bissau. Kuiah’s letter, filed a week earlier, told a third version entirely. And the ship’s Automatic Identification System — the transponder every large vessel must broadcast, showing position, speed, and declared destination — placed it in open West African waters, moving at a crawl, declaring a destination of Lomé, Togo. Not Sierra Leone. Not Guinea-Bissau.

A 41-year-old cargo ship, flagged in Comoros — a registry international shipping analysts describe as asking few questions of anyone — moving at less than a third of a knot is not a ship in transit. It is a ship waiting. And in the days after it first appeared, intelligence sources told FrontPageAfrica that a smaller, unidentified vessel approached it and appeared to attempt passing something aboard. Officials have never said what, or whether the attempt succeeded. But the detail reframes everything that came before it: not a disabled ship asking for mercy, but a ship parked at a fixed position, waiting for a delivery that Liberia’s institutions were too slow, or too divided, to intercept.

The week nobody was in charge

Ask three Liberian security institutions who was responsible for the IB Atlantic IV in its first days in Liberian waters, and — as this newspaper found when it tried — you get three different answers that all point somewhere else. LiMA said it had “information relative to the vessel” and had passed it along to the National Security Agency. The NSA said the Coast Guard was aware. The Coast Guard’s own chief of staff was, according to the NSA, personally monitoring the situation.

Everyone was watching. No one was catching.

That is the sentence this episode leaves behind, and it is the sentence Liberia’s Legislature should sit with before it advances a bill to break the National Port Authority into four separate regional operators. A government that could not coordinate a single response to one suspicious ship, watched by three agencies for the better part of a week, is being asked to prove it can coordinate four ports instead of one. Nothing about the events of the last three weeks makes that case. If anything, the IB Atlantic IV has made the opposite case for free.

What comes next

The ship is now sitting in an Ivorian port, in Ivorian hands, waiting on a Liberian government trying to arrange its own passage home. Whether the coming search finally answers the question that has hung over this entire saga — was there ever anything aboard — will determine whether this story ends as a costly false alarm or the confirmation of exactly what critics of Liberia’s port security have warned about for months.

Either way, the country got lucky this time only in the sense that a neighbor caught what it could not. That is not luck built to last, and it is not oversight built to repeat.

World.title: Mr. President, Be Straight with Liberians – And Let the Chips Fall Where They May
World.content:
President Boakai has given his own Minister of Justice 48 hours to report on his own drug chief. That deadline is the easy part. The harder part — the part that will tell Liberians whether “no sacred cows” was ever more than a good line in a good speech — is what he does with the answer once it lands on his desk.

WE GIVE PRESIDENT BOAKAI CREDIT for the 48-hour order. Asking the Minister of Justice for a detailed report on the allegations against LDEA Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago, on a fixed timeline, with his own name attached to the demand, is more than his government has done for most of the officials swept up in this scandal. It suggests, at minimum, that the president understood how badly this allegation — a truck, a second vehicle, a bar owner already facing prosecution — needed an answer that didn’t come from the accused agency itself. That instinct was right. What happens next will determine whether it meant anything.

HERE IS THE PLAIN truth this newspaper thinks the president already knows: a 48-hour report that Liberians never see or see only in a carefully worded summary designed to close the story rather than settle it, will do more damage to “no sacred cows” than if the deadline had never been set at all. Liberians have watched this pattern before. A dismissal here, a recusal there, a promise of a thorough investigation, and then silence — while the case quietly stops making headlines and the official in question either fades from view or, eventually, fades back in. Mark Kuiah has been out of a job for weeks without a single charge filed. Inspector General Coleman’s own claim that trafficking was “sanctioned at very, very senior level” has never been followed by a name, from him or from anyone above him. If the Biago report follows that same script — findings received, reviewed, and never fully disclosed — the president will have taught the country exactly the opposite lesson from the one he delivered at last week’s commissioning ceremony.



WE ARE NOT ASKING the president to prejudge his own drug chief, and we are not asking him to treat a 48-hour investigation as a trial. Biago is entitled to the same presumption of innocence as anyone else this scandal has touched, and if the allegations against him do not hold up, Liberians deserve to hear that plainly and specifically, not simply assume it from the agency’s continued silence. But due process and public transparency are not in conflict here. The president can honor both by committing, now, before the report is even finished, to release its substantive findings to the Liberian people — not a press statement engineered to sound decisive while saying nothing, but the actual basis for whatever decision he makes. If Biago is cleared, show us why. If he isn’t, say so, and let the same legal process now underway against Moses Jallah and George Harris apply to him without exception. Liberians are not asking their president to fabricate guilt. We are asking him to let the facts speak, out loud, regardless of whose name they land on.



THAT, IN THE END, IS WHAT “let the chips fall where they may” requires of a president, and it is a harder standard than it sounds. It means being willing to let a report embarrass his own appointee if that is what the evidence shows. It means resisting the very instinct to manage a story quietly rather than confront it publicly, especially when the person under scrutiny sits atop an agency the president himself elevated. And it means treating Senator Konneh’s warning — that this could become the president’s own “Containergate,” a scandal that defines a presidency rather than merely interrupting one — not as an attack to be weathered, but as an accurate description of the stakes. Rhetoric got Liberians’ attention at the commissioning ceremony. Only transparency, applied without exception to the government’s own people, will keep it.



FORTY-EIGHT HOURS is a short window. What the president does with what comes out of it will be remembered far longer than the deadline itself. Be straight with the Liberian people, Mr. President. Show us the report. Let the chips fall where they may — even if, especially if, they fall on someone wearing your own government’s badge.

World.title: Liberia: Suspended Prison Superintendent Says He Was “Set Up”; Justice Ministry Says He Was “In the Way
World.content:
Strip away the titles and the procedural language, and what happened at Monrovia Central Prison on the afternoon of August 1 comes down to a very human moment: a career officer, watching two men in prohibited clothing bluff their way past his gate, trying to decide how far to push back against people who outrank him on paper but not, in his telling, in judgment.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

That officer, Jackson K. Kolako, has now told his version of events in a lengthy public statement — one considerably more textured, and considerably more defiant, than the bureaucratic language the Ministry of Justice used to answer him days later. Read side by side, the two accounts agree on almost nothing except the outline: a prison, a drug case, an inmate, and an arrest that neither side disputes actually happened.

A gate, not an interrogation room, is where this starts

The Ministry’s version begins clinically — NSA personnel arriving to interview an inmate “in furtherance of the investigation.” Kolako’s version begins with a detail the Ministry’s statement omits entirely: that the two men who showed up claiming to be NSA agents were, in his account, dressed in shorts — a violation of prison protocol — and refused to sign the visitor logbook or explain themselves beyond saying their mission was covert. It is the kind of granular, sensory detail that rarely survives into an institutional press release, and its absence from the Ministry’s account is itself notable. The Ministry’s statement treats the encounter as a straightforward operational visit; Kolako’s account treats it as the moment he first suspected something was procedurally wrong.

From there the two stories diverge sharply on a second point: who was informed, and when. Kolako says that when he asked whether his superiors — the MCP’s Chief Superintendent and the Assistant Minister for Corrections — had been told about the visit, he was informed they had not, and that the visit’s authority superseded the Corrections Department entirely. He says he then called both men directly and that each expressed surprise at the operation. If accurate, that detail cuts against the Ministry’s framing that Kolako’s objections amounted to interference with a lawful, properly-sanctioned operation — it suggests that even his direct superiors in Corrections had not been looped in.

The moment of arrest, told two ways

The most striking gap between the accounts is the arrest itself. The Ministry describes a sequence in which intelligence “subsequently made available” indicated Kolako had contact with the inmate before the interview, that the inmate initially refused to cooperate, and that only after Kolako’s removal did the inmate allege he’d felt intimidated. It is a bureaucratic passive-voice account: things became known, information was received.

Kolako’s account is far more immediate and personal. He says he had already ordered the inmate — who he says was outside simply for exercise — back to his housing unit and returned to his ordinary duties overseeing roughly 1,800 inmates and around 100 officers, before Siafa Bahn Kemokai arrived with police officers and ordered his arrest without acknowledging Kolako’s salute. Kolako describes this refusal of customary courtesy, and what he calls Kemokai’s public, almost theatrical manner of ordering the arrest, as a deliberate provocation — one he worried was calibrated to trigger resistance from his own officers and potentially a riot that inmates could exploit. His response, he says, was to walk away quietly rather than let his officers witness the arrest.

Whether or not one credits the specific charge of provocation, the underlying image — an experienced officer choosing self-restraint precisely because he understood the security stakes of an 1,800-inmate facility better than the people arresting him — is a more sympathetic and more detailed picture than anything in the Ministry’s statement, which addresses Kolako’s ​twelve years of service only to argue that his seniority did not entitle him to advance knowledge of the operation.

What happened after the arrest is where the accounts stop touching at all

Here the Ministry’s statement goes essentially silent, and Kolako’s fills the gap with the most serious allegations of the whole affair. He says he was held from August 1 to August 7 without the police taking any formal statement from him; that on the night of August 3, Ministry officers, NSA agents, and a police unit compelled him to surrender his phones and passwords; that he was accused that same night of being connected to a drug cartel and receiving payments from it; and that when told to go home the next day, he refused, unwilling to leave custody without assurance of his safety. He says he was eventually released on August 7 still without his phones, was handed a suspension letter the same day citing disruption of the inmate interview, and points out — pointedly — that if such an infraction occurred, the Ministry has its own disciplinary board, raising the question of why the matter was routed through the police at all.

The Ministry’s statement, dated after Kolako’s, never mentions the six days in custody, the confiscated phones, the cartel accusation, or the suspension letter’s specific wording. Its account of “money allegedly being provided to him” through an outside contact reads, against Kolako’s statement, like a paraphrase of the same cartel allegation he says was leveled at him directly on August 3 — except the Ministry frames it as an open investigative question rather than something already put to him as an accusation days earlier.

Two different appeals to legitimacy

The rhetorical strategies are as different as the accounts themselves. The Ministry leans on institutional language — need-to-know principles, chains of authorization, the presumption against guilt before findings are concluded — to argue that what looks irregular from outside was, in fact, procedure. Kolako leans on personal biography: nine years as a teacher, three as a transit conductor, twelve in law enforcement, a salary that never topped $224 a month, and what he describes as an unblemished record he says he has refused to trade for money. He closes not with a request for due process in the abstract, but with a direct, public appeal — naming the Attorney General, the heads of the NSA, the Ministry of National Defense, and the police, and even invoking the U.S. Embassy — asking that drug-case detainees be moved to a secure facility abroad so the investigation cannot be compromised from within. He also names four individuals he asks the public to remember as the investigation proceeds, a move that reads less like a defense and more like a warning.

What the contrast reveals

Neither statement is a neutral document — one is an institution defending a decision it has already made, the other is a man defending a record he says has never been in question. But the specific, checkable claims in Kolako’s account — who he called, what time the suspension letter arrived, how long he was held, when his phones were taken and by whom — give reporters concrete threads to pull that the Ministry’s more abstract statement does not offer. Whether Colonel Roosevelt Varney and Assistant Minister Gabriel Fayiah Ndupellar confirm they were uninformed of the operation, whether police records show a formal statement was ever taken from Kolako during his custody, and what the suspension letter actually says about the alleged disruption are all now matters of record that could be verified rather than argued. Until they are, the public is left with two accounts of the same afternoon that cannot both be complete.

World.title: What Trump’s New Order Means for Liberia — and Why Liberia’s Own Law Looks Nothing Like America’s
World.content:
What Trump’s New Order Means for Liberia — and Why Liberia’s Own Law Looks Nothing Like America’s

Washington is fighting over whether being born on American soil should be enough to make you American. Monrovia settled that question generations ago and settled it the opposite way. The two debates rarely touch — until an executive order like this one lands, and Liberians realize how differently their own country answers the same question.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – The story behind this summer’s executive orders begins with a defeat. Trump’s original January 2025 order sought to end birthright citizenship outright for children born in the U.S. to undocumented or temporary- visa parents — a direct challenge to more than a century of settled interpretation of the 14th Amendment. The Supreme Court rejected it on June 30, 2026, ruling 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that birthright citizenship remains a constitutional guarantee the president cannot unwind by executive action alone.

Rather than drop the fight, the administration narrowed it. The first of the two new orders carves out specific, smaller exclusions from automatic citizenship — children born to employees of foreign governments, such as embassy or consulate staff, and children whose parents are members of designated foreign terrorist organizations or are found to have engaged in fraud to obtain citizenship. The second, the “Ending Birth Tourism” order, is broader in practical reach: it directs the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to deny visas, revoke travel authorization, and impose permanent entry bans on any foreign national a consular or border officer determines is traveling to the U.S. primarily to give birth. Neither order has been finally tested in court, and legal challenges are expected, but as of this writing both remain in effect.



Where Liberia Fits

Liberia does not appear by name in either order, and there is no evidence in U.S. government data or reporting that Liberia is a significant source country for birth tourism — the countries named repeatedly in coverage of the new policy are China, Russia, Nigeria, and parts of Latin America, including Cuba. But the absence of Liberia’s name from that list is not the same as immunity from the policy’s reach. Liberia has never been part of the U.S. Visa Waiver Program, the roughly 40-country list, dominated by Europe and wealthy Asia-Pacific nations, whose citizens can travel to the U.S. without a visa. Liberians applying for a B-1/B-2 visitor visa now do so under a system in which the consular officer reviewing that application has explicit new authority to deny it, or revoke it later, based on a judgment about the traveler’s intent to give birth in the United States. For the ordinary Liberian traveler — a business visitor, a student’s parent, a relative attending a graduation — the practical change is a wider door for discretion at the visa window, not a new restriction that names Liberia specifically.



The Wider African Picture

The birth tourism order is, in scale, a modest addition to a far larger tightening of U.S. immigration policy toward Africa that was already well underway before it was signed. In December 2025, a separate proclamation placed Nigeria under a near-total visa freeze effective January 1, 2026, blocking new tourist, business, and student visas for Nigerian applicants — a country that had been receiving an average of roughly 128,000 U.S. immigrant and nonimmigrant visas a year, among the highest of any African nation. Existing visa and green card holders were left largely unaffected, but the freeze effectively cut off new legal travel from the continent’s most populous country. Nigeria is not alone: of the 39 countries currently under some form of U.S. travel restriction, 26 are African, and 12 of those are in West Africa, Liberia’s own subregion. Liberia itself has not been placed under a Nigeria-style freeze, but the pattern across the region gives the new birth tourism order an added weight for African readers: it arrives as one more layer in a broader American posture that has grown steadily more restrictive toward the continent over the past year, not as an isolated policy confined to its own narrow purpose.

Liberia’s Own Birthright Rule Is Already Stricter Than America’s Old One

Here is where the comparison becomes genuinely striking rather than merely topical: Liberia never had anything resembling the American tradition Trump has spent two years trying to unwind. Under the Liberian Constitution, a person is a citizen at birth only if they are of Negro descent and born to Liberian citizen parents. Liberia has never granted automatic citizenship simply for being born on Liberian soil, regardless of a parent’s status — there is no Liberian equivalent of the unconditional jus soli the U.S. 14th Amendment has guaranteed for a century and a half. A child born in Monrovia to two foreign nationals gains no automatic claim to Liberian citizenship at all, a position considerably more restrictive, on its face, than even Trump’s rejected 2025 order, which targeted only children of undocumented or temporary-visa parents rather than all foreign nationals categorically.

Liberia is not alone in this approach, but the company it keeps is notable. Analyses comparing citizenship regimes worldwide, including research drawing on the Global Citizenship Observatory’s dataset of national citizenship laws, group Liberia with countries like Israel and Haiti as nations that apply race- or ancestry-based criteria rather than granting citizenship automatically based on birthplace alone. A Pew Research Center analysis found that roughly 32 countries worldwide, most of them in the Western Hemisphere, have birthright citizenship laws substantially like the traditional American model, while around 50 others have more limited variations. Liberia’s model — ancestry and racial descent, not geography — sits outside both groups, closer to the narrower, identity-based citizenship regimes found in parts of Europe, the Gulf, and East Asia than to its own regional neighbors in the Americas that share the U.S. approach.

The Dual Citizenship Reversal

For decades, Liberia compounded that restrictiveness with an outright ban on dual citizenship, forcing members of its own diaspora to formally choose between Liberian nationality and whatever citizenship they acquired abroad. That changed in July 2022, when the Legislature passed, and President Weah signed, an amendment to the 1973 Aliens and Nationality Law repealing the dual citizenship ban and, separately, granting Liberian women the same right as men to pass citizenship to their children — a gender inequity that had persisted in Liberian law for decades.

The 2022 reform did not simply throw the doors open, however. Dual citizenship under the amended law is available to people born outside Liberia if a parent was a Liberian citizen at the time of that person’s birth — an extension of the same ancestry-based logic that governs citizenship at birth, not a break from it. Foreign nationals of Black African ancestry may apply for Liberian citizenship after two years of residence; non-African applicants remain ineligible under current law regardless of how long they have lived in the country. And dual citizens face specific limits once naturalized or reclaimed: they are barred from serving as Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Minister of Defense, or Executive Director of the Central Bank of Liberia, an acknowledgment that Liberia’s own lawmakers were not fully comfortable extending dual nationality into the government’s most sensitive financial and security posts.

A Global Outlier, Either Way

Set side by side, the two systems make an uncomfortable kind of sense together. The United States built its citizenship law on the presumption that geography confers belonging — born here, American, full stop — and has spent the past two years fighting in court over how much of that presumption an administration can chip away by decree. Liberia built its citizenship law on the opposite presumption entirely: that belonging flows through ancestry and race, not geography, and that even reversing a strict ban on dual nationality required careful boundaries around who qualifies and what offices they can hold once they do. Liberians reading about Trump’s birth tourism order and the legal fight behind it are not encountering a foreign concept so much as an inverted mirror of their own country’s much older and, in some respects, considerably stricter rules. Whether that makes the American debate easier or harder to relate to may depend less on the policy details than on which side of the ancestry-versus-geography divide feels more familiar to begin with.

World.title: Liberia: Debt Court Begins Contempt Process Against Finance Minister, LEC MD Over US$415K ELTEL Judgment
World.content:
Contempt proceedings have been initiated at the Debt Court of Montserrado County against the management of the Liberia Electricity Corporation and the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning over alleged non-compliance with a final judgment of US$415,327.08 in favor of ELTEL Network Liberia.

By Victoria G Wesseh

The proceedings were triggered by a Bill of Information filed by ELTEL, asking the court to compel enforcement of its February 4, 2026 payment order.

According to court records, on July 7, 2026, the Debt Court issued show-cause summonses ordering LEC Managing Director Mohammed M. Sheriff and other senior LEC executives to appear before the court to explain why the judgment remains unsatisfied.

In its latest filing, argued last week, ELTEL is also asking the court to extend the show-cause action to include Finance and Development Planning Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, on grounds that the Ministry is the fiscal agent for payment of judgments against state-owned enterprises.

The court has not yet made any finding of contempt against Minister Ngafuan or MD Sheriff. A show-cause summons is not a conviction – it is an order to appear and explain.

Why ELTEL Filed For Contempt

According to ELTEL’s petition, LEC acknowledged liability for the debt on February 3, 2026, and on February 4, 2026, the court entered judgment for US$415,327.08. The court said the sum comprises an arbitral award of US$364,322.00 plus statutory interest, attorney’s fees and court costs.

ELTEL alleges the amount has not been paid more than five months later.

Counsel for ELTEL further alleged in court that the matter was referred to the Executive Mansion and that on July 3, 2026, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. directed the Ministry of Finance to intervene to satisfy the judgment. That alleged directive has not been independently verified by this paper, and no public response from the Ministry on that specific allegation is on the court record as of press time.

On that basis, ELTEL is praying the court to find willful disobedience and to impose contempt sanctions.

Sanctions under Liberian law for civil contempt may include a fine, an order for coercive imprisonment until the contempt is purged by payment, or other enforcement orders. Such sanctions are discretionary and are imposed only after due process.

The Debt Court is expected to decide whether to grant a final enforcement ultimatum – such as a 72-hour order for the US$415,327.08 to be transferred to the court’s escrow account, or set a full contempt hearing date where Minister Ngafuan and MD Sheriff would be required to appear personally or through counsel to show cause.

Both officials remain entitled to the presumption of compliance until the court rules otherwise, and to present their defense.

The case file shows the underlying dispute stems from a 2016 contract for low-voltage materials that ELTEL alleges it supplied to LEC. The original suit was filed in June 2024 through Attorney-in-Fact Hans Armstrong.

World.title: In Loving Memory of Hon. Sylvester Mondubue “Greg” Grigsby October 15, 1950 – August 9, 2025
World.content:
One year later, from his wife and daughters One year ago today, we said goodbye to our husband and father, Sylvester Mondubue “Greg” Grigsby. The world knew him as a statesman – a diplomat, a Minister of State, a proud son of Sinoe County who gave more than forty years of his life to the service of Liberia. We knew him as the man who came home.

The one who carried cash in his pocket just so he could tip an Uber driver. The one who loved game shows and corrected the history in our television shows. The one whose laugh you could hear from the next room and never mistake for anyone else’s. For fifty-one years, he was a husband. For all of our lives, he was our father. He crossed oceans and boarded late trains for us. He washed dishes, organized closets, and cooked corned beef and rice when one of us was unwell. He played monopoly with his grandchildren. He believed in showing up to show his love, and he showed up.

World.title: Liberian Mining Superintendents at ArcelorMittal Complete Advanced Drill & Blast Training in Brazil
World.content:
ArcelorMittal Liberia (AML) has reaffirmed its long-term commitment to developing Liberian professionals into world-class mining leaders following the successful completion of an advanced international Drill & Blast training program by five of its senior Liberian mining superintendents in Brazil.

According to a release, the specialized technical program was held at ArcelorMittal’s Serra Azul Mine in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, where mining professionals from various ArcelorMittal operations around the world gathered to exchange knowledge and strengthen expertise in modern mining techniques, operational excellence, environmental stewardship, and safety management.

The training exposed participants to internationally recognized best practices in drill and blast engineering, including blast design optimization, fragmentation control, ground vibration monitoring, powder factor management, explosives performance, environmental impact mitigation, and community safety. Participants also received practical, field-based instruction on improving productivity while ensuring responsible and sustainable mining practices.

The Liberian delegation consisted of five experienced operational leaders from AML’s Mines Department including Hamilton S.S. Kamara – Superintendent, ROM & Stockpile Management, Solo B. Gbayor – Superintendent, Mines, Ferrison Saye Andrews – Superintendent, Production, Theresa Mamie Nuah Koah – Superintendent, Pit and Toney Bazee Kamara – Superintendent, Drill & Blast.

Their participation reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader strategy of continuously investing in Liberian professionals by providing access to international technical training, leadership development, and global knowledge-sharing opportunities.

Building World-Class Liberian Mining Leaders

For more than a decade, ArcelorMittal Liberia has consistently prioritized the training and professional development of Liberian employees as part of its commitment to local capacity building. Through scholarships, vocational education, graduate development programs, international exchanges, technical certifications, leadership courses, and specialized overseas training, the company continues to prepare Liberians to occupy increasingly strategic positions across its operations.

The Brazil program represents another milestone in AML’s long-term vision of creating a highly skilled Liberian workforce capable of managing complex mining operations that meet international standards.

Rather than relying indefinitely on expatriate expertise, the company continues to build a pipeline of competent Liberian engineers, geologists, mine planners, production supervisors, and operational managers who can lead modern mining activities safely, efficiently, and responsibly.

This investment is particularly significant as Liberia’s mining industry continues to expand and demands a new generation of technically competent local professionals capable of leading large-scale industrial operations.

Preparing Liberia for the Future of Mining

Speaking following the completion of the program, AML General Manager Selmah Jallah emphasized that exposure to global mining operations is essential for developing the next generation of Liberian mining professionals.

“Liberia’s growing position as a key mining destination requires highly skilled professionals who can operate responsibly while protecting the environment,” Selmah said.

“International development opportunities are essential in preparing Liberian employees for future leadership roles as our mining sector increasingly relies on local talent and expertise.”

She noted that world-class mining is no longer defined solely by production volumes but also by operational safety, environmental responsibility, technological innovation, and strong leadership.

According to Selmah, every international training opportunity strengthens Liberia’s own mining capacity by allowing Liberian professionals to bring home globally tested knowledge and practical experience that can be applied across AML’s operations.

She further commended the five superintendents for their professionalism, discipline, and commitment throughout the program while encouraging all employees to continue demonstrating accountability, integrity, and compliance with company policies.

“Leadership is earned through consistent performance, professionalism, and continuous learning,” she added.

A Culture of Continuous Learning

The training also highlights AML’s philosophy that learning does not end with technical competence but continues throughout an employee’s career.

Production Superintendent Ferrison Saye Andrews described the Brazil program as another important milestone in his professional journey.

Andrews previously benefited from the AML Mineral Development Agreement (MDA) Scholarship Program in 2022, which enabled him to obtain a master’s degree before returning to Liberia to continue contributing to the company’s mining operations.

He said the opportunity to learn alongside mining professionals from different countries broadened his understanding of modern mining techniques and reinforced the importance of continuous professional development.

Similarly, Mines Superintendent Solo B. Gbayor described representing Liberia among mining experts from across the global ArcelorMittal Group as both an honor and an invaluable learning experience.

He noted that interacting with international specialists exposed the Liberian delegation to innovative operational approaches that will help improve safety, efficiency, and productivity within AML’s mines.

The other members of the delegation echoed similar sentiments, expressing appreciation to the company’s management for investing in their careers and providing opportunities to gain practical knowledge from one of the world’s leading mining organizations.

Investing in Liberian Talent

The Brazil exchange forms part of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader human capital development agenda, which continues to prioritize Liberians for technical and leadership advancement.

Over the years, the company has sponsored numerous employees for master’s degree programs, specialized mining certifications, engineering training, equipment operation courses, vocational education, leadership development initiatives, and international technical exchanges across multiple countries.

These investments have steadily increased the number of Liberians occupying senior operational and management positions within the company.

By transferring global technical expertise to local professionals, AML is helping develop a workforce capable of managing increasingly sophisticated mining operations while supporting Liberia’s long-term economic development.

As the company continues implementing major expansion projects, the demand for highly skilled Liberian professionals will continue to grow. Programs such as the Brazil Drill & Blast training demonstrate AML’s determination to ensure that Liberians are not merely participants in the country’s mining industry but are equipped to become internationally competitive professionals and world-class mining leaders.

The successful completion of the advanced Drill & Blast program therefore represents more than an individual achievement for the five superintendents. It reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s enduring commitment to empowering Liberian talent, strengthening national capacity, and creating a future where Liberians lead every aspect of modern mining—from the pit to the boardroom.

World.title: VEEP Commissions K6.8 million Power Project
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has commissioned the 13 kilometres Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project which has been constructed by the Rural Electrification Authority (REA) at over K6.8 million in Mukupa-Katandula chiefdom of Kaputa District of Northern Province.

Ms Nalumango stated that the rural electrification is one of the key pillars in the national development agenda hence government is constructing electricity infrastructures in rural areas to give citizen access to electricity.

She stated that the rural electrification program has seen local business grow with confidence that comes with reliable electricity.

Ms Nalumango urged people of Mukupa-Katandula chiefdom to take full use of the opportunities that government has taken to them and ensure their homes are connected.

She said with the coming of electricity in the area, government expected to see better service delivery to the people from public institution which will create great economic activities.

The Vice President said the Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project has answered the electricity need that has existed for many years.

She also appealed to the community to take care of the infrastructure which government through the REA has constructed at a huge cost so that it can save its purpose effectively.

And Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Beauty Undi-Phiri who was represented by Northern Province Assistance Secretary Jordan Mwenya thanked government for constructing and commissioning the project which she said demonstrates governments commitment to ensuring that no part of the country is left behind.

Ms Undi-Phiri added that the electricity which has been connected in Mukupa-Katandula is not merely a utility but as a powerful enabler of opportunities.

She said that the project marks the fulfillment of long held aspiration to have access to reliable electricity as an essential service that will improve livelihood and unlock new opportunities for social and economic development.

Ms Undi-Phiri stated that the commissioning of the Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project by the Vice President is a great encouragement to the people of Kaputa district as it reflected governments resolve to bring development closer to the people and ensure equitable access to essential services across the country.

REA Board Chairperson Charles Mboma noted that communities evolve faster when they are connected to electricity.

Mr Mboma said REA with the support of the government will continue to construct and connect rural communities to electricity to ensure development is delivered.

He indicated that the Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project has been constructed at a cost of over 6.8 million Kwacha adding that over 100 thousand beneficiaries will be connected to power.

Mr Mboma added that the 13 kilometres electricity distribution line which has been constructed and commissioned has connected over 15 public infrastructures in Mukupa-Katandula chiefdom.

He said the project will enhance the businesses and improve local economy in the area.

Meanwhile, Chief Mukupa Katandula of theTabwa people of Kaputa District described the commissioning of the project as a clear demonstration of governments commitment to taking development to all areas including the remotest part of the nation.

The traditional leader said the completion and commissioning of the Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project government through REA was key to transforming the livelihood of the people of Kaputa.

The traditional leader said the Mukupa-Katandula Grid Extension Project is significant to the people of Mukupa-Katandula.

He said the commissioning of the project was a huge milestone as it represented a concrete step towards national energy vision.

World.title: President Hichilema pledges more development for Milenge.
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured the people of Milenge District that Government will continue delivering development to the area if re-elected for a second term.

Speaking during a community engagement meeting in Milenge, President Hichilema said Government will prioritise the improvement of road infrastructure in the district, including the Kasanka-Milenge Road, Mwang’uni-Milambo Road and feeder roads connecting communities from Chief Sokontwe’s Palace.

“We will continue working on the roads in Milenge. We will look at the Kasanka-Milenge Road, the Mansa-Milambo Road and the feeder roads from Chief Sokontwe’s Palace so that our people can move easily and participate in economic activities,” President Hichilema said.

He said improved road infrastructure will enhance connectivity, facilitate the movement of people and goods and open up more opportunities for communities in the district.

The President also pledged to work on the Kapalala Pontoon, saying the intervention would provide a shorter route between Milenge and Ndola.

“We will work on the Kapalala Pontoon because we want to shorten the distance between Milenge and Ndola. Our people should not continue travelling long distances when there is an opportunity to create a shorter and more efficient route,” he said.

The president further said Government will also prioritise the improvement of water schemes in the district to ensure that communities have access to reliable water supplies.

“We do not want to see our women walking long distances looking for water. We will work on the water schemes because water is a basic need and our people must have access to it closer to their homes,” President Hichilema said.

Meanwhile, President Hichilema has pledged to improve the Kampala rural Health centre and ensure that it has water and a maternity annex.

He said improving health infrastructure will strengthen access to quality healthcare services and ensure that women in the area receive maternal healthcare closer to their communities.

“We will work on the Kampala Health Facility and make sure that there is a maternity annex because our mothers should not travel long distances to access maternity services,” he said.

President Hichilema further announced that all volunteer teachers and nurses in Milenge have been employed, recognising their contribution to the provision of essential services in the district.

“We have heard you on the issue of volunteer teachers and nurses. These people have been serving our communities, and Government will ensure that they are given an opportunity to be employed,” President Hichilema said.

President Hichilema said although Government had already delivered a number of development projects in Milenge, more interventions would continue to be implemented across the district.

He said the Government remains committed to ensuring that development reaches all parts of the country, including rural communities.

World.title: Feira Constituency Receives Ballot Papers
World.content:
Feira Constituency in Luangwa District has received ballot papers ahead of the General Election taking place on Thursday, 13thAugust, 2026.

Acting District Electoral Officer Paul Siyanga confirmed receiving one pallet of ballot papers at 21:53 hours yesterday, whose delivery was witnessed by stakeholders before the materials were secured in the strong room upon arrival.

Mr Siyanga, who is standing in for District Electoral Officer Greyson Sakala, explained that the ballot papers were received intact without any breakage on the seals and locks.

“I can assure the public that all stakeholders witnessed the arrival of the ballot papers and that they have been secured amidst tight state security of the Zambia Police until 13th August, 2026,” he explained.

Mr Siyanga thanked the stakeholders for a peaceful process of receiving the ballot papers and urged them to maintain this peace and order exhibited before, during and after the elections.

Socialist Party District Campaign Manager Canaan Mukanka appreciated the professionalism exhibited by the Electoral Commission of Zambia during the exercise.

Mr Mukonka explained that the tight security by the Zambia Police played a key role in ensuring that the ballot papers are not tampered with during transportation from Lusaka to Luangwa.

And National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) District Chairperson Obert Tembo expressed satisfaction with the way the Electoral Commission of Zambia handled the stakeholders at the civic centre.

Mr Tembo explained that the stakeholders were given ample time to inspect anything they felt needed to be checked for transparency purposes.

“We just had a concern as stakeholders on the safety of the strong room provided for the safe keeping of the ballot papers but we have been assured that tight security will be provided,” he expressed.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) District Youth Chairperson Kelly Kasongole said his party has confidence in the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

“We are not worried about the safety of the ballot papers because we believe in a transparent and professional process where no one can tamper with the election materials,” Mr Kasongole explained.

World.title: Luangwa Political Players Commended for Peaceful Campaigns
World.content:
Luangwa District Commissioner Luke Chikani has commended political players for maintaining peace and order during the campaign period in the district.

Mr Chikani says no violence has been recorded since the commencement of the campaigns, citing unity and love being promoted by government.

Speaking when a team of Election Observers who are in the country from the European Union paid a courtesy call on him, Mr Chikani emphasised that Zambia is a peaceful nation that does not promote violence.

“I must confess that the country has never had peaceful campaigns such as these since Zambia gained its Independence from the colonial masters and we are happy as a country and of course as a district that each political player has a fair playing ground,” he explained.

Mr Chikani further explained that the institution mandated to handle the elections at district level was doing everything possible to ensure that the process was transparent and professional from the voter education component to the actual voting day.

He said political players in the district have strictly adhered to the laid down guidelines by the Electoral Commission of Zambia leading to a safe political environment in the district.

The DC called on the public and all political players to maintain the love, peace and unity that has been exercised from the beginning of the electoral exercise.

European Union Long Term Observer, Milan Kuksa explained that the role of the European Union was to follow the electoral process in the field until the Election Day on 13th August, 2026.

Mr Kuksa said the observers meet key stakeholders and report regularly to the core team.

“My colleagues Claudia Kamariza and Suzen Mwape are part of the team that is monitoring and observing the electoral process in Chongwe, Rufunsa and Luangwa Districts and therefore, you will be seeing us quiet often,” he explained.

World.title: ZYAFAC Urges Monitors to Remain Neutral
World.content:
The Zambia Youths Association in the Fight Against Corruption (ZYAFAC) has urged its election monitors to remain neutral, professional and non-partisan during the August 13 General Elections.

ZYAFAC Board Chairperson Rickson Kanema says the monitors have a responsibility to observe and document the electoral process without supporting any political party or candidate.

Mr Kanema noted that the 250 monitors accredited by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) should act as the eyes of communities at polling stations and promote the integrity of the electoral process.

He was speaking in Lusaka during a ZYAFAC Election Monitoring Training Workshop at Ndeke Hotel.

He added that the organisation expects the monitors to contribute to peaceful, free, fair and credible elections through responsible and non-partisan monitoring.

“You are not here to campaign, you are here to observe, document and promote integrity.” he said

Mr Kanema also said ZYAFAC has also engaged the Electoral Commission of Zambia, Anti-Corruption Commission, Drug Enforcement Commission and the media as resource persons.

He emphasized that ZYAFAC expects the training to strengthen its monitoring and reporting system and enhance public confidence in the electoral process through credible and non-partisan youth-led election monitoring.

Mr Kanema further reminded the monitors that their participation in the elections should be guided by national interest and the desire to contribute to a peaceful and credible electoral process.

World.title: HH, UPND favoured for first-round win, new analysis shows
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema is favoured to retain the presidency in Thursday’s general election, with the United Party for National Development handed a 70 to 80 percent chance of securing an outright first-round victory, a new pre-election analysis has found.

The briefing, titled Zambia’s 13 August General Election: Assessing the Route to the Presidency, puts the likelihood of a run-off at 15 to 25 percent. It is authored by Southern Africa Coalition for Democracy and Accountability executive director Blessing Vava and Masosote Institute for Political Economy director Tamuka Chirimambowa, and was published by the Public Affairs Research Institute in Africa on 8 August.

The analysis finds that Hichilema is favoured to cross the mandatory 50 percent threshold required to avoid a second round. It cautions, however, that the reasoning behind the projected outcome is not as simple as incumbent popularity.

“A first-round UPND victory is the most likely single outcome,” the briefing states.

Ballot access emerges as the clearest structural advantage identified in the report. UPND has fielded candidates in all 226 National Assembly constituencies, compared with 156 for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity. The ruling party is also contesting 115 of the 116 mayoral and council chairperson positions nationwide.

“Ballot access is the clearest measurable difference between the two campaigns. The UPND contested effectively every seat available. The NRPUP did not,” the report states. “The gap is not a matter of interpretation, it is recorded in the nomination returns, and it compounds downward, widest at ward level, where the machinery of election day actually sits.”

That gap widens further down the ballot. UPND has fielded candidates in wards countrywide, while NRPUP is contesting fewer than two-thirds of Zambia’s 1,858 wards.

The disparity matters beyond vote counting, the authors argue, because ward-level candidates are central to placing polling agents and monitoring the counting and aggregation of results on election day itself.

“The NRPUP’s decisive weakness is organisational rather than rhetorical,” the report says.

Opposition fragmentation stands out as the single biggest factor working in the incumbent’s favour, according to the analysis. Fourteen presidential candidates appear on Thursday’s ballot, splitting the anti-incumbent vote across a crowded field rather than consolidating it behind a single challenger.

Even so, the authors caution against reading the projected UPND victory as a sign of overwhelming popularity. The report points to an underlying anti-incumbent sentiment that persists among a segment of voters, suggesting the ruling party’s advantage rests more on organisational depth and opposition division than on broad public enthusiasm.

Zambians go to the polls this Thursday to elect a president, members of parliament and local government representatives.

World.title: ECZ Praises Siavonga Parties for Peaceful Campaigns
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commended political parties and their supporters in Siavonga District for conducting peaceful campaigns ahead of the August 13 General Elections.

Siavonga District Electoral Officer Kennedy Shombo, speaking at Lake View Lodge when he opened a Poll Day briefing meeting for political parties, Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), church representatives and members of the media, said the district has so far recorded no cases of political violence since the commencement of the election campaigns.

Mr Shombo urged political parties and their supporters to continue adhering to the Electoral Code of Conduct and maintain peace before, during and after polling day and called on the media to verify information before publication and help promote peace and prevent the spread of misinformation.

Mr Shombo also reminded voters that political regalia will not be allowed at polling stations on polling day.

Meanwhile, Siavonga District Returning Officer Steven Mbita reaffirmed the ECZ’s commitment to delivering a credible election.

In a presentation, Assistant Returning Officer Mutinta Mutoloki highlighted key electoral processes and procedures, including the deployment of poll staff, timelines, conflict resolution mechanisms, verification of ballot papers and account forms, as well as results management.

Mr Mutoloki said the Commission was fully prepared and that all necessary arrangements were being put in place ahead of polling day.

The briefing was aimed at equipping stakeholders with information on Poll Day activities, operational arrangements, electoral procedures and their respective roles in ensuring a smooth, peaceful, transparent and credible electoral process.

World.title: Government launches wetlands Input distribution in Mpika
World.content:
Government has commenced the distribution of fertiliser and seed packs under the Wetlands Cropping Programme, being implemented through the Food Security Pack Programme in Mpika District of Muchinga Province.

Mpika District Commissioner David Siame says the distribution exercise has started in Chailo Zone, where 200 beneficiaries have so far received farming inputs.

Mr Siame said the exercise is expected to be completed by Wednesday next week.

He said more than 1,000 vulnerable but viable households in Mpika District are earmarked to receive fertiliser and vegetable seed packs under the Wetlands Cropping Programme.

Mr Siame described the programme as an encouraging initiative aimed at improving household food security in the district.

He said Government remains committed to supporting vulnerable but viable households in Mpika District.

He explained that programmes of this nature are intended to cushion families against food insecurity while promoting sustainable agricultural practices in wetland areas.

And Mpika District Community Development Officer-in-Charge, Precious Lungu, said the inputs will be distributed to beneficiaries in 10 selected Community Welfare Assistance Committees (CWACs) in the district.

Ms Lungu said her department will closely monitor the distribution and implementation of the programme to ensure that the inputs are used for the intended purpose.

She said the involvement of CWACs at community level was intended to enhance transparency and accountability in the selection and verification of beneficiaries.

“Beneficiaries must make good use of the inputs to boost household food production and reduce dependence on relief support,” she said.

Ms Lungu further emphasized that the Wetlands Cropping Programme forms part of broader Government efforts to strengthen food security among vulnerable households in Mpika District and Muchinga Province at large.

Meanwhile, one of the beneficiaries from Chibansa area, Matilda Kalounde, thanked Government for providing the farming inputs, saying the support has come at an opportune time.

Ms Kalounde said the inputs will go a long way in improving the livelihoods of vulnerable but viable households.

“This will go a long way in improving the livelihoods of many vulnerable but viable households,” she said.
