World.title: Moody’s affirms Romania’s sovereign rating, sees risks of slower fiscal consolidation
World.content:
International rating agency Moody’s on August 7 affirmed Romania’s fragile Baa3 sovereign rating, along with its negative outlook, linked to high implementation risks related to the country’s ambitious multi-year fiscal consolidation programme. Compared to a year ago, the fiscal deficit narrowed faster than expected, but there is less clarity on further steps towards a sustainable deficit, the rating agency concluded.

Just like Fitch a week before, Moody’s signalled that the political consensus on fiscal consolidation beyond 2026 emerged as the key driver for further rating actions, despite the fiscal consolidation having outperformed expectations so far.

While Romania managed to reduce the deficit somewhat more quickly than Moody’s expected in its September 2025 country update, the rating agency assesses political conditions as more challenging following the passage of the no-confidence vote against the government in May.

The rating agency remarks that political fragmentation has delayed the formation of a new government, but expressed expectations that a new administration will take office after the summer break.

Moody’s says that passage of a deficit-reducing 2027 budget before the end of 2026 and of an adequate public wage law would signal political consensus in favour of implementing and maintaining a large fiscal effort beyond 2026. The outlook could return to stable if it is clear that such a political consensus still exists in favour of implementing and maintaining a large fiscal effort beyond 2026.

Conversely, “a political and policymaking environment that is unlikely to be conducive to sustaining a large fiscal effort over a number of years” would exert negative pressure (prompting a downgrade to non-investment region).

Separately, the rating agency notes risks stemming from geopolitical risk emanating from the war in Ukraine or any other developments that could jeopardise the funding of the country’s wide current account deficit, with a negative impact on its rating.

Technically, Moody’s expects Romania's 2026 headline deficit to decline significantly to 5.8% of GDP this year, down over two percentage points in one year, thanks to expenditure restraint and revenues holding up in spite of challenging macroeconomic conditions.

Despite the slightly faster-than-expected deficit reduction, the rating agency expects Romania's interest burden will still increase in the coming years given high financing needs and the prevalence of market-based funding. Interest costs will increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2028 from 2.8% of GDP in 2025, up from 2.0% of GDP in 2023.

As a result of still elevated primary deficits and rising interest costs, Moody’s expects the debt burden to continue to increase, albeit at a slower pace than it anticipated at the time of its last rating committee in September 2025. Just like Fitch, Moody’s projects debt will increase to 64.5% of GDP in 2028 (above the projected peer median of 57.9%) from 59.3% in 2025. The rating agency’s current baseline assumes a gradual further reduction in deficits that stabilises the debt burden at around 66% of GDP by the end of this decade.

World.title: Sculptures destroyed in 1944 reinstalled on University of Bucharest pediment
World.content:
Video

The University of Bucharest (UB) reinstalled the eagle and two griffins on the pediment of the UB Palace, located in downtown Bucharest, on Saturday, August 8.

This is the first step in the full restoration of the original pediment of the palace, a project that will continue over the next two years, culminating in the complete reconstruction of the sculptural ensemble designed by architect Alexandru Orăscu and created by sculptor Karl Storck between 1862 and 1869, UB said.

The original pediment of the University of Bucharest Palace, designed in the Neoclassical style, was known as “Minerva Protecting the Arts and Sciences.” The artistic composition was conceived by Theodor Aman, while the bas-relief, carved in Rusciuc stone by Karl Storck and his collaborators, depicted the goddess Minerva crowning the sciences and arts, surrounded by allegorical representations of academic disciplines and the fine arts. Above the pediment stood an ensemble consisting of a crowned eagle and two griffins, symbolizing the state's protection of knowledge and the university institution. The ensemble was almost entirely destroyed in the 1944 bombings. During the post-war reconstruction, the facade of the central section was simplified, and the sculptural elements that had defined the appearance of the University Palace for almost a century disappeared, UB explained.

The ensemble installed over the weekend is made of bronze and consists of an eagle weighing approximately one tonne and two griffins weighing around 300 kilograms each, bringing the total weight of the ensemble to 1.6 tonnes.

The work, with a total value of approximately RON 2 million, was created by sculptor Alexandru Siminic together with his collaborators, Teodor and Ștefan Siminic. It was produced using the lost-wax bronze casting technique, followed by chasing and patination, and is based on the original work by sculptor Karl Storck.

The investment is funded through the National Public and Social Interest Construction Program, administered by the National Investment Company (CNI) under the authority of the Ministry of Development, Public Works and Administration. The project aims to structurally strengthen the entire complex, restore the facades and historic elements, create a museum space dedicated to archaeological remains discovered in the inner courtyard, and incorporate modern architectural lighting solutions, ensuring that the historic heritage is preserved and made accessible to future generations. The strengthening, restoration and modernization works are being carried out by the consortium comprising Construcții Erbașu (leader), Terragaz Construct, Euras and Polarh Design.

World.title: Romanian shipyard delivers hull of largest cable-laying ship in Japan
World.content:
The VARD shipyard in Tulcea, eastern Romania, has completed the construction of the hull of “Discovery,” the largest vessel intended for the installation of submarine cables and the first such project delivered by the VARD group for the Japanese market.

The ship, valued at over USD 200 million, will have an important role in the development of infrastructure for offshore wind energy and the transport of electric energy through submarine cables.

The construction of the vessel’s hull was carried out in Romania, at the VARD shipyards in Tulcea and Brăila, and after launching, it was towed to the VARD Langsten shipyard in Norway, where the specialized equipment was installed, and the final tests were carried out before delivery. The vessel was officially handed over to the Japanese company Toyo Construction at the end of June and is currently heading to Japan, where it will be based in the port of Ishikari Bay.

“Discovery” was designed to meet the specific conditions in Japan, where the water depth increases rapidly near the coast. The vessel can operate both in shallow waters and offshore, where future floating wind farms will be installed.

The vessel is approximately 151 meters long, 28 meters wide, and can transport up to 9,000 tons of submarine cables, distributed in two carousels with capacities of 4,000 and 5,000 tons.

On board, the ship has a main crane with a lifting capacity of 400 tons and an auxiliary crane of 100 tons. The vessel is also equipped with a dynamic positioning system, a heliport and equipment for the operation of remotely operated underwater vehicles.

In addition to the installation of submarine cables, “Discovery” can also be used for offshore construction works, including the installation of foundations for wind turbines and anchoring operations for floating turbines.

The vessel is equipped with a hybrid propulsion system, in which diesel engines are used to produce electric energy, while propulsion is provided by electric motors. The system includes batteries and the possibility of shore power supply during stationing, in order to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. Up to 90 crew members and technicians can work on board.

The Japanese government has set the rapid expansion of offshore wind energy capacities as an objective in the coming period, and this vessel will be used for the installation of the submarine electric cables necessary to connect the new farms to the energy grid.

For VARD, the project marks the first delivery to the Japanese market in the segment of specialized vessels for the offshore wind industry. In recent years, the VARD Tulcea shipyard has specialized in the construction of the hulls of some of the most complex vessels intended for the offshore industry, including vessels for the installation of submarine cables and for the development of offshore wind energy projects.

Several of the most advanced vessels of this type currently used worldwide were built in Romania and subsequently equipped at the VARD group’s shipyards in Norway.

World.title: Romania’s eMAG to come under sole control of Naspers after EU approval
World.content:
The European Commission has approved, under the EU Merger Regulation, the acquisition of sole control over Dante International of Romania by South African investment fund Naspers Limited.

"The Commission concluded that the notified operation does not raise competition concerns, as the companies are not active on the same markets or on markets that are in a vertical relationship, and the impact on the market structure is limited. The transaction was examined under the simplified merger control procedure," the EC stated in a press release.

Last month, businessman Iulian Stanciu announced the sale of his stake in the eMAG Group to global consumer internet and technology investment group Prosus, 17 years after taking over the company and 14 years after signing the partnership with Naspers, the owner of Prosus.

After the sale, eMAG will continue its development and extensive investment plans, with RON 1.2 billion budgeted in this fiscal year alone for technology, logistics and financial services, with the support of Prosus and an experienced management team, company representatives stated. They also noted the regional growth potential of e-commerce, which remains significant, with growth rates of up to three times in the coming years, compared to the current penetration rate of 11-12% of total retail.

"The investments will be directed predominantly toward logistics and delivery infrastructure, AI and financial services, consolidating the foundation for a strong digital economy in the region. I want to thank Iulian for his dedication, vision, and for keeping us focused on the customer and on continuous personal development," said at that time Tudor Manea, CEO of eMAG Group, cited by News.ro.

At group level, eMAG recorded in fiscal year 2025 a turnover of RON 11.4 billion (USD 2.64 billion), up 11% compared with the previous financial year. The eMAG Group portfolio includes the eMAG brand, the Fashion Days online store, Romania’s 100% online hypermarket Freshful, the IT and electronics specialist store PC Garage, the Romanian national and international express courier company Sameday, the Depanero repair workshop, the most relevant recommerce platform in South-Eastern Europe Flip, as well as the financial services company HeyBlu.

World.title: In Solving World War II ‘Puzzle’, Young Greeks Help ‘Heal a Wound’
World.content:
After wading through the archives at Arolsen, municipal registers, the Internet and other documents, the tram was able to return a wristwatch to the family of Vangelis Kerasiotis, who spent time in a forced labour camp in Germany in 1944, aged 19.

Having worked at the camp as an interpreter, Kerasiotis returned to Greece in 1945, where he moved in with a Jewish woman and joined the police. He died at the age of 25.

“The objects are of zero value in terms of their literal value, but they are of enormous value in terms of mental upliftment,” said his niece, Chrysanthi Kerasotou, who received the watch with her sister and mother during an event organised by the Greek government in late June.

Hotzidis, a historian, said that between 50,000 and 60,000 Greek Jews perished in the Nazi camps and at least 10,000 other Greeks were sent to labour camps, including leftists involved in the resistance against the Nazi occupation of Greece.

“We do not know if Kerasiotis was engaged in any political activity,” Hotzidis said. “The relatives did not mention anything, but even if wasn’t, his name was certainly heard somewhere by Greek collaborators of the German battalion security forces and some gendarmes who collaborated with the Germans.”

“It is important to remember, because this way we know not only our recent history, but we can think that it is good that all these events do not happen again,” he said. “So, first we must know them and secondly remember them, ensuring they are never forgotten.”

In Arolsen, Meiwes said that some 2,000 envelopes remain. For some, they known neither the nationality nor the identity of the person whose belonging are inside.

“It is possible that some of these still belong to Greek nationals,” she told BIRN.

The Nazis turned people into numbers, Meiwes said, so it is important “to give them back their names and to tell their stories”.

World.title: A Decade After North Macedonia’s Deadliest Floods, Dangers Remain
World.content:
On August 6, 2016 torrential rain triggered a devastating flash flood in the north-east outskirts of Skopje, killing 22 people and causing more than 30 million euros in damage.

Suburbs of the capital like Singelic and Cento, villages like Stajkovci and Aracinovo, and surrounding areas were among the worst hit, as torrents of water and mud swept through streets and homes within minutes.

“We narrowly escaped death. The water was almost two metres deep. I have never seen this kind of weather,” one Stajkovci resident said at the time. “It was terrible. We had only half a minute to get outside [the house] and save ourselves when the water surged,” said another.

In the aftermath, experts pointed to several factors that had turned an extreme weather event into a disaster. Around 93 litres of rain per square metre fell on the heavily deforested southern slopes of Skopska Crna Gora Mountain in just four hours, allowing water and mud to rush towards the settlements below.

World.title: Albania Could Face Costly Arbitration Battle After Scrapping Vlora Airport Plans
World.content:
An international arbitration dispute is looming after Albania’s Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy announced last week that it has officially started the procedure to terminate the concession contract for Vlora International Airport.

The decision follows a bitter legal tussle between the two consortium partners, Mabco Construction and 2A Group, which began in the autumn of 2025 over a dispute concerning the division of shares between them.

There have also been large confrontations between workers from the two companies over access to the site, and a series of court rulings. The deadlock persisted even after the Supreme Court in May rejected 2A Group's requests for interim measures to secure its lawsuit. That decision was later followed by additional blocking rulings issued by the Court of First Instance Tirana.

World.title: Albanian Court Puts Turkish Activist in Custody After Extradition Demand
World.content:
Protesters rally with pictures of victims of the 2013 Gezi Park protests in Istanbul, April 2022. Photo: EPA-EFE/SEDAT SUNA.

The Tirana Court on Friday ordered a custody remand for Julide Yazici, who is wanted for extradition by Turkey to serve a prison sentence for aiding a terrorist organisation – charges that she claims are motivated by her political activism.

Yazici was arrested on August 4 at Tirana Airport while travelling from France to Albania after it was discovered that she was wanted for extradition to Turkey.

The judge granted the prosecution’s custody request despite Yazici’s lawyer’s arguments that his client “holds political asylum status in France and poses no danger”, and could be placed under house arrest instead.

The lawyer, Artan Shllaku, said that the decision will be appealed.

Shllaku added that Yazici, who teaches at an elementary school in France, had visited Albania a year earlier to see relatives and had encountered no issues.

Yazici is wanted by Turkish authorities to serve the remainder of a four-year prison sentence – three years, five months and 22 days – for providing logistical support to and participating in a terrorist organisation.

According to a decision by the French National Court of Asylum dated November 2020, a document obtained by BIRN, Yazici was involved in political activism in Turkey and participated in the Gezi Park mass protests in 2013 against the administration led by Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

She actively supported the former People’s Democratic Party, HDP, a left-wing political group that supported Turkey’s Kurdish minority, and which later became the DEM Party.

The French court decision granting asylum to Yazici stated that she was arrested in January 2016 “for having allowed a young woman she did not know, who had been introduced to her by a friend, to stay in her student room”.

The French court decision in the document that Yazici had “a well-founded fear … of being persecuted if she returns to her country due to her political activism”.

Yazici is not the first Turkish national to be arrested in Albania for extradition in controversial circumstances in recent years. Teachers and others linked to the movement previously led by the now-deceased cleric Fethullah Gulen, which is classified as a terrorist organisation by the authorities under Erdogan, have also been detained and then deported in line with Ankara’s demands.

World.title: Secrecy Surrounds Croatia’s Arrest of Alleged Serbian State-Linked Hacker
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH.

The Croatian and Serbian authorities are remaining tight-lipped over the arrest last week of a Serbian businessman named as Georgije V., 33, on suspicion of hacking into the computer systems of various Croatian state institutions and public agencies.

The Serbian man is reportedly suspected of hacking into the Croatian Interior Ministry, the Central Register of Pension-Insured Persons, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, the Croatian Regulatory Agency for Network Activities, the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, the Croatian Tax Administration and the Croatian Automobile Club.

Tomo Medved, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, was asked about the case on Friday but declined to provide details.

“I would like to commend the entire security and intelligence system for its responsible and vigilant monitoring and protection of the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Given the ongoing proceedings, I cannot comment further than that,” Medved told journalists.

Croatian daily Jutarnji list has reported that the arrest took place on July 28, when Georgije V. was on holiday in Croatia. He had arrived with his wife, two children and mother at a tourist resort on the Adriatic coast a few days earlier.

Following his arrest, police searched his electronic devices, vehicle and accommodation under court orders. They seized items and digital data allegedly linking him to criminal acts, including two mobile phones and a laptop containing a large amount of data.

The court ordered one month of pre-trial detention, despite the man offering 20,000 euros in bail money and his family home in Novi Sad as collateral.

Croatia’s Chief State Attorney, Ivan Turudic, initially sparked public interest on Monday when he made a comment about a case related to national security. It was then reported by Jutarnji list that Turudic was referring to the arrest of an alleged hacker linked to Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA.

It is not known whether the suspect’s alleged access to the computer systems of various institutions and agencies endangered Croatia’s national security in any way, or what he did with any data he may have obtained.

Nera Gajdarov Beg, the suspect’s lawyer, told Jutarnji list that the court’s custody order is being contested.

“An appeal has been filed against the decision to order pretrial detention because we believe that not all legal requirements for such a decision have been met. At this point, I cannot provide details of the defence because the proceedings are in the investigation phase, which is secret,” Gajdarov Beg said.

The Serbian authorities have not commented on the arrest so far. However, Serbian media have reported that Georgije V. is the owner of an active Novi Sad-based company specialising in computer programming and cybersecurity.

World.title: Croatian Serb Leader Deplores Hate Speech at Operation Storm Commemoration
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milorad Pupovac, president of the Independent Democratic Serb Party, SDSS, and MP, on Friday said that slogans and chants heard on the streets of Knin on August 5, the day marking the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, represented a “serious attack on constitutional values and democracy”.

Pupovac, leader of the main party representing Serbs in Croatia, argued that “hatred and incitement to crime are incompatible with true patriotism”.

At a press conference, he showed a compilation of recordings from Knin, the town that was the headquarters of a rebel Serbian statelet crushed by the Croatian Army’s Operation Storm in 1995.

They included sports fans and army veterans singing songs glorifying the Ustasha – the army of the Independent State of Croatia, NDH, a World War II fascist puppet state operating under the patronage of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

The recordings also showed people chanting: “We Croats do not drink wine, only the blood of Chetniks [Serbian nationalists] from Knin”; “The battle is fought, it is fought, the Ustasha flag is flying”, as well as insults directed at St Sava, the patron saint of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

“Those who have been trying to pass this off as an act of patriotism for years are actually seriously violating the true values of patriotism. In peacetime, the greatest patriotic virtue is constitutional patriotism,” Pupovac said.

He added that such behaviour was a “vicious attack on democracy”.

The SNV cited articles of the Croatian Constitution that it believes were violated by the shouting of the Ustasha salute “For the Homeland, Ready” and other glorifications of the NDH. The violations came after, not during, the official anniversary celebrations, it said.

Every year, Knin hosts a commemoration of Operation Storm, which liberated about 18 per cent of Croatia’s territory from rebel Serb forces and was followed by the flight of around 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. Some of them later returned.

SDSS leader Pupovac also criticised the Croatian judicial authorities, questioning why the State Attorney’s Office often does not react to hate speech and incitement to violence, appealing for an end to what he called a policy of appeasement.

He warned that failure to condemn such phenomena represents a direct threat to the Serb community in Croatia, and to all citizens who advocate for a state governed by the rule of law.

World.title: Week in Review: The Electoral Merry-Go-Round
World.content:
Last week, a no-confidence motion in the Serbian government was held in the country’s parliament. A boisterous discussion ensued between ruling and opposition MPs, but the motion failed – as expected.

Its real significance was not so much the outcome as the fact that the holding the vote, tabled at the beginning of the year, cleared an important obstacle to calling early parliamentary elections.

President Aleksandar Vucic has fuelled speculation that polls are imminent. Our analysis takes a look a look at what will determine when they happen – and whether they will happen at all.

World.title: One Year in the Palace: How Nawrocki Made the Polish Presidency His Own
World.content:
Nawrocki vetoes again and again

At home, he has repeatedly used his veto to frustrate the government. In his first year, Nawrocki vetoed 41 bills, more than any other Polish president since the fall of Communism. Among the most consequential were legislation linked to Poland’s access to nearly 44 billion euros under the EU’s SAFE defence program, bills concerning the justice system and public finances, two laws expanding rights for unmarried couples and, three times, legislation regulating the crypto-assets market.

The conflict, however, extends beyond legislation. Forty four ambassadorial nominations remain unsigned amid a long-running dispute between the palace and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski. Poland still has no fully accredited ambassador in Washington, one of its most important diplomatic postings; Bogdan Klich continues to run the embassy as chargé d’affaires.

But Nawrocki has also been unusually active in proposing legislation of his own. In a year, he submitted 22 bills; if he continues at this pace, he is on course to breaking another record by the end of his term. His predecessor Andrzej Duda by comparison submitted 32 during the entire first five years of his presidency.

“I want, in fact, to change the model of the presidency,” Nawrocki told the crowd on Thursday. “The president is not only there to review the law and deal with bills that come from parliament. The president is also there to come forward with legislative initiatives and carry your voice and your demands.”

That ambition goes beyond the number of bills. Poland is a parliamentary democracy in which the government runs most day-to-day policy, while the president has important but more limited powers, including the veto and a role in foreign and defence affairs. Nawrocki has repeatedly floated constitutional change and has been pushing the Presidential Palace towards something closer to a parallel centre of power. His ministers regularly speak on the same issues as their government counterparts, while the 17 presidential councils that aid him, involving around 700 people, are working on a broader development strategy that Nawrocki says he will unveil within months.

“I deeply believe that the presidential development strategy… will become, in the next parliamentary elections, a point of reference for all those who aspire to govern Poland,” he said.

Tusk has accused Nawrocki of trying to change Poland’s political system in practice without changing the constitution. Government spokesman Adam Szlapka described the first year of the presidency as a “bad time”, accusing Nawrocki of thinking primarily in political terms and obstructing government policy.

So far, however, the confrontation has not hurt the president much. Nawrocki remains Poland’s most trusted politician: an IBRiS poll published in late July found that 51.3 per cent of respondents trusted him.

Foreign policy has been another central part of his presidency. Nawrocki has worked hard to cultivate ties with Donald Trump and the US, while taking an increasingly confrontational line towards Ukraine over the historical legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for massacres of Polish citizens during World War II.

On Thursday, he again tried to hold both positions at once. It was in Poland’s strategic interest, he said, for Ukrainian soldiers to keep Russia as far from Poland as possible. But it was also in Poland’s interest that “Banderite flags” should not fly in Warsaw, referring to the common term used for fighters of the UPA. “You can help and you can demand.”

World.title: MP: Estonia has a top public servant competition instead of presidential elections
World.content:
Newly independent MP Meelis Kiili told ERR that while he respects Ülle Madise as justice chancellor, he cannot support her as a presidential candidate until he hears her views on foreign policy, national defense and social policy.

"We don't have a presidential election; we have a competition for a top public office. An election requires at least two candidates and a debate, but we don't have that right now," Kiili told ERR.

He added that he has great respect for Ülle Madise both as a person and as a legal expert, but that does not mean he would vote for her on that basis alone. Kiili said he does not know Madise's positions on her role as supreme commander of national defense, or on foreign policy, social policy and other issues.

Regarding his departure from the Reform Party, Kiili said he made the decision a week and a half ago.

"My own reflection told me that we no longer have any common ground. I continue to support a liberal economy, but we disagree on the issue of the nation-state and particularly on matters concerning national defense," he said.

Kiili said he cannot currently say whether he plans to join another political party or whether he will run in the next Riigikogu elections.

"One thing at a time. So far, I have tried to work across party lines. If I can continue working in national defense and security, then I may continue in politics. If not, I don't have to."

Asked what will happen to the National Defense Committee now that both he and committee chair Kalev Stoicescu have left parties in the governing coalition, Kiili said they would have to wait until the committee meets. According to Kiili, the National Defense Committee is unusual in that votes do not fall along coalition and opposition lines.

"Decisions there were based on expertise and the stronger argument," he said.

Kiili, who until now had been a member of the Reform Party, announced Monday that he had decided to leave the party and continue serving in the Riigikogu as an unaffiliated MP.

World.title: Estonia's ruling coalition loses majority after 2 MPs quit parties
World.content:
Estonia's two-party governing coalition lost its majority on Monday after two members of parliament resigned from their respective parties, reducing the number of seats to 50 of 101.

Eesti 200's Kalev Stoicescu and Reform's Meelis Kiili separately announced they were leaving their parties. Stoicescu made the announcement on social media on Sunday evening, while Kiili did so on Monday morning.

Kalev Stoicescu

According to Stoicescu, the decision had been a long time coming and he had considered whether he wanted to remain in politics at all.

"I stepped down from the party's board back in February 2024. I did not run in the local elections in October 2025. I thought for a long time about whether to continue in politics at all. People close to me and voters have unanimously encouraged me to continue and run in the next Riigikogu elections. I trust myself and the people close to me," the politician said.

Stoicescu also said he has already received offers to join other parties but has not yet made a decision.

"I want to continue contributing to Estonia's future, particularly in the areas of defense, security and foreign policy," Stoicescu said.

Meelis Kiili

"This is not a decision made on the spur of the moment. I have arrived at it over a longer period of time, primarily because my views on Estonia's national defense and security and their long-term development have increasingly diverged from the party's political choices," he said, explaining his decision.

Kiili said he does not regret joining the Reform Party.

"I have met many good people in the Reform Party and made good acquaintances and friends. I am grateful for that. But in politics, there comes a point when you have to ask yourself whether belonging to a party helps you stand up for the principles that brought you into politics or whether it begins to constrain you. For me, the answer to that question is now clear.

Meelis Kiili. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"That is why the Reform Party and I are going our separate ways."

"I will continue in the Riigikogu as an unaffiliated MP and will keep working on issues where my knowledge and experience can benefit Estonia."

Meelis Kiili joined the Reform Party ahead of the last Riigikogu elections, on November 2, 2022. He ran in Ida-Viru County, received 1,289 votes and was elected.

Following Kiili's departure from the Reform Party and its parliamentary group, as well as Kalev Stoicescu's announcement a day earlier that he was leaving Eesti 200, the governing coalition now has 50 MPs in parliament, effectively making it a minority government.

Stoicescu associated with Parempoolsed

Stoicescu himself said he intends to run in the next Riigikogu elections and has already received offers to join other parties.

ERR has been told that Stoicescu is most likely to join the nonparliamentary Parempoolsed (Right-wingers) ahead of the Riigikogu elections. Polling firms Emor, Norstat and Turu-uuringud currently put the party's support at 6–7 percent. Parempoolsed have struggled with a lack of well-known figures and Stoicescu joining would certainly help them.

It will also be interesting to see how Stoicescu's departure from Eesti 200 affects the dynamics of the Riigikogu's committees, particularly the National Defense Committee, which Stoicescu currently chairs. The National Defense Committee has 11 members, and before Stoicescu left Eesti 200, the governing coalition held a narrow six-member majority.

The next Riigikogu elections will take place March 7, 2027, seven months from now.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) and Eesti 200 head Kristina Kallas. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

World.title: Tartu Old Town bar owners concerned about residential development
World.content:
Several bars in Tartu's Old Town are concerned about apartments due to be completed in the heart of the city in a few years and potential conflicts with the new residents who will move into them.

The building on the corner of Gildi and Rüütli streets in Tartu's Old Town, built in 1838, has served as a broadcloth factory, a girls' school and a polyclinic. Now, after standing empty for several years, the building is being converted into office space and 53 apartments, mostly one- and two-room units. Nearby bars are concerned about their potential new neighbors, fearing noise complaints and conflicts similar to those surrounding Genialistide Klubi, which Tartu has been trying to resolve for the past year and a half.

"Rüütli tänav is Tartu's main downtown street. This is where the nightlife is most concentrated. We already have noise problems, which have been discussed extensively in Tartu, so how do you resolve a situation where short-term rental apartments are allowed on the main downtown street, which is the center of nightlife? Why are short-term rental apartments allowed on this street? It's clear from the outset that there are going to be problems here and experience so far has shown that I have to resolve all these problems out of my own pocket, with my own money, nerves and everything else," Kivi bar owner Karin Kiplok said.

Jaan Tover, who owns several bars near the new apartments, said they are also concerned because the city is not taking steps to prevent problems related to nightlife. When problems arise, businesses on Rüütli tänav are left to resolve them themselves. The developer said its plans have taken the location into account.

"These are mostly smaller homes that will probably attract younger people without children who may be less bothered by the associated disturbance. The other thing is that, from a construction standpoint, we have to take great care to make sure the windows are very well insulated. Also, there won't be any ventilation openings in the wall," said Kaarel Kiidron, managing partner at developer Livida.

Although prospective apartment buyers are informed about the bustle on Rüütli tänav, some residents who expected noise and people on the street have encountered issues they did not anticipate.

"The vibration that comes through the window on weekends is actually pretty bad, and it's specifically from the music. I knew there would be noise, but I didn't expect the vibration to come through the walls of the building. It's coming through from the building next door. I knew there would be a lot of people here, and people don't bother me, but there could be less music here," said Triin Varul, a Rüütli tänav resident.

Tartu's Rüütli tänav. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

Tartu Deputy Mayor Kertu Vuks said the city's vision is for the Old Town to accommodate both housing and bars and cafes. If new Old Town residents encounter problems with noise, the city will address them on a case-by-case basis. At the same time, the city would like bars outside the Old Town to be viable as well.

"The city's hope and vision is also for other locations — not just Rüütli tänav — and neighborhood bars to be viable," Vuks said. She added that, ultimately, bars will not have to leave Rüütli tänav and businesses are free to choose the locations that suit them best.

World.title: Estonia axes unemployment benefit for young people finishing conscription
World.content:
New eligibility requirements mean that young graduates cannot receive unemployment benefits after finishing school or completing military service, unless they have previously worked for at least eight months.

A young person who goes straight from school into compulsory military service may be surprised to discover that, when looking for work after completing their service, they will have to rely on someone else for financial support because the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund will not pay them benefits. The exception is if they managed to work enough while still in school.

Previously, both school graduates and young people completing military service were eligible for unemployment allowance, but that form of support ceased to exist at the beginning of this year. Unemployment insurance benefits are now available, with eligibility depending on a person's previous participation in the labor market, said Kirsti Melesk, head of the employment department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.

"As with any other type of insurance, the system works so that a person becomes entitled to benefits if they have contributed to the insurance system and the insured event then occurs. In the case of unemployment insurance, that means becoming unemployed. The same principle can be compared with home or auto insurance: If a person has never paid insurance premiums, they cannot claim an insurance payout when an insured event occurs. The purpose of unemployment insurance benefits is to partially replace income previously earned from employment during the period when a person is looking for work, rather than directly guaranteeing an income to everyone who is out of work, including those who did not previously have such an income," Melesk said.

She said conscripts are in the same position as school graduates who also have no previous work experience when they begin looking for work after graduation and have to manage without financial support from the state. Young people can nevertheless register as unemployed and make use of services designed to help them find work.

"We currently have no plans to create any kind of exemption for conscripts. Instead, we consider it important to support young people in their job searches, helping them gain their first work experience and get a foot in the door of the labor market. Since the beginning of this year, for example, the Unemployment Insurance Fund has also had youth counselors who specialize specifically in supporting young people's job searches and providing them with counseling," Melesk said.

In certain cases, however, young school graduates may still be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits if they managed to work while attending school. To qualify, they must have worked during at least eight months over the preceding three years, for at least one day in each of those months.

"A person must have accumulated at least eight months of unemployment insurance coverage. This can be accrued, for example, through employment under an employment contract, and if a person has worked under an employment contract for eight months, the requirement has already been met," said Vadim Djomin, head of unemployment insurance benefits at the Unemployment Insurance Fund. There are, however, exceptions.

"If a person works under a contract governed by the law of obligations, there must be eight payments from which unemployment insurance premiums have been withheld. In the case of employment contracts, a person must have worked for eight months and those months do not have to be consecutive. They can be under different contracts and in different months, but there must be at least eight months in total," Djomin said.

According to Djomin, a young person could accumulate the required eight months by working over three summers and would then be eligible for benefits from the Unemployment Insurance Fund after graduating.

Viru Infantry Battalian conscripts' passout, June 10. Source: mil.ee

The Estonian Defense Resources Agency has not discussed providing conscripts with financial support while they look for work after completing their service. If such support were introduced, it would have to come from the defense budget at the expense of specific military capabilities, the agency's director general, Anu Rannaveski, said.

"What is military service if not another form of training? Just as people study different fields at university, military service itself is training in national defense. Of course, as a society, we want to make it as easy as possible for young people to enter the labor market. I think military service itself already gives a young person a very strong competitive advantage. The studies we have conducted also show that, in the future, young people who have completed military service earn more than those who have not," Rannaveski said.

She said the trend in recent years also shows that a significant number of young people remain in the Estonian Defense Forces as active-duty personnel after completing their military service. They account for around 7.5 percent of conscripts.

World.title: Natalie Mets: Youth unemployment will not fix itself
World.content:
Vocational education must be a deliberate and valued choice for young people in Estonia, rather than a fallback option for those who did not get into university, writes Natalie Mets.

Estonia's youth unemployment rate is at its highest level in recent years, at 18.2 percent. But we should also be increasingly concerned about young people who are not in education, employment or training (the so-called NEET group). In Estonia, approximately one in 10 young people aged 15–26 falls into the NEET category.

Estonia's problems are often blamed on our small population. Yet youth unemployment is also rising in much larger countries. The root of the problem, therefore, is not that there are too few Estonians. The labor market has changed rapidly and getting that first opportunity is becoming increasingly difficult for young people. It is no longer only those who do not want to work who are unemployed — increasingly, even young people who are actively looking for work cannot find a job.

But what lies behind these figures? A young person who is neither studying nor working unfortunately ends up on the margins of society. Inactivity can quickly turn into loneliness and isolation. Days are spent in front of a computer screen and — as anyone who has spent a long time unsuccessfully looking for work probably knows — confidence in oneself and in the idea that there is a place for them in the labor market quickly disappears. The longer a young person remains without work or study, the harder it becomes to enter the labor market later.

Against this backdrop, it was particularly dismaying to hear Tallinn Deputy Mayor for Education Andrei Kante's (Center Party — ed.) explanation for Tallinn Technology College's lack of popularity among girls. In his view, the problem is that the college does not offer enough programs that interest girls. Fortunately, representatives of the college immediately rejected this view, saying that such thinking is outdated and harmful to society.

When a politician in power essentially says that technology-related fields are not meant for girls and that more suitable programs should be created for them, he is reinforcing precisely the stereotypes that Estonia should have left behind long ago. Through the deputy mayor's words, Tallinn is sending the message that higher-paying occupations with better career prospects — engineer, mechanic or IT specialist — are for boys, while girls should choose service, care work or other traditionally lower-paid fields that are supposedly more likely to "interest" them.

This kind of thinking is just as harmful to boys as it is to girls. If a boy wants to study to become, for example, an early childhood teacher, occupational therapist, speech therapist or nurse, prejudice and misplaced embarrassment may prevent him from making that final decision. There is extensive research on this and the OECD has reached the same conclusion: perceptions of which occupations are "women's work" or "men's work" directly influence young people's choices of fields of study.

Yet the fields mentioned above are precisely the ones that need more men. Children benefit when both male and female teachers work in kindergartens and schools. Every field stands to benefit from greater diversity.

There are occupations in which biological differences may, on average, give one sex an advantage, such as strength-based activities at the absolute elite level or the most physically demanding tasks. Most modern occupations, however, require knowledge, teamwork, creativity and dedication, not lifting rocks.

At a time when artificial intelligence will inevitably change the nature of work and affect almost every occupation, politicians should be sending a very different message. Instead of crudely dividing occupations into "women's" and "men's" work, we must do everything possible to ensure that every young person acquires the skills needed to adapt in a rapidly changing world.

Those who know how to use technology, acquire new skills, combine different fields and think critically will succeed. We cannot afford to leave some young people with the impression, while they are still in school, that certain opportunities simply are not for them.

Only systemic change can address the current situation. Vocational education must become a deliberate and valued choice for young people in Estonia, rather than a fallback option for those who did not get into university. That requires closer cooperation with employers, more internship opportunities and greater societal respect for skilled trades.

At the same time, hiring young people must be made more attractive to employers. One option worth considering would be reducing employers' tax burden on young workers, making it less risky for businesses to offer someone their first job.

The Riigikogu's decision to allow 16-year-olds to serve alcohol was also a step in the right direction, but that alone is not enough to improve young people's prospects in the labor market. A broader package of measures is needed to support young people's education and their transition into employment.

Higher education, for example, could be made more flexible so that parents can study part time free of charge and having a child does not mean interrupting their education or facing a financial penalty. The public sector, one of Estonia's largest employers, could also launch a pilot program to create more first-job opportunities specifically for young people.

Youth unemployment will not decline on its own. It requires political decisions that expand young people's opportunities, whether in education or in getting their first job, and that help break down outdated notions about which choices are "right" for them.

World.title: EKRE head: Ülle Madise's election in the Riigikogu could be contested in court
World.content:
Martin Helme said his party would not support Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a potential candidate in the presidential election and that the chancellor's conflict of roles in the election could lead to the result being challenged in court.

"Ülle Madise has now essentially declared herself a presidential candidate because she is bargaining with the Riigikogu to secure cross-party support. She does not have that support, because at the very least our party does not support her election," Helme wrote on social media.

"At the same time, she has a very serious conflict of interest by indicating that she wants the support of all parties while serving as chancellor of justice, who oversees the work of parliament," he said, adding that such a conflict of roles could result in the election result being challenged in court if Madise is elected.

The EKRE chair said Madise's potential candidacy creates a bad impression.

"The chancellor of justice is playing a game in which she acts as though she is not a candidate, thereby avoiding the debate and heightened media and public scrutiny that should be a matter of course for someone seeking high office. At the same time, she is consistently signaling that she is interested in the office, provided the votes for her are already secured," Helme said.

He said Madise has systematically passed up opportunities to say that she will not run and is not interested in doing so. "Today (Saturday — ed.), she once again confirmed that she is interested in the presidency, except that she wants to see sufficient support first."

"This kind of game allows her to pop up as a candidate at the last minute and, assuming the votes are indeed secured, walk straight in through the back door of Kadriorg. As I said, all of this is very poor form and flagrantly at odds with the basic principles of democracy," the EKRE chair added.

Helme said EKRE is the only party to have approached the presidential election seriously and professionally, while also treating voters with respect. He emphasized that the party nominated Mart Helme as its candidate in the spring.

"I continue to urge people to support Estonia's only official presidential candidate, Mart Helme," he concluded.

Eesti 200 Chair Kristina Kallas said Thursday that Madise currently has the support of 67 members of the Riigikogu and that Züleyxa Izmailova, who left Eesti 200 and joined the Social Democrats, does not support Madise. Izmailova, however, told ERR that the vote is secret and that she would not stand in the way of electing a president.

The Riigikogu's Council of Elders will discuss the presidential election Tuesday.

At least 21 members of the Riigikogu are required to nominate a presidential candidate. A candidate would need at least 68 votes to be elected president by the Riigikogu.

Key dates:

• Aug. 21-24: Candidate nominations

• Sept. 2: First round of voting in the Riigikogu

• Sept. 3: Second and third rounds of voting in the Riigikogu, if necessary

World.title: Asian stocks track Wall St higher after US job losses ease rate fears
World.content:
Hong Kong – Stocks rose Monday as investors pared their bets on a US interest rate hike after data showed thousands of jobs were lost in July, though sentiment was dented by another spike in oil prices as hopes for an end to the Middle East crisis fade.

Tech firms enjoyed a fresh bout of buying following a volatile run in recent weeks, with Japanese and Korean chipmakers leading the charge.

The positive mood was fuelled by figures from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics that showed 23,000 jobs were lost last month, while growth in May and June was revised down.

The reading suggested the world’s number one economy was slowing, though traders welcomed the prospect the Federal Reserve will hold off hiking borrowing costs for the time being.

The chances of an increase in September were slashed to about 43 percent from 64 percent a week ago, according to Bloomberg.

Inflation data due later this week will be the next guide for investors.

The news helped Wall Street higher, with the S&P 500 ending at a fresh record high, while tech firms — which benefit from lower rates — helped the Nasdaq pile on more than one percent.

And the gains filtered through to Asia, with Tokyo climbing two percent thanks to healthy advances for Kioxia, Tokyo Electron and Advantest. Seoul was also up as chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung rallied.

Hong Kong, Taipei, Shanghai, Wellington and Jakarta were also up.

“Markets treated the report as a meaningful challenge to near term Fed rate hike expectations, effectively concluding the Fed has time on its side,” wrote National Australia Bank’s Rodrigo Catril.

But he added: “The report reduces the case that the labour market is adding inflation pressures, but it does not provide a clean green light for a dovish pivot.

“The report is unlikely, by itself, to deter a September hike… inflation remains the more pressing side of the mandate. The next (consumer price index) prints (for July and August) ahead of the September Federal Open Market Committee meeting are the key data releases to watch.”

The dollar clawed back the losses suffered Friday in reaction to the jobs figures, and continued to gain against the yen after plunging earlier this month when US and Japanese authorities embarked on a historic joint intervention to support the Japanese unit.

Crude prices jumped around one percent to extend gains at the end of last week as Iran’s Revolutionary Guards insisted Sunday that they would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States complied with a list of demands.

Tehran insists on retaining control of the waterway — through which a fifth of world oil and LNG pass — after the war and wants to charge tolls for passage, which Washington has pushed back against.

Attacks in the strait, which was free to transit before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have urged both sides to return to the terms of a subsequent June memorandum that set out a path for peace talks.

Iran on Saturday released a list of conditions for reopening the strait, including an end to the war on all fronts, the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen assets and compensation for wartime damage, the Tasnim news agency reported.

Those conditions echoed the terms of the June agreement, which included a provision to create a $300 billion reconstruction fund for Iran.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday that their strategy was to maintain their blockade “until the enemy accepts all our conditions… the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway”.

For his part, US President Donald Trump said in an interview: “We are low-keying it.”

“We are only semi-negotiating with them,” he was quoted as saying. “We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.”

“It will work out,” he added. “It’s like a chess game.”

World.title: NBA champion player and historic coach Nelson dead at 86
World.content:
San Francisco – Don Nelson, who won the second-most games of any coach in NBA history and five NBA titles as a player with the Boston Celtics, died on Sunday, his family announced. He was 86.

Nelson was a member of NBA championship teams with Boston from 1966 to 1976 and the Celtics retired his jersey number 19.

As a coach, Nelson finished with a record of 1,335-1,063 — what had been an NBA record until Gregg Popovich passed him in 2022 — in stints with Golden State, Milwaukee, New York and Dallas from 1976 to 2010.

“Don Nelson revolutionized NBA basketball through his fearlessness, ingenuity and deep conviction,” NBA commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement.

“He spent nearly 50 years in the NBA -– winning five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics before building one of the most successful and pioneering coaching careers in league history.

“He brought an unmistakable personality to everything he did, and his impact on our sport will continue to be felt for generations.”

Nelson, who was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2012, never reached the NBA Finals as a coach but was remembered as a historic figure among bench bosses.

“The Golden State Warriors mourn the passing of Hall of Fame head coach Don Nelson,” the team said in a statement.

“‘Nellie’ was one of the most innovative and influential coaches in NBA history and an iconic figure in Warriors history…

“More than anything, Don Nelson will be remembered for his authenticity, larger-than-life personality, and incredible passion for basketball and his influence on the Warriors franchise will endure for years to come.”

Steve Kerr, the current Warriors coach, recalled Nelson as a visionary whose influence remains with the modern era of the league.

“Don Nelson was a true innovator whose influence on the game of basketball is still felt today,” Kerr said.

“He consistently challenged conventional thinking, experimented with different lineups and styles of play, and saw possibilities in the game that others often did not.

“So much of what is now commonplace in the modern NBA can be traced back to the way Nellie approached the game.”

The Celtics paid tribute to Nelson’s playing career in a statement.

“Nellie was a tough and reliable all-around player whose tenacity and ability to ‘think the game’ was on full display throughout his 11 seasons with the Boston Celtics, where he was a key member of five championship teams across two eras,” the Celtics said.

The Bucks paid tribute to Nelson’s first NBA coaching stint.

“During his 11 seasons as Bucks coach from 1976-1987, Nellie won two of his three NBA Coach of the Year awards and established himself as one of the most innovative and visionary leaders in basketball history,” the Bucks said.

The Dallas Mavericks called him an innovator and legend whose “impact will never be forgotten,” saying he left “an incredible mark on our franchise and the game of basketball.”

World.title: Zambia vote to test Hichilema’s economic record
World.content:
Lusaka – Zambians vote Thursday in a closely watched presidential election that will test whether recent economic gains can offset frustration over the high cost of living in one of Africa’s most stable democracies.

Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema faces Brian Mundubile, a former ally of late president Edgar Lungu, who surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.

Up to 8.7 million voters — a majority of them women — will decide whether Hichilema’s economic reforms deserve another term or whether the opposition can turn widespread discontent into a comeback.

Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), won the presidency in 2021 on his sixth attempt, inheriting a country in sovereign default after years of heavy borrowing under Lungu.

His victory marked a rare peaceful transfer of power to an opposition party through the ballot box in Africa.

The government has since secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restored an International Monetary Fund programme and returned the economy to growth, winning praise from international lenders and investors.

But many Zambians say the benefits have been slow to reach ordinary citizens. Rising food prices, unemployment and persistent poverty remain dominant concerns in a country where more than 70 percent of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, according to World Bank data.

“Worldwide there has been recognition that we are doing well but he needs to bring it home,” medical student Semi Malama, 26, told AFP.

Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and the government has set an ambitious target of tripling production by 2031.

Chinese companies are major players in the mining sector, underscoring Beijing’s outsized economic influence in the country.

– Continuity vs change –

The opposition has sought to exploit the squeeze on household finances, arguing that reforms have failed to improve livelihoods despite signs of recovery.

Until the opposition coalesced behind Mundubile, re-election had looked all but certain for the 64-year-old Hichilema, widely known as “HH”.

Although 14 candidates are on the ballot, analysts say the race has narrowed into a two-horse contest between Hichilema and Mundubile, a 55-year-old former minister.

“The opposition alliance is bringing energy to their rallies and appealing to youth, women, and rural voters,” Joseph Siegle, director of research at the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, told AFP.

Mundubile’s challenge is built around “mopping up” the support base of Lungu’s Patriotic Front, particularly in the north and east, where the former ruling party has historically held sway, political analyst Louw Nel said.

But his relatively late entry into the race and association with the Lungu era could limit his ability to expand beyond that base, he said.

Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc.

“Ultimately, the election will hinge on whether voters believe continuity offers the best chance of consolidating recent economic reforms, or whether they conclude that change is needed to address immediate economic pressures,” Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.

– Tensions –

The campaign has been marked by pockets of violence and allegations of intimidation.

Police have used tear gas to disperse clashes between rival supporters, while Mundubile’s National Republican Party (NRPUP) has accused authorities of restricting its campaign activities.

The opposition leader last week alleged that snipers were deployed at a campaign event in Mongu, about 580 kilometres (360 miles) west of Lusaka, calling the tear gas “just the tip of the iceberg.”

Polling stations open Thursday at 0600 local time (0400 GMT) and close 12 hours later.

Zambians will also elect an expanded parliament, with directly elected members of parliament rising to 226 from 156.

Presidential results are due August 17, according to the electoral commission’s calendar. A candidate needs more than 50 percent of valid votes to win outright; otherwise, the top contenders face a run-off.

The outcome could hinge on “relatively small swings” in support across Zambia’s 10 provinces, Simakoloyi said.

The vote will also test Zambia’s reputation for political stability amid growing concerns over restrictions on dissent and a narrowing political space.

World.title: No mercy for corrupt officials as Al-Zaidi widens Iraq crackdown
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s anti-corruption effort has shown no signs of stopping, with arrests and investigations ranging from senior Oil Ministry officials to MPs, former provincial leaders, and other government figures since he assumed office.

One of the main early instances involved Adnan Al-Jumaili, the former deputy oil minister for refining affairs, whose imprisonment was a key development in the probe.

Statements gathered from Al-Jumaili assisted authorities in expanding their investigation into a larger network of politicians and officials accused of profiting from government contracts and state resources.

That probe culminated in a spectacular operation on June 28, when Iraqi security forces blocked off access to Baghdad’s highly defended Green Zone and conducted coordinated raids on political and government heavyweights.

Iraq’s national news agency first claimed 47 arrests, including 12 current parliamentarians, a former legislator, a former aide to former Prime Minister Mohammed Shia Al-Sudani, and a top Oil Ministry official.

According to sources inside Iraq’s anti-corruption authorities, there were 67 people held during the first phase of the “Dawn Crackdown”.

Ali Maarij, Iraq’s Deputy Oil Minister for distribution and another key player in the country’s energy industry, was among those held.

According to prosecutors, the larger investigation turned up claims of the misuse of public resources, government contracts, and commissions for personal or political gain.

Authorities also recovered a considerable quantity of assets related to the investigations. Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council said in July that 375 kg of gold had been confiscated as part of the al-Jumaili probe, with more cash and gold found in subsequent operations.

Instead of finishing with the first Green Zone attacks, the campaign lasted all of July.

Between July 20 and July 26, Iraqi police apprehended 31 persons in seven corruption cases, reflecting the government’s escalating enforcement campaign.

So far, August has delivered a slew of high-profile cases.

Former Salah al-Din governor Ahmed al-Jubouri, also known as Abu Mazen, was held as authorities investigated claims involving public finances, while former Finance Minister Taif Sami was allegedly called by the court for a separate inquiry.

On Sunday, police detained Hashem al-Sudani, the director general of the state-owned General Automobile and Machinery Company, on suspicion of corruption regarding a Ministry of Defense contract.

The specifics of the alleged infractions and the contract’s worth have not yet been released.

The financial impact of the crackdown is becoming significant.

The Eco Iraq Observatory said on Sunday that police had recovered around 482.6 billion Iraqi dinars ($371.6 million) in stolen assets, including cash and gold.

Taken together, the arrests convey an increasingly clear message from Al-Zaidi’s government: senior political ties, legislative standing, or positions inside major ministries should not exclude people from scrutiny.

However, arrests alone will not decide whether Iraq eventually succeeds in combating corruption.

Success will be predicated on transforming the present campaign into long-term institutional transformation via open government contracts, improved audits, digital financial systems, independent investigations, and tighter controls over public funds.

This is especially crucial as Iraq pursues tens of billions of dollars in foreign investment and works to strengthen economic ties with the United States, Europe, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and other Gulf nations.

Investors need to be confident that predictable rules govern contracts and public institutions rather than political interference.

The crackdown has also received backing from key international partners.

During a phone call with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saturday, Macron reaffirmed France’s support for Iraq’s anti-corruption drive and economic reforms, as well as continued cooperation on counterterrorism and strengthening the capabilities of the Iraqi armed forces.

But the problem goes beyond financial corruption.

Al-Zaidi has committed to reinforce state power and bring armaments under government control, adding to the administration’s already arduous task of dealing with entrenched political and economic interests.

Iraq’s long-term goal must consequently be greater than capturing people.

Baghdad needs institutions strong enough to prevent corruption and foreign intervention from resurfacing under new political networks, whether sponsored by Iran or another external entity.

If Al-Zaidi can combine rigorous enforcement with due process and institutional change, the campaign might greatly boost trust in the Iraqi government.

Without such institutional improvements, even hundreds of arrests risk becoming a momentary crackdown rather than the long-term transformation Iraq requires.

World.title: Iraq opens its first IMAX cinema in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has inaugurated its first IMAX theater at the Iraq Mall in Baghdad, introducing the premium large-screen movie format to the nation for the first time.

Sarwa Abdul Wahid, the Acting Minister of Culture, Tourism, and Antiquities, formally opened the new Iraqi Cinema branch in the mall, adding to Baghdad’s fast expanding entertainment and leisure sector.

According to IMAX’s official listing, the Iraq Mall site in Baghdad has an IMAX with Laser auditorium and stadium seating.

The launch allows Iraqi consumers to see important worldwide movies in IMAX without having to fly abroad, like Christopher Nolan’s 2026 blockbuster The Odyssey.

The film, starring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Robert Pattinson, and Lupita Nyong’o, was the first feature film filmed exclusively on IMAX film cameras.

The Odyssey has also emerged as one of 2026’s greatest box office triumphs, earning more over $260 million globally in its first weekend.

Iraqi Cinema is now offering daily IMAX screenings of the film at its Iraq Mall location.

IMAX brings another worldwide entertainment option to Baghdad, as Iraq seeks additional investment in retail malls, restaurants, hotels, theaters, and other leisure developments, while also growing its domestic tourist and entertainment sectors.

World.title: Iraq arrests senior Trade Ministry official Hashem Al-Sudani
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi prosecutors detained Hashem Al-Sudani, the director general of the state-owned General Automobile and Machinery Company (GAMCO), on Sunday for suspected embezzlement in a contract with the Ministry of Defense.

The contract’s specifics, including its value and the particular alleged infractions under investigation, have not been released. Al-Sudani’s arrest is part of Iraq’s growing anti-corruption effort, which targets prominent government officials, legislators, and business leaders.

The new arrest comes as Baghdad ramps up the “Dawn Crackdown,” an anti-corruption operation that began on June 28 by Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi to probe big crimes involving public contracts and state finances.

The initiative has gained traction among senior and politically connected individuals.

Recently, police arrested former Salah al-Din governor Ahmed al-Jubouri, also known as Abu Mazen, while former Finance Minister Taif Sami was allegedly called by the court as part of a separate inquiry.

Al-Zaidi’s administration has prioritized combating corruption and reclaiming public monies, with authorities attempting to show that probes would extend to officials regardless of party or institutional affiliation.

Corruption has long been a major impediment to Iraq’s growth, depleting state resources, degrading public services, and deterring private and international investment.

The ongoing arrests imply Baghdad’s new effort is spreading to official institutions, but anyone arrested or interrogated has not been convicted and is still subject to due process.

World.title: Five dead in new Russia, Ukraine strikes
World.content:
Kyiv – Russian strikes killed two people and wounded dozens across Ukraine overnight Saturday and Sunday, while a Ukrainian drone attack killed three people in Russia’s Belgorod region.

The World Health Organization denounced a strike that destroyed a warehouse in Ukraine holding medical supplies.

More than four years after the start of Russia’s large-scale offensive against Ukraine, both countries are ramping up long-range strikes. The resulting civilian casualties led the United Nations to condemn both sides last week.

Russia is relying on “ballistic terror,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday on social media, stating that 61 missiles of various types had been fired at Ukraine this week.

“More pressure, more sanctions against Russia and more air defence for Ukraine are needed,” he added.

The two people killed by a Russian drone strike were in the major northeastern city of Kharkiv, where four floors of a residential building were also destroyed, said Zelensky.

Twenty-three people were also wounded, according to regional governor Oleg Synegoubov, sharing images of a gutted building with emergency services working at the scene.

Zelensky said eight people had also been wounded overnight in Odesa, where strikes damaged the power grid, the port, and residential buildings.

He condemned another “absolutely brutal” strike targeting energy infrastructure near a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, in the Dnipropetrovsk region that wounded nine people, including four children.

– WHO condemns warehouse strike –

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said a WHO warehouse stocking medical supplies in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro had been destroyed in strikes on Friday.

“I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros in a post on X Sunday.

“Even wars have rules. One of those is that health must be protected!”

In Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack on the border city of Belgorod killed three people, according to the region’s acting governor, Alexander Shuvaev.

Twenty-five people, including children aged four and nine, were also wounded, he added.

Fires broke out in cars, two apartment buildings, and a house, said Shuvaev.

A video released by Russian media shows an apartment building engulfed in flames at night, watched by residents gathered across the street.

On the front line, the Russian army said Sunday they had captured two small villages in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The claim has not yet been independently verified.

One of them, Vasiutynske, is about 10 kilometres (six miles) from the city of Kramatorsk, a Ukrainian urban and logistical hub.

– Zelensky defends strikes –

Zelensky, in his evening address on Sunday, defended Ukraine’s responses to Russia’s attacks — including strikes on oil refineries, air-defence systems and radar stations — as “truly just responses”.

“The Russian war will be increasingly felt at home, in Russia,” he said.

On Thursday, United Nations chief Antonio Guterres condemned both sides for their repeated attacks on civilian areas.

“Attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure are a clear violation of international humanitarian law, and must stop immediately,” he said.

The Russian invasion, which began four and a half years ago, continues with prospects of a peace agreement largely stalled.

World.title: Como sign England defender Chalobah from Chelsea
World.content:
Milan – Como have completed the signing of England centre-back Trevoh Chalobah from Chelsea for a reported fee of 30 million euros ($34.5 million), the Serie A club announced Sunday.

The 27-year-old has penned a five-year deal with Cesc Fabregas’s ambitious side, who will play in the Champions League for the first time this season.

“I can’t wait to bring my experience to the team, feel the incredible atmosphere at the stadium, and connect with the fans,” said Chalobah, who made 151 appearances for Chelsea.

“I will give my absolute all every single day to make history together.”

Como pipped AC Milan and Juventus to Italy’s fourth and final Champions League place last season.

Scudetto holders Inter Milan had also been heavily linked with a move for Chalobah, before reportedly deciding the asking price was too high.

“Trevoh is an important signing for us and a player who represents the level of ambition we have at this club,” said Como coach Fabregas, a former Chelsea midfielder.

“He is a leader who can raise the level of the team, and I am very happy that he has chosen Como.”

Chalobah was part of the England squad which finished third at the World Cup last month, after receiving a late call-up as a replacement for the injured Tino Livramento.

He could make his Como debut when they visit Udinese in their Serie A opener on August 22.

World.title: 'Our mother tongue is as pure as our mother': Vijay moves Tamil anthem resolution; DMK, AIADMK back it
World.content:
Tamil Thai Vazhthu is an invocation to Mother Tamil from Manonmaniam, a play written by Manonmaniam Sundaranar in 1891. (Photo: PTI)

What does the resolution say?

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday moved a government resolution in the assembly making the rendition of Tamil Thai Vazhthu, the state song, mandatory at the beginning of official programmes across the state.Moving the resolution in the state assembly, Vijay said his Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam government would not compromise on Tamil Nadu's linguistic and cultural rights and urged legislators to set aside political differences in supporting the measure."Our mother tongue is as pure as our mother," Vijay said in an emotive speech, adding that, "Tamil is not only a language but also our life and emotions.""Tamil means pride, Tamil means power. The moment you say 'Tamil', the entire Tamil Nadu will come together and stand as one," he said."Tamil Thai Vazhthu must hold the first place in Tamil Nadu. Giving first place to Tamil Thaai Vaazhthu is our state right," he noted."Saying that Tamil Thai Vazhthu should be sung first does not need to become a political debate," the Tamil nadu CM said, appealing to members across party lines to support the resolution.Under the resolution, Tamil Thai Vazhthu will be sung first at programmes held by educational institutions, universities, government offices, public sector undertakings and other public institutions in Tamil Nadu.The resolution received support from both DMK and AIADMK legislators, with members backing the government's move to mandate the singing of the state song at official functions.The move comes amid a recent advisory from the Union home ministry asking states and Union territories to comply with its January 28 directive on playing Vande Mataram before the National Anthem at official events.It also comes against the backdrop of a July 9 communication from the ministry of home affairs regarding the singing of state songs at official programmes.The resolution describes Tamil Thai Vazhthu as an expression of respect for the Tamil language and culture and links its mandatory rendition to the linguistic and cultural rights guaranteed under the Constitution."Therefore, this House ( Tamil Nadu Assembly ) emphasises that "Tamil Thai Vazhthu" is an expression of respect for the Tamil language and Tamil culture. In accordance with the linguistic and cultural rights guaranteed by the Constitution of India, and with a view to preserving the Cultural identity of Tamil Nadu, the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly unanimously resolves that "Tamil Thai Vazhthu" shall be mandatorily sung first, before the commencement of programmes held by all Educational Institutions, Universities, Government Offices, Public Sector Undertakings and other Public Institutions in Tamil Nadu," the resolution said.The resolution also notes that Tamil is one of the world's oldest classical languages and describes Tamil civilisation as one of the world's oldest cultural traditions.Tamil Nadu had first directed that Tamil Thai Vazhthu be sung at the beginning of official functions through a government order issued on November 23, 1970.The state government formally accorded the song the status of the state song on December 12, 2021, making its rendition mandatory at official programmes and institutions across the state.Tamil Thai Vazhthu is an invocation to Mother Tamil from Manonmaniam, a play written by Manonmaniam Sundaranar in 1891.
