World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.title: Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.content:
A Beijing court has ruled in favor of a mother seeking to inherit her late son’s 87 online gaming accounts, selecting the dispute as an example case to provide judges with legal direction on similar future proceedings involving digital assets.

The case, reported Monday by the People’s Court Daily, a newspaper affiliated with China’s Supreme People’s Court, involved the inheritance rights to the accounts of an avid gamer surnamed Gu, who passed away last year at 36 due to oral cancer.

With China’s internet penetration rate reaching 80.1% by the end of 2025, the case comes as the country faces increasing pressure to handle the growing volume of digital assets left behind by deceased users.

Since China’s Civil Code — which states that digital assets are protected by law — took effect in 2021, courts have increasingly recognized the property value of digital assets. In 2025, the Supreme People’s Court created a separate case category for disputes involving data and online virtual property.

Between 2010 and 2021, Gu registered accounts on games by Chinese game developer Changyou, acquiring valuable in-game assets due to having “built up the accounts” over the years, according to the report.

After Gu’s passing, his mother, surnamed Chen, asked the company to transfer the accounts into her name so she could sell them to help cover her living expenses, as she relied on a low income and no family support.

The company denied her request, however, citing their user agreement, which states that it retains ownership of all account-related data, including account information, game characters, virtual items, and in-game currency.

Chen then sued the company. In April, the Beijing Shijingshan District People’s Court ruled that although ownership of the accounts rested with the company, the accounts had independent economic value because Gu had invested time, effort, and money in them. As a result, the court found that the right of use of the accounts, though not their ownership, could be inherited.

The court ordered the company to complete the transfer of the accounts’ real-name registration to Chen within 15 days after the ruling took effect. Chen is the sole legal heir to the accounts, as Gu’s daughter waived her inheritance rights.

Many online platforms prohibit account transfers or inheritance. But platforms’ user agreements cannot override a user’s legal inheritance rights, Zhang Yingzhou, the judge presiding over the case, told local media.

“Heirs inherit the economic interests attached to the right to use an account, not ownership of the account itself,” the judge said.

Other incidents related to the transfer of digital assets have made headlines in China recently, including a case related to the recycling of popular Chinese-American singer Coco Lee’s phone number by her telecom operator after she committed suicide in 2023.

In 2025, a user who registered for domestic music streaming platform NetEase with a newly purchased mobile phone number was inadvertently logged into Lee’s verified artist account. NetEase explained that the phone number originally linked to Lee’s account had been reassigned to a new user without unbinding the account link to NetEase. The incident sparked widespread discussion on domestic social media about digital privacy, account security, and the management of digital assets after death.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.title: The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.content:
JIANGSU, East China — “We are looking for a factory that can produce acrylic mahjong tiles.”

Hua Fangyi repeated that pitch at nearly 30 factories in Taixing, a city in eastern China’s Jiangsu province known for manufacturing mahjong tiles. “Almost every factory refused,” she says.

After quitting her job to start an export business last October, Hua, 28, spotted a surge in overseas demand for American mahjong. Believing the opportunity might last only a few months, she planned to test the market with just a few dozen sets.

But Taixing’s factories were built for large runs of traditional Chinese mahjong, not the small batches of brightly colored acrylic tiles overseas buyers wanted. Some produced only conventional melamine sets; others required minimum orders far beyond what Hua could afford.

Then Hua found a factory with 20 American mahjong sets in stock. She bought the entire batch, and it sold out almost immediately.

Within months, she had built a company shipping more than 5,000 sets a month and generating roughly $400,000 in monthly sales. Across Taixing, factories that had once turned away from American mahjong were now chasing the same overseas buyers.

“Almost every factory is now making American mahjong,” Hua says.

The shift came as rising material costs and intensifying competition squeezed margins on traditional sets. Overseas demand offered higher returns, prompting established factories to buy equipment, hire workers, and adapt their production lines to the elaborate designs sought by American buyers.

The opportunity has also drawn a new generation of entrepreneurs to Taixing: former tech workers, salespeople, and export traders hoping to manufacture the tiles and build brands of their own.

Together, they are all betting on a boom whose limits remain unclear. For now, overseas orders have given Taixing’s mahjong industry fresh momentum, sending an old manufacturing center racing to master a game it barely recognized a year ago.

Follow the dots

Growing up around her family’s garment factory and later working in international e-commerce at Alibaba, Hua had experience with both manufacturing and overseas sales. She began searching for products that could find a market abroad.

She continued using the habits she developed in product operations, tracking trends on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook and monitoring sales performance on overseas independent websites. American mahjong stood out.

The game itself, however, has a long history in the U.S. The governing body for American mahjong, the National Mah Jongg League, was founded in 1937 with 32 members; it now has more than 350,000 members and publishes a new card of official hands and rules each year.

More recently, American brands such as Oh My Mahjong have helped recast mahjong tiles as colorful, premium lifestyle products, while influencers and social clubs have brought the game to younger players seeking in-person connection.

In April 2026, review platform Yelp reported that U.S. searches for mahjong clubs had jumped 4,467% between September 2024 and August 2025, compared with the previous 12 months. Oh My Mahjong’s sets now sell for $350 to $475, with most priced around $400 — versus the roughly 100 yuan ($15) many Chinese sets sell for in China on e-commerce platform Taobao.

But Hua initially expected the opportunity to be short-lived. Without historical data on American mahjong, she looked to previous domestic product cycles, which often peaked around specific festivals. She expected demand to surge around Christmas, just two months after she first spotted the trend.

Moving quickly to find a supplier, Hua and her father, who runs the family’s garment factory, drove several hundred kilometers from Ningbo, in neighboring Zhejiang province, to Taixing.

But many workshops had no obvious signs and appeared on maps only under broad categories such as “entertainment products.” From the road, little revealed what was being made inside.

Hua struggled to understand the local dialect, so her father asked residents and security guards where they could find factory owners. “We’d only know we’d found the right place after spotting a set or two of mahjong tiles,” she says. “They’d point us to a building and a floor, and we’d keep looking until we found the boss.”

The industry was all around them. A search for “mahjong” on Qichacha, a Chinese corporate database, returns nearly 180 businesses in Taixing, many of them small workshops specializing in a single stage of production.

The cluster grew from a household trade dating to the 1980s, when local families cut and polished tiles by hand from bamboo and ox bone. Over time, production split among specialized workshops handling tile blanks, engraving, polishing, printing, and packaging.

“If one family made money from it, the neighbors would learn too,” says Zhu Ronggen, whose father was among Taixing’s earliest mahjong makers. “One person taught another, and slowly the whole village started making mahjong.”

Zhu grew up inside that manufacturing network. After studying mechanical engineering, he returned to Taixing in 2015 and opened his own factory. By the following year, he was producing traditional sets for China’s domestic market.

So when a customer first asked him to make an American set, Zhu, now 48, assumed it would be a minor variation on a familiar product.

“Chinese mahjong designs have barely changed for decades,” Zhu says. “American mahjong is completely different. A circle tile could be a football or a bunch of grapes. One grape stands for one dot, and nine grapes represent nine dots.”

American sets also include Arabic numerals and joker tiles, while familiar symbols are constantly reworked around seasonal themes and customers’ ideas. Summer collections feature seashells and aquatic plants; Christmas designs use Santa hats and trees.

And while traditional Chinese sets are usually molded from melamine in a narrow range of colors, American buyers prefer acrylic tiles with richer palettes, sometimes built from six or seven colored layers visible along the edge.

“Every customer wants their own concept,” Zhu says. “The color palettes are also much richer than those used in China.”

Chinese players, he says, tend to value weight, legibility, and how the tiles feel in the hand. American buyers, by contrast, want sets distinctive enough to display and expressive enough to reflect their tastes.

“I gradually understood that they weren’t just buying mahjong to play mahjong,” Zhu says. “A lot of the time, they’re buying a lifestyle.”

Factory reset

Inside Zhu’s factory, traditional Chinese mahjong and its American reinvention sit side by side. Dust-covered melamine slabs are stacked near the entrance, while baskets of brightly colored acrylic tiles and export cartons crowd the corridors beyond.

By 4 p.m., Zhu is usually outside the workshop, surrounded by cardboard boxes as he seals packages and confirms overseas delivery addresses with couriers. He moves between the packing area and loading site until sunset.

After the workers leave, he returns to his office to answer inquiries that accumulated during the afternoon. His wife stays at the UV printer, often working until midnight.

At 7 a.m. the next day, Zhu unlocks the factory gate and starts again.

For years, inquiries from new buyers came weeks or even months apart. Orders from Zhu’s long-term domestic clients remained steady, but rising material costs and intensifying competition had squeezed profits. To keep costs down, he and his wife took on work once handled by employees.

Now, he receives dozens of inquiries every day — from foreign trade companies, Amazon sellers, independent online retailers, and buyers on Alibaba.

“I used to make just 20 sets of American mahjong a year,” he says. “Now, I can turn out 200 sets a day.”

Unlike traditional Chinese sets, which can be reproduced using fixed molds, each American order requires new adjustments to engraving, printing, and coloring. A batch of 300 to 400 acrylic sets takes 15 to 20 days to complete — three to five days longer than the same number of Chinese sets.

“People buy them the way they buy clothes,” Zhu says. “What’s fashionable this year may be completely different next year.”

To keep up, Zhu has invested another 1 million yuan ($148,000) in laser engravers, UV printers, and other equipment. But he has hired only two or three additional workers, leaving his family to absorb much of the extra labor.

At the center of the workshop, a giant white sack hangs above a mound of acrylic tiles. Zhu’s parents, both in their 80s, sit on opposite sides of the pile, lifting the pieces one by one and arranging them into neat rows, every face turned in the same direction. Their hands move with a steady, practiced rhythm.

They work from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., the same hours as the factory’s other employees.

“I can do 100 sets a day,” Zhu’s father says. “Workers’ wages aren’t cheap. At least the two of us can save a few hundred yuan.”

A few steps away, Jin Guihua, 62, sorts black tiles before they are colored. Their engraved patterns are barely visible against the dark surface, so she lifts each rack toward the window, tilting it until the light catches the shallow lines.

She scans the rows for matching designs, tapping each selected tile against the edge of the table before setting it aside. Sometimes she checks more than five tiles before finding the next match.

Jin once sorted about 150 sets a day. The smaller tiles and changing patterns of American mahjong have reduced her output to about 60.

“The designs are more complicated and harder to identify,” she says.

Brand new

This past March, five young entrepreneurs arrived in Taixing to start a mahjong business.

A few minutes from Zhu’s family-run factory, they turned a village house into a workshop. Machines occupied the ground floor; their bedrooms were upstairs. There were no fixed hours or weekends.

Between them, the five had experience in sales, technology, and international trade. None had ever made a mahjong tile.



Li Mingzhi, 30, leads the venture, which operates under the name SenJoy Mahjong. A former Alibaba employee, he saw American mahjong as a chance to sell a higher-value product overseas. He recruited his former colleague Wang Hao, his younger brother, and several childhood friends from northwestern China’s Gansu province to build the venture.

“I never imagined I’d move to such a remote village to start a business,” says Wang, 28.

Zhu estimates that nearly 30 new factories have sprung up in Taixing over the past year as entrepreneurs rush into American mahjong. The town’s fragmented supply chain has allowed outsiders to enter without building a factory from scratch.

“Here, you don’t need to build an entire production line yourself,” Li tells Sixth Tone. “You can outsource each step and focus on design and branding.”

In practice, however, the workshop became a crash course in manufacturing.

“Every day is unpredictable,” Li says. “Customers can call at any time, and problems can emerge at every stage — production, design, communication, quality inspection. Working until 3 or 4 a.m. is normal.”

The new equipment offered precision but no ready-made solution for mahjong production: sizes varied, hand-cut pieces did not match machine-cut ones, and every fault required another round of testing.

“Almost every step brought a different problem,” Wang says.

The UV printer proved especially difficult. Each design had to be aligned by hand, and a shift of just 1 millimeter could push the ink outside the engraved lines.

The night before Sixth Tone’s visit, all five stayed up until 3 a.m. trying to solve the problem. “Before entering the industry, I thought making mahjong would be simple,” says Wang. “Once I started, I realized American sets are closer to handicrafts.”

Despite the setbacks, the team produced and sold about 1,000 sets in its first few months, generating roughly 230,000 yuan in sales. Its customers included businesses selling on Amazon.

Li put 1.5 million yuan of his own savings into the venture. “Based on our current orders,” says Li, “we expect the business to recover that investment within six months.”

To avoid becoming another contract manufacturer in Taixing’s crowded supply chain, the team began working with outside designers to develop original sets. It also launched an independent website and overseas social media accounts.

“For us, building a brand starts with original design,” Li says. “We might become the first company in Taixing — and perhaps one of the first in China — to build a real mahjong brand instead of simply manufacturing for others.”

The team hopes to reach buyers directly through social media, influencers, online sellers, and brick-and-mortar retailers.

Their bestseller uses a coral-reef theme. Against a shimmering blue base, coral motifs represent bamboo tiles, shells stand in for circles, and small fish serve as jokers.

“As long as the designs aren’t ugly, we’re not worried about sales,” Li says. “Right now, demand far exceeds supply.”

Wang is more cautious. Today’s buyers, he says, remain a relatively small group with strong spending power. If American mahjong reaches a broader market, more manufacturers will follow, he says, adding: “Price wars are unavoidable.”

Hua, one of the first Chinese traders to bet on American mahjong, has watched competitors multiply within months.

When she launched the business, Hua handled every part of the operation herself, often staying up late to respond to customers in the U.S. and sleeping as little as two hours a night. Today, her Ningbo-based company employs about 10 people and provides customer service around the clock.

But the market that once seemed wide open has become more crowded. Designs that once sold out quickly are now easier to source, and more suppliers are competing for the same orders.

“The conversion rate isn’t as good as before,” Hua says. Her sales data show that fewer visitors become inquiries, and fewer inquiries turn into confirmed orders.

“The profit margins were much higher in the beginning, but now they have dropped significantly,” she says. “I think this is probably an inevitable stage for any viral product.”

She, too, has started developing designs of her own.

Last month, she began experimenting with AI to create early concepts before working with freelance designers to refine them. Her first ideas included themes inspired by witches, tennis, flowers, and Christmas.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Workers sort uncarved and unpainted mahjong tiles at Zhu Ronggen’s factory in Taixing, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.
