During expanded talks with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the two sides discussed their strategic partnership, trade, energy, transport, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Bayramov reiterated the need for an early end to the fighting and a diplomatic settlement based on international law, while reaffirming Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

He said Azerbaijan’s total humanitarian assistance to Ukraine had exceeded 50 million US dollars. Bayramov also highlighted reconstruction projects in Irpin and rehabilitation programmes for children.

During his meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the discussions focused on Russian attacks, the situation in the Black Sea, the disruption of grain export routes, defence cooperation, and cooperation in the energy, oil and gas, and agricultural sectors.

Zelensky thanked Azerbaijan for its energy and humanitarian assistance, as well as for maintaining constructive dialogue. Bayramov, in turn, spoke about the post-conflict situation in the South Caucasus and reconstruction efforts in the territories regained by Azerbaijan.

As part of his official visit to Ukraine 🇺🇦, FM of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Kyiv.



The Minister met with the Embassy staff and received a comprehensive briefing on the Mission’s activities. pic.twitter.com/UPqN5Hn9rx — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

At a joint press conference, particular attention was drawn to Bayramov’s remarks on possible gas supplies: “If the need arises, we will be ready to supply gas to our friendly Ukraine.”

He highlighted SOCAR’s long-standing presence on the Ukrainian market, as well as the importance of Ukraine’s underground gas storage system – the largest in Europe – for regional energy security.

The statement can be seen as signalling Azerbaijan’s willingness to contribute to the diversification of Ukraine’s energy supplies, while also supporting alternative routes for Caspian gas exports to Europe. Against the backdrop of Russia’s strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Ukraine, Baku’s offer also underscores the importance of competition and diversification in the energy sector.

During meetings with Kyrylo Budanov and Ihor Klymenko, the sides also discussed regional and international security, as well as prospects for energy cooperation. They reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders.

Expert: “Azerbaijan will continue to provide Ukraine with political, economic and humanitarian support”

lkhan Shahinoglu, head of the Atlas Research Centre and a political commentator considered close to the Azerbaijani authorities, wrote that the visit is being closely watched by Russia:

The Kremlin will closely monitor Jeyhun Bayramov’s meetings in Kyiv. Azerbaijan’s partnership with any country is an exclusive sovereign right, and no other state has the right to interfere in that process.

At the same time, Russia, which is waging a war of conquest against Ukraine, closely watches those who cooperate with Kyiv. President Ilham Aliyev‘s response to the same question from Ukrainian journalist Gordon, asked at the Shusha Global Media Forum two years in a row – that ‘Ukraine should not reconcile itself to occupation’ – angered chauvinistic circles in Russia. They believe Azerbaijan should accept the annexation of Crimea and the occupation of Ukrainian territories.

Just as Jeyhun Bayramov visited Moscow some time ago, he has now travelled to Kyiv. Ukraine is Azerbaijan’s partner, and Baku will continue to provide it with political, economic and humanitarian support.”

World.title: Giga Avaliani case: Two more arrested 10 months after Georgian teacher’s murder
World.content:
Two more arrested in Giga Avaliani murder case

Two more suspects have been identified in the high-profile murder case of a 28-year-old teacher in Georgia. On 5 August 2026, two teenage girls – Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili – were arrested.

Giga Avaliani, a mathematics teacher, was killed in October 2025. Five people have already been convicted over his murder, while the trial of a sixth defendant is still under way. With the arrest of the two girls, the total number of suspects in the case has risen to eight – all of them minors.

The arrests of Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili, after several convictions had already been secured, mark an unexpected and significant development in the Giga Avaliani case.

Nia Imnadze was one of Giga Avaliani’s former students and the girlfriend of the principal defendant, Aleksandre Gabashvili. Prosecutors accuse her of incitement to commit the crime.

According to local media, Anastasia Beruashvili is a friend of both Nia Imnadze and another convicted defendant, Giorgi Rikadze. She has been charged with failing to report the crime.

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics tutor, was returning home late on 1 October 2025 when he was attacked outside his apartment building. He fell into a coma following the assault and died on 24 October without regaining consciousness. Investigators say the attack was motivated by jealousy and what they describe as “unwanted communication with a girl”. The defendants have given a similar account. According to their version of events, Avaliani sent sexually explicit messages to his student Nia Imnadze, who told her boyfriend, prompting him to confront the teacher. Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, rejects that account. She says Nia had been skipping lessons and that Avaliani informed the girl’s mother, angering the student. According to Kupatadze, the attack was planned afterwards.

The Giga Avaliani case has become one of Georgia’s most high-profile criminal cases in recent years. Much of the public attention surrounding it has been driven by Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, who campaigned for what she said should be a thorough and impartial investigation. Her efforts also helped generate significant public pressure over the handling of the case.

From the outset, Kupatadze maintained that Nia Imnadze bore primary responsibility for what had happened and repeatedly called for her arrest. The recent detention of the two girls has therefore raised new questions.

But the key question remains: if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, why were the two girls not arrested earlier? Was their detention the result of new evidence, or did it come only after sustained public pressure and Eka Kupatadze’s campaign?

Detention of two girls

Both girls were arrested late on the night of 5 August, in what appeared to be coordinated operations. News of the arrests first emerged through a video of Nia Imnadze’s detention, which was released by her lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili.

The footage is deeply distressing. It shows a large number of police officers arriving at Nia’s home. Her mother, visibly distressed, pounds on the front door, shouting: “Come in, all of you!”, “Maniacs!”, “Murderers!”, “Do you know that Niako is innocent?!”

The girl’s father, meanwhile, tells the police: “You are going to make me do something the whole of Georgia will be talking about. If you treat my child so unjustly, I will do it.”

Police officers try to calm the distraught parents.

“Why are you taking my child? On what grounds? What does the court order say?!” the mother asks.

“The lawyer has reviewed the court order,” one of the officers replies.

“Giorgi, on what grounds are they arresting her?” the mother asks the lawyer.

“On the basis of a court order containing only formal wording, nothing specific,” the lawyer replies.

Nia sits in the hallway on a sofa, curled up with her face buried in her hands. The video is being filmed by her lawyer, who occasionally strokes her hair.

Shortly after the video was released, reports began circulating on social media that the second girl, Anastasia Beruashvili, had also been detained. No footage of her arrest was made public, but the Ministry of Internal Affairs later confirmed that she had been taken into custody.

During her arrest, Nia Imnadze became unwell and was taken to hospital, where she spent the night. On 6 August, she was transferred to a pre-trial detention centre. Anastasia Beruashvili was also taken there.

Minors charged in Giga Avaliani's murder case in Georgia – read more Five people have already been convicted in connection with Giga Avaliani’s murder: Aleksandre Gabashvili – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. He was the principal defendant in the case and was found guilty of organising a group assault and intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm as part of a group, resulting in the victim’s death. Giorgi Rikadze – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. A friend of Aleksandre Gabashvili, he was convicted on the same charges. Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Odesa in summer 2026: Life between sea and war. VIDEO
World.content:
Beaches, bomb-damaged homes and explosions in broad daylight. In the summer of 2026, Odesa is caught between its traditional seaside resort atmosphere and the constant threat of Russian attacks. While some people relax by the sea and stroll through the city centre, others sift through the rubble left by the latest strike.

JAMnews visited Odesa to show what life in the city looks like today.

Odesa and the surrounding region remain frequent targets of Russian strikes. Residential neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and port facilities have all come under attack.

Russia has carried out combined attacks using drones and missiles, seeking to overwhelm Ukraine‘s air defence systems.

The impact of these attacks is visible across the city. Residential buildings have been damaged, windows blown out and flats destroyed. Strikes have also hit Odesa’s historic centre, including heritage buildings and universities.

Ports in Odesa Region, along with the logistics hubs and warehouses that support them, are also regularly targeted. Attacks on port infrastructure have disrupted Ukraine’s transport network and Black Sea export routes.

The strikes often occur in broad daylight, when the streets are busy, cafés and shops are open, and beaches are filled with residents and visitors. At any moment, the familiar sounds of the city can be interrupted by explosions, air defence fire or the buzz of attack drones.

On several occasions, missiles have been intercepted directly over the coastline while beaches were crowded with people.

Today, it is possible to spend the day at the beach and the night in a bomb shelter.

World.title: “Russia’s annexation of Georgia’s regions would not go unanswered” – embassies on 18th anniversary of August war
World.content:
France, Germany, Italy, Britain: Russia’s annexation of Georgia

France, Germany, Italy and the UK issued a joint statement marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 Russo-Georgian war, reaffirming their support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

18 years after the Russian aggression, we reaffirm our full support to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Georgia within its internationally recognized borders. We welcome Republic of Naoero’s decision to withdraw its recognition of the so-called independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

We urge states that have established diplomatic relations with these entities to follow this example,” the statement said.

August 7, 2026 marks 18 years since the start of the Russo-Georgian war over South Ossetia. In the 2008 war, 412 Georgian military personnel and civilians were killed, along with 365 people on the Ossetian side. Some 20,000 ethnic Georgians were displaced. Georgia also lost control of 125 more villages in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia is recognized by Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

August 7, 2026 marks 18 years since the start of the Russo-Georgian war over South Ossetia. In the 2008 war, 412 Georgian military personnel and civilians were killed, along with 365 people on the Ossetian side. Some 20,000 ethnic Georgians were displaced. Georgia also lost control of 125 more villages in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). The independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia is recognized by Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

France, Germany, Italy and the UK condemned Russia’s military presence in Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

ЭWe reiterate our condemnation of Russia’s ongoing military presence in the occupied breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia in violation of international law as well as Russia’s obligations under the six-point agreement of 12 August 2008.

Russia’s ongoing militarization of Georgia’s occupied territories poses a serious threat to the security of Georgia and to regional and European stability,” France, Germany, Italy and the UK said.

The statement also referred to rulings by the European Court of Human Rights.

In October 2025, the court found Russia responsible for a number of violations in the occupied regions, including the use of excessive force, ill-treatment, unlawful detention and restrictions on movement between Georgian-controlled territory and areas occupied by Russia.

“We urge Russia to implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights relating to this situation and to fully fulfil the commitments it made on August 12 and September 8, 2008,” the statement said.

The four countries also expressed concern over recent developments in South Ossetia.

They said the so-called “Agreement on Deepening Alliance and Cooperation,” signed by Moscow and the de facto authorities in South Ossetia on May 9, 2026, further violates Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and is incompatible with international law.

“This is a clear violation of international law. This document, as well as the appointment of a Russian citizen to head the region raise concerns on a possible full-fledged annexation of the region, which would not go unanswered,” the statement said.

Support for the Geneva International Discussions, co-chaired by the EU, OSCE and UN, was reaffirmed.

They said it is the only format that allows the parties to work towards a peaceful resolution of the conflict.

The statement also stressed the importance of the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia and said its work would continue to be supported in the future.

News in Georgia

World.title: Coalition calls on Albanese to apologise to Japan's PM over melon gesture
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing pressure to apologise to his Japanese counterpart over a gesture he made about two melons she gifted him, which his office insists was not a crude joke.

In an interview last month, Mr Albanese gestured to his chest when recalling the melons during an exchange with Bush Deep podcast host Nikki Osborne, who asked how the fruit had been smuggled into the country.

The incident resurfaced this morning after former Australian ambassador Shingo Yamagami criticised the exchange in The Australian, labelling it "insulting", ignorant and a betrayal of the "close relationship" between Australia and Japan.

Anthony Albanese is facing backlash from another gaffe during his appearance on the Bush Deep podcast last month. (Supplied: YouTube)

The former Ambassador suggested Mr Albanese was making a quip about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's body, but a spokesperson for Mr Albanese told The Australian, "this assertion is wrong".

The comment has not been supplied to the ABC despite multiple requests.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was beneath the office of the prime minister, and demanded Mr Albanese apologise.

"They were insulting, and the prime minister should make a personal apology. He's done it through a statement. I mean, the hypocrisy of Labor and the foreign minister on this topic," Mr Taylor said.

Angus Taylor has called on Anthony Albanese to apologise. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The gaffe occurred during the same podcast that landed Mr Albanese in hot water when he said he would shag Kylie Minogue during a game of "shag, marry, date". He later apologised for those comments.

While Mr Albanese was condemned by several female parliamentarians at the time, including Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson, the main focus was on Minogue and not Ms Takaichi.

Liberal Deputy Leader Jane Hume added to the criticism, calling the comments "grubby" and "inappropriate".

Labor ministers defend PM

Senior cabinet ministers have again been forced to defend Mr Albanese's appearance on the podcast.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek today deflected criticisms and disagreed with Mr Yamagami's interpretation.

PM apologises for shag comment Anthony Albanese made the comments during a game of "shag, marry, date" on the Bush Deep podcast.

"We have an excellent relationship with Japan. Japan is a very important strategic and economic partner … and I think the former ambassador is wrong in his interpretation," she told Sunrise.

Health Minister Mark Butler reiterated Australia's strong economic and security ties with Japan.

"It's very close. It involves constant communication between our two countries, two at the highest level. I know Prime Minister Albanese feels the deepest respect for that relationship," he told reporters.

The federal Transport Minister Catherine King argued the comments were being blown up by the opposition.

Comments 'unfortunate' but not Japan's primary concern

While officials may have winced in private, nobody in the Japanese government has publicly commented about Mr Albanese's gaffe.

Ms Takaichi's first visit in May solidified Australia's place as a critical energy partner for Japan, and an increasingly important security partner as well.

When the episode first came out, officials in the Japanese government told the ABC they were not focused on the exchange and that Tokyo would not comment on a minor episode, particularly given the scale of cooperation between the two countries.

The episode has also drawn little attention so far in the Japanese press, aside from one scathing opinion piece in the English-language Japan Times which lambasted Mr Albanese and accused him of rank sexism.

Shingo Yamagami says it shows cultural ignorance and is insulting to the partnership between Japan and Australia. (Perth USAsia Centre: Kelly Pilgrim-Byrne)

But one member of the Australian business community with close links to Japan said the exchange "had absolutely not gone unnoticed" among Japanese elites, even if they were publicly silent about it.

In his criticism, Mr Yamagami pointed out that Ms Takaichi has already copped sexist and derogatory attacks from Chinese state media, but it was not expected from Japan's strategic partner.

Innuendo aside, the former diplomat also highlights that Mr Albanese's comments ignore the cultural significance of crown melons, which are intensely cultivated luxury fruits in Japan.

Australia and Japan sign agreements on energy, defence and critical minerals Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Japanese counterpart Takaichi Sanae agreed to bolster cooperation on energy, defence and critical minerals.

In the face of an "increasingly dangerous" geopolitical climate, he urged the prime minister to show greater focus.

"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.

Mr Yamagami had a fraught relationship with Labor when he was in Canberra and was particularly angry when Foreign Minister Penny Wong urged him, while she was still in opposition, to pull back his public criticisms of China.

World.title: What have we learnt from Origin Energy's data breach?
World.content:
Three weeks ago, Origin Energy told 900,000 former and current customers that their information had been exposed in a data breach.

The major cybersecurity data leak made headlines and raised the alarm that the threats were becoming more prevalent.

It also showed that anyone with their information online could be vulnerable, according to Curtin University Associate Professor in AI and Cybersecurity, Mihai Lazarescu.

"There is no such thing as 100 per cent security," he said.

Associate Professor Lazarescu, who has worked in cybersecurity for over 16 years, said whenever anyone put information online, there was a chance it could be compromised.

That included commonly used details, such as email addresses and first and last names.

"Never give your full name and date of birth because that is identifiable evidence," he said.

How did Origin Energy compare to Australia's biggest data breaches?

Origin's breach affected hundreds of thousands of customers, but it wasn't technically the largest.

Australian companies such as Canva, Optus, and Qantas had data breaches that affected millions of customers.

Canva Read more Australian online design tool Canva suffered a data breach impacting 137 million of its users in 2019. A cybercriminal identified as Ghosticplayers breached Canva's defences but was stopped by Canva when it detected malicious activity in its systems.

Access to usernames, real names, email addresses, country data, encrypted passwords and partial payment data of users was leaked. Latitude Read more In March 2023, Latitude, the Australian personal loan and financial service provider, was affected by a data breach that impacted more than 14 million people from Australia and New Zealand. The Latitude breach was one of Australia's largest breaches in recent history.

The attack occurred when one set of employee credentials was stolen, allowing access to Latitude's customer data, including full names, physical addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, driver's licence numbers and passport numbers.

Much of the information was data stored from 2005, which drew questions on why companies continue to store customer records beyond the required seven-year time frame. Optus Read more In September 2022, the Optus data breach impacted 9.8 million customers. The security incident brought up questions about Australian data security policies and how companies handled them.

Cybercriminals believed to be working for a state-sponsored operation breached Optus's internal network, compromising personal information and impacting up to 9.8 million customers, almost 40 per cent of the population.

Personal data included names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, passport information, driver's license numbers, government ID numbers, medical records & Medicare card ID numbers. Medibank Read more In December 2022, Medibank, the Australian health insurance giant, was the victim of a data breach affecting the personal details of 9.7 million customers. The attack was believed to be linked to a well-known ransomware group based in Russia, the REvil ransomware gang.

The privacy breach was first discovered when REvil posted on a dark web blog a folder that contained 6GB of raw data samples, indicating that they had larger amounts of data to release, and demanded a $10 million ransom. The data included names, birthdates, passport numbers, medical claims data, and medical records. Qantas Read more In July 2025, up to 6 million Qantas customers were affected when the Australian airline confirmed a data theft incident that impacted a significant portion of its customer base. Data compromised included names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and frequent flyer numbers.

The breach was reportedly attributed to a cyber attack targeting the airline's call centre. Origin Read more In July 2026, Origin Energy, Australia's largest energy retailer with more than 4.8 million customers, announced that the information of 900,000 current and former customers was accessed during a data security breach. The energy provider confirmed it first became aware of a potential security threat in early July but initially did not believe it credible.

The company said it was still working to determine the total number of people affected and would notify impacted customers.

While there is no indication full payment card details were compromised, experts say the stolen information remains highly valuable and are urging affected customers to remain cautious about unsolicited emails, text messages and phone calls long after the breach.

The information included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, home addresses and email addresses, as well as the last four digits of some credit cards and the last three digits of some bank account numbers.

What does the Origin breach reveal about cybersecurity?

Associate Professor Lazarescu said the fact that a power company was potentially breached should have been expected, given how easy data could be accessed online.

"It will get worse," he said.

"99 per cent of people have no understanding of how difficult it is to protect data.

"It requires both the technical and administrative aspects of security to be perfect."

He said the only way to be fully protected online was to be "checking all the time", from bank statements to which information was given online.

Recent data from the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) showed most of the leaked customer information in data breaches included contact details, financial details and identity information.

Associate Professor Lazarescu said social media was also one of the easiest ways for criminals to access data.

"You see people posting online with photos with specific locations, timing. These are not secure," he said.

"When you have criminal groups that are very well organised and make a lot of money out of what they do, these are not beginners.

" I've seen groups that were based in Europe where there were 11-year-olds coding. "

Associate Professor Lazarescu said having data leaked could not only put people at risk of being hacked but, in worst-case scenarios, their data could be sold on the dark web to criminal groups.

"It could create a situation that's expensive and complicated to fix," he said.

He said serious discussion should be taking place that outlined to customers what the risks of data leaking could entail and the potential consequences if security measures failed.

Hidden costs of data leaks

The severity of a data breach depends on the sensitivity of the data and the nature of the exposure, rather than just the total number of people affected.

Charles Sturt University computing professor Yeslam Al-Saggaf said the Origin data breach was "more concerning" than the Canva breach, despite fewer customers being affected.

"The value of data is low as these students don't have credit cards, don't have car loans, mortgages, and don't have driver's licences," Professor Al-Saggaf said.

Origin Energy confirms hack Energy company Origin has confirmed that there has been unauthorised access and disclosure of some customers' data, a day after it announced it was investigating a "potential" breach.

"Whereas in the Origin data breach financial details of individuals and businesses have been compromised."

He said when individuals' and businesses' financial details were published online, it exposed them to a range of risks, such as losing money through payment redirection attacks and identity theft.

He said businesses and individuals could also face a situation with additional costs and an increase in insurance premiums.

Cyber insurance providers have noted the increase in cyber-attacks and, in turn, are raising premiums.

According to a 2025 report by the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Australian Cyber Security Centre responded to 1,200 cybersecurity incidents in the last financial year, an 11 per cent increase.

The average self-reported cost of a cyber incident for a small business had risen to 14 per cent, while medium businesses have seen a 55 per cent increase.

Cyber-hacking number one cause of data breaches

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) received 1,205 data breach notifications in the 2025 calendar year, representing an 8 per cent increase from 2024, according to OAIC data.

Cyber hacking remains the primary cause of data breaches reported to the OAIC.

Of the data breaches notified in 2025, the majority were attributable to malicious or criminal activity.

Health service providers were the most commonly affected, accounting for 19 per cent of the total.

How can we protect our data from being leaked?

The Australian government said it had revised its cybersecurity policies to strengthen resilience against nation-state threat actors amid the rise in cyber attacks.

In 2025, the OAIC launched a new Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) statistics dashboard to keep the public informed on the volume and type of data breaches occurring.

Professor Al-Saggaf said "people are becoming numb to the drama of data breaches", and people who remained naive to cybersecurity were most at risk.

"They happen every day in Australia because Australians are trusting, affluent, speak English, and some are not technically savvy," he said.

"We need to improve our literacy with respect to cybersecurity hygiene practices."

AI has changed what criminals can do with your stolen Origin data The theft of names, addresses and phone numbers may seem less serious than stolen bank details, but cyber experts say AI is changing what criminals can do with that information.

He advised using a strong, unique password that differed for each account, or using a password manager, to help protect individuals.

He said enabling multi-factor authentication could provide an additional layer of verification, and using secure payment methods on secure websites could also help avoid potential security risks.

But as scammers started to integrate artificial intelligence into their operations, he warned regular security measures would need to be strengthened.

"AI is going to make impersonation more sophisticated, so use more than one method to communicate with your close contacts if they ask for financial assistance, and keep an eye on bank balances and credit card statements," he said.

World.title: Former kindergarten cleaner jailed over AI-produced child abuse material
World.content:
A Mildura man who possessed thousands of child abuse images, including hundreds he produced himself has been jailed for four-and-a-half years.

The actions of Christopher Rankin, 36, were described as abhorrent during sentencing in the Victorian County Court on Monday.

Rankin offended across an eight-month period at a north-west Victorian home between November 9, 2024 and June 6, 2025.

His offending directly involved five children and six adults known to him, as well as a number of unidentified child victims.

Not isolated or sporadic

The former teacher's aide and kindergarten cleaner was found guilty of possessing a total of 3,638 images and videos of child abuse material.

Almost 3,300 of the files were not created by Rankin, and were described as perverse, depraved and disgusting by Judge Krista Breckweg.

Christopher Rankin, 36, had served 81 days in detention prior to sentencing. (Supplied: Facebook)

Those videos and images related to the sexual abuse of unknown child victims, some as young as one-year-old.

Across the offending period, Rankin himself created more than 350 explicit videos and images, either through covert filming or use of artificial intelligence.

While the material did not feature sexual abuse, it was described as "nevertheless predatory".

The court heard he installed a black covert pinhole camera in a home bathroom in Mildura, producing explicit videos and images of two children known to him.

Christopher Rankin 's moral culpability was described as high. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

He also used AI software to transpose the faces of a total of four children and six women onto the bodies of unknown naked female children and adult women.

Judge Breckweg said the offending was not isolated or sporadic, as there was evidence Rankin had moved the child abuse material files across multiple devices and had encrypted access to them.

A serious sexual offender

Rankin was described as a deviant offender, who was assessed a moderate risk of sexual reoffending.

Judge Breckweg said Rankin's prospects for rehabilitation remained guarded.

She acknowledged the material Rankin possessed on his devices was for personal use, and was not obtained for the purposes of blackmail, revenge or sale.

He was sentenced to a combined total sentence of four-and-a-half years imprisonment, and would be eligible for parole in three years.

Christopher Rankin was arrested on June 5, 2025. (Facebook)

Upon release he will be put on a two-year good behaviour bond, and he will need to complete a sex offender program and alcohol abuse rehabilitation program within two years.

He must also report to Mildura Police Station, and is barred from travelling interstate or overseas without permission.



Rankin also will have lifetime reporting obligations, due to being sentenced as a serious sexual offender.

Judge Breckweg said if he did not enter a guilty plea, Rankin would have been sentenced to six years imprisonment.

World.title: Coal train derails weeks after runaway train incident
World.content:
A coal train has derailed in the NSW Upper Hunter less than two weeks after a runaway unmanned train operated by the same company reached 90 kilometres per hour.

The Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) confirmed it was notified about an incident just before midday.

ARTC was advised the lead wheel, or bogie, of the Pacific National coal train derailed at Ardglen Loop, a stretch of track between the Upper Hunter and Tamworth.

Pacific National has confirmed the incident.

"The incident occurred on the Ardglen loop and has resulted in disruption to rail traffic through the area," a spokesperson said.

"There have been no reports of injuries to the train crew.

The train derailed at Ardglen just before midday on Monday. (ABC News: Peter Sanders)

"The train has been secured and our teams are responding to the incident."

ARTC said the site had been "preserved" pending the arrival of investigators from the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR).

The derailment comes three weeks after an incident involving an unmanned Pacific National train travelling up to 90km/h over 20 kilometres without a driver on board.

The train started moving unmanned before it was stopped several kilometres away. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

An interim report found the three locomotives and 96 wagons reached speeds well over the safe limit on July 25, and only came to a halt after rolling backwards for 5 kilometres.

Last week ONRSR updated its advice about reporting requirements for rail transport operators.

It said "a notifiable occurrence means an accident or incident associated with railway operations that must be reported to ONRSR".

World.title: AGL fined $60k after workers exposed to lead during power plant deactivation
World.content:
Energy giant AGL has been convicted and fined $60,000 after workers were exposed to lead during a decommissioning project at an Adelaide power station.

The company pleaded guilty to failing to comply with a health and safety duty to its employees, after SafeWork SA lodged criminal proceedings over the plant's decommissioning process at the Torrens Island A Power Station.

In 2024, the ABC revealed workers, including AGL employees, had been affected by lead exposure during the works between October 2022 and April 2023.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said testing found five employees had elevated blood lead levels, after the presence of lead was detected in workplace dust.

AGL was sentenced in the South Australian Employment Tribunal on Friday.

SafeWork SA said the exposure occurred when "large quantities of paper insulated lead covered (PILC) cables were required to be de-energised, cut and removed".

AGL says it cooperated fully throughout the process. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The statement said that process involved cutting cables into 1-metre lengths and placing them into drums for disposal.

"The work generated dust and debris, including lead dust," the statement said.

"Workers undertaking the task were provided with personal protective equipment including long sleeves, long pants, boots, safety glasses, hard hats and gloves.

"However, respiratory protection to prevent inhalation of lead dust, such as full-face respirators, was not provided."

Torrens Island lead exposure Sean Gibbons says he started experiencing fatigue, stomach upsets, pins and needles in his legs, and insomnia after helping decommission AGL's Torrens Island power plant.

In his sentencing remarks, Deputy President Judge Miles Crawley said the work "should have been an obvious source of the risk of lead exposure needing to be addressed".

"Risk assessment protocols are only as effective as the way in which they are implemented," he said.

As well as the $60,000 fine, the company was convicted and ordered to pay SafeWork SA's costs of $2,640.

SafeWork SA executive director Glenn Farrell said the case "demonstrates the importance of thorough hazard identification and risk assessment processes for known materials that are known to cause harm".

"Lead exposure remains a significant workplace health risk, particularly during demolition, decommissioning and maintenance activities where hazardous materials may be disturbed," he said.

"Employers must ensure all foreseeable sources of hazardous exposure are identified and appropriate controls are implemented before work begins."

Glenn Farrell says lead exposure is a significant workplace health risk. (Supplied: SafeWork SA)

Mr Farrell said where lead hazards were present, workers must be provided with suitable protective equipment and safe systems of work to minimise exposure.

"Effective safety management depends not only on having systems in place, but on correctly identifying and addressing workplace risks before workers are put in harm's way," he said.

AGL says it 'won't happen again'

In a statement, a spokesperson for AGL said the energy provider had cooperated with all aspects of the investigation and had "taken actions to ensure the event does not happen again".

"Health and safety is a core value of AGL and is an integral part of the way we work," the statement said.

"While we acknowledge that on this occasion AGL fell short of our own standards, the health and safety of our people, both employees and contractors, remains our highest priority."

The spokesman said AGL had updated written procedures to include a new working with lead procedure, hazard identification risk assessments, and is educating employees and contractors.

World.title: Renaming of electorate for Aboriginal leader abandoned after disagreement
World.content:
The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) has abandoned a controversial plan to rename a Tasmanian electorate after an Aboriginal resistance leader.

WARNING: This article contains a depiction of an Aboriginal person who has died

The AEC proposed renaming the electorate of Franklin, which takes in Hobart's eastern shore and southern Tasmania, to Tongerlongeter — an Aboriginal leader and warrior who died in 1837.

The proposed change was canvassed at the same time as the AEC announced an electoral boundary redistribution, which will see more than a quarter of Tasmanians voting in a new electorate.

The AEC said the new boundaries would take effect from the next federal election, but all electorates would retain their current names, including Franklin.

The proposed name change to Tongerlongeter was suggested to honour the Aboriginal resistance leader and warrior who died in 1837. (Watercolour by Thomas Bock, 1832 — British Museum)

"The panel considered the case for the proposed name to be very strong — including Tongerlongeter's strong connection to the area encompassed by the new boundaries of the electorate of Franklin," Australian Electoral Commissioner Jeff Pope said.

Racism inquiry hears from groups A national inquiry into racism, hate and violence towards First Nations people has come to Hobart to hear from the state's Aboriginal groups and people with lived experience of racism.

"However, public submissions not only indicated a level of disagreement among Tasmanian Aboriginal organisations and individuals about the proposed name but also highlighted a broad sentiment that further consultation was required.

"While other name options were put forward — including Mathinna, Rooke and Woureddy — the panel had to reach its final decision based on the evidence and views already received.

" The redistribution process allows no more time for further consultation. "

The boundary changes will see more than a quarter of Tasmanians voting in a new electorate. (Supplied: AEC)

'Makes no sense': TAC reject renaming

The proposal had been criticised by the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC), which said the warrior's name was actually Tukalunginta.

Electoral boundary changes to affect more than 100,000 Tasmanians More than a quarter of Tasmanians will vote in new electorates under a long-awaited boundary redistribution announced by the Australian Electoral Commission.

TAC campaign manager Nala Mansell welcomed the move to abandon the proposal to name the electorate after Tukalunginta, who had resisted British invasion.

"They were fighting against the replacement of an Aboriginal political system that had been in place for thousands of years," she said.

"It makes no sense, for people who fought so fiercely against the establishment of a white political system, to name the same system in their honour."

She said the AEC should have consulted the TAC earlier.

"If the idea is to include Aborigines or acknowledge our ancestors, it's important to give Aborigines the opportunity to discuss it, think about it and provide our feedback," she said.

The AEC had consulted with the public since October last year on the new electoral boundaries, but did not reveal the proposed name change until July 15.

The commission said by that point, it only had seven days for further consultation.

"The panel did seek to engage the various members of the Tasmanian Aboriginal community on the question of the name of the electorate, and a number of organisations and individuals from the Aboriginal community took the opportunity to express their views through a formal submission," Mr Pope said.

"This outreach included contacting the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre before and after a name was proposed, to encourage the TAC to consider making a submission, noting the submissions process is the formal way the panel can receive input under redistribution laws."

The AEC decided any change to electorate names would be best considered at future redistributions, when it could conduct further consultation.

After July's announcement of the name change and new boundaries, the AEC received 272 written submissions.

In their submissions, both the First Peoples (Tasmania) Aboriginal Corporation and Parrdarrama Pungenna Aboriginal Corporation both endorsed the name change to Tongerlongeter.

If the change had gone ahead, it would have been the first time a Tasmanian electorate was named after an Aboriginal person.

World.title: Adelaide waterfalls roar to life as reservoirs receive decade-high deluge
World.content:
Waterfalls in the Adelaide Hills have roared to life as reservoirs in the region received their highest inflows over a 24-hour-period in nearly 10 years.

Lightning, heavy rain and small hail swept over Morialta Conservation Park east of the city at about 2:30pm yesterday, turning its usually gentle waterway into a raging torrent reminiscent of tropical Queensland.

Across the Mount Lofty Ranges, about 18 billion litres was injected into the state's metro reservoir system in the 24 hours to 8am today, according to SA Water, lifting their combined level by 9 per cent to 73 per cent of capacity.

"This was the highest daily volume of combined reservoir inflows since September 2016," Water Futures and Security senior manager Ashley Kingsborough said.

Loading...

He said Mount Bold, the largest reservoir with a capacity of 46.4 gigalitres, received more than 5 billion litres of water, lifting its storage level by 13 per cent to 82 per cent of capacity, with Kangaroo Creek increasing by 19 per cent.

"Relative to the size of their catchments, Little Para and South Para reservoirs were some of the main beneficiaries of this rainfall, with their storage levels increasing by 7 per cent and 10 per cent respectively," Dr Kingsborough said.

More than 71 billion litres of water has flowed into the metro reservoirs since the beginning of winter, leaving them well over the storage holding of 55 per cent at this time last year.

"A wet start to winter laid the groundwork by helping increase soil moisture across our catchments, and we're now seeing the benefit of this on our reservoirs, through the cumulative impact of rainfall events like yesterday," Dr Kingsborough said.

Mount Bold is the biggest of SA Water's primary reservoirs and can hold 46.2 gigalitres. (Supplied: SA Water)

The last time SA Water needed to release water at Mt Bold, which is typically triggered when storages reach above 95 per cent of capacity, was in November 2022.

"We will continue working in partnership with the Bureau of Meteorology [BOM] to monitor forecast rain and water levels in our reservoirs, to guide any potential releases of water from Mt Bold," Dr Kingsborough said.

"Our reservoirs are in a healthy position heading into spring, and we will keep a close eye on our storage levels to ensure a secure water supply for our customers in advance of what the BOM is forecasting to be a dry late winter and spring."

Bushwalkers urged to use caution

The Kaurna name for Morialta Conservation Park's Fourth Creek is Moriatta, which means "ever flowing", although that is no longer the case due to upstream dams and agriculture.

Rain halts play during SA flooding Three people were rescued after attempting to drive through floodwaters, following a weekend of heavy rainfall and storms across South Australia.

Its water flows through Morialta and into the River Torrens system, but occurs below reservoir catchments so does not impact upon storage levels.

Bushwalkers visiting the site are urged to stick to trails and stay behind guardrails as it has been the site of several rescues and fatal accidents.

"Visitors are responsible for their own safety and should follow advice from park rangers, comply with all warnings and other park signage, stay on marked trails, and remain behind safety barriers that are installed to protect the public," a Department for Environment and Water spokesperson said last month.

Several South Australian towns recorded record-breaking August rainfall totals across Saturday and yesterday, including 110 millimetres at Lenswood, 101mm at Coromandel East and150mm in some parts of the state's far north.

World.title: Labor candidate stands by comments on party's 'skeletons' and culture of silence
World.content:
Western Australian Premier Roger Cook has described Labor's Secret Harbour by-election candidate as someone who "doesn't take bull crap", after old comments she made about her own party’s culture of silence on sexual harassment in the workplace resurfaced.

In July 2021, Labor candidate Georgia Tree spoke on a political podcast about the actions of the federal Australian Labor Party (ALP) amid allegations from former Liberal staffer Brittany Higgins that she was raped by her colleague Bruce Lehrmann.

Two Federal Court judgements later found Mr Lehrmann did, on the balance of probabilities, rape Ms Higgins at Parliament House in 2019, after a night out with other Liberal staffers.

It was a saga that gripped the national conversation after Ms Higgins went public in February 2021, leading to a national reckoning over women's safety in the workplace.

In her podcast appearance months later, Ms Tree described instances of Labor members erring on the side of caution when attacking political opponents to avoid drawing attention to Labor’s own faults.

Georgia Tree told the podcast Labor would deal with things "in-house" so it did not "taint the brand". (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"You would have people offhand say, 'Oh God, like we probably shouldn't go too hard on X because what about like, the skeletons in our closet?'" she said.

"It's like the Catholic Church, right, like we don't want to taint the brand, so let's deal with everything in-house, and everyone just shut up."

'Things have changed'

Asked about the comments this morning, Mr Cook was staunch in his defence of Ms Tree.

"What it shows is that Georgia Tree stands up for her community," he said.

" She doesn't take bull crap, she calls it out when she sees it. "

The premier said he was "sure" Ms Tree did not still hold the same views about the ALP, and denied WA Labor had any "skeletons" in its closet.

Premier Roger Cook and Georgia Tree walking and talking in Rockingham prior to a press conference. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

"The context in which she was speaking was five years ago, in the context of the accusations by Britney Higgins against a Liberal member of parliament," he said.

"Things have changed significantly over the last decade in relation to the way people conduct politics."

Meet the candidates in the Secret Harbour by-election Here's everything you need to know about the Secret Harbour by-election, which is shaping up as one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

More women in politics

Ms Tree said she stood by her 2021 comments, but added that her party had changed since then.

"I've always been outspoken, and I will always fight for what is right — particularly when it comes to women," she said in a statement.

"Both the federal and WA Caucus is now made up of more than 50 per cent women.

"This is one of the reasons why I am running, we need to see more young women entering politics to fight for change and not be afraid to stand up, speak out and take their seat at the table."

The Secret Harbour by-election is shaping up to be one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

The battle for the outer suburban seat in Perth's south is expected to be a major test of One Nation's popularity in the state, and the ability of the Labor and Liberal parties to fight back.

Secret Harbour has long been considered a safe Labor seat, with the by-election triggered by last month's retirement of high-profile minister Paul Papalia, who represented the electorate for almost two decades.

World.title: ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Elliot Constable was named winner of the ABC’s rebooted reality series Race Around the World. The competition, which sent six young filmmakers – Constable, Jayden O’Neill, Kate McGuinness, Lucinda Price, Mikaela Zuiderduyn and William He – around the world to each film 10 videos in 100 days, was caught up in controversy towards the end, when billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart threatened legal action against the public broadcaster over a film that featured commentary about her. The film, by Kate McGuinness, was also reported to the ABC Ombudsman, but the complaint was thrown out. ABC boss Hugh Marks also issued an apology about the offending episode, saying the content “has fallen short of community expectations”. Constable spoke to national TV editor Louise Rugendyke about his experiences on the race, the controversy and which film he watched to relax. Race Around the World winner Elliot Constable (middle) with (from left) judge Danny Philippou, former winner Olivia Rousett, host Zan Rowe, judge Margaret Pomeranz and judge and former contestant John Safran. Elliot Constable in Nepal for episode six of Race Around the World and his film The Ghurka Detox. Congratulations Elliot! You have been back in the country for about 10 days now, do you finally feel like you have landed on earth? That’s just wild that it’s been two weeks already. It’s so overwhelming. I’ve been receiving so many lovely messages. I don’t think it’s fully sunk in yet because we filmed the [final] episode about a week ago [and it was broadcast last night], so I’ve just been sitting around, sleeping on my couch.



That final episode must have been very overwhelming, because you had only just landed back in the country from Brazil, you were face-to-face with the judges, and then you beat Kate by only one point. Related Article ★★★★

Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks My film went first, and I was like, “OK, that was well received” and then when I saw Kate’s film, that was maybe one of my favourite films of the entire season. And when [judge] Margaret [Pomeranz] said, “Elliot” [to announce the winner], it was quite surreal. I would have been happy if anyone else had won it as well. Obviously, I’m stoked that I won. But I truly was surrounded by incredible filmmakers, talented artists, lovely individuals. There was a comment online like, “Why didn’t you write a speech?” Not that I didn’t believe I was going to win or anything, but the whole thing was this kind of dream, really. I spoke to you before you left and you seemed quite overwhelmed about the task ahead of you. When did you feel like you hit your stride? Elliot Constable in Norway in episode four of Race Around the World. I always felt like I could do it, that’s why I applied for the show. I tried to do it years ago when I started this whole [filmmaking] thing out in South America, [where I would] make little films and try and sell them back to Australia. I didn’t realise how crazy or how intense the experience would be. I think [we were up to filming] episode five when it started going to air, which added another layer of intensity, because then you had the Australian public watching your films and commenting. So we were in a bit of a bubble, and then it was just like, “Whoa”. But obviously the first film [about a woman in Moldova trying to return to Kyiv for cancer treatment] was received really well. I got a lot of points. That was when I was like, “OK, maybe I do want to win this.” What was the most challenging part?



Related Article ★★★

Review Ted Lasso goes beyond extra time with its fourth season, and we pay the penalty It just didn’t stop. It was very hard to switch off because you put everything into a story, you’re editing every night, you’re filming day and night. And I think, maybe, one or two films I edited before the deadline, whereas every other film, it was just to the deadline. I was exporting [files] a few minutes before it was due because you just want it to be perfect. And then you submit it, and the next day you’re presenting your film to Australia, and then they tell you where you’re going, and two hours later, you’re on a flight. So you pack up your hotel room, or wherever the hell you’re staying, and then you’re on a flight, and you immediately go back to, “OK, what am I going to do there?” So it was just not switching off. I don’t know how many flights I got. I watched one movie in the entire three or four months. When I was on the plane, I was either sleeping or studying. I struggled even speaking to friends and family. It’s hard to explain what’s going on, and you’re always up against it. I went from California to the North Pole. I think it took 40 hours to get there, so the jet lag, my body just started to [go], “All right, here we go again.” That was the challenge, just surviving: “Have I eaten today? What is the time? Am I in California now?” Elliot Constable in episode two, in South Africa for his film about wildlife poaching, Guardians of the Wild. What was the movie you watched? Marty Supreme. I love those directors [Josh Safdie, who used to work with his brother Benny]. Before this show, I would love flights, I love plane food, sitting there and watching the latest Hollywood movie with a glass of wine and butter chicken or whatever, but it was just non-stop. How did you cope with the public feedback? As you said, it wasn’t until you were up to filming episode five that you were able to see what the public thought of your work.



I read the feedback. I probably had the better end of the stick, but then it started to get more negative. One of my favourite comments was, “Hell is Lucinda filming something and Elliot sound mixing it.” I gave her a call and we had a good laugh about that. So there is some funny feedback, then it starts to get a little bit nastier. And the girls were treated far worse than me. But there is good feedback as well, and stuff that you’re like, “Oh yeah, fair.” Filmmaker Kate McGuinness in her controversial Race Around the World film. ABC What was the discussion among the contestants when the backlash began over Kate’s film? We were in contact all the time. I looked at a lot of the feedback, but you try and disconnect yourself a little bit from that. So I can’t really comment on that specifically, I was just trying to put one foot in front of the other. I found it really hard when there was negative feedback and hate on my colleagues, my friends. Is she OK? Yeah, yeah, she’s OK. You said the girls suffered a bit more with negative feedback. That really says everything about being a woman on television, doesn’t it?



Well, I mean the feedback inherently on [online comment forum] Reddit is just sexist. They got a lot more hate than the guys, so I think that says everything. But we all supported each other, and most of us stayed off those comments. Race Around the World’s new contestants (from left) Lucinda, Mikaela, Jayden, Elliot, Kate and William. Do you think the ABC should have apologised for Kate’s video? That’s far above my pay grade. I’m not even sure what the situation is now, to be honest. Which film – that wasn’t one of yours – was your favourite?

Far out. That’s 60 films. The last episode was spectacular. I thought Kate’s film [about the dad in China] was just brilliant. Kate’s Utah film [about data centres] is one of my favourites, like top three, and Mikaela’s film [in Mongolia] was incredible. Lucinda’s last film [about ageing in Los Angeles] was incredible. I loved William’s bull-riding film [in Madagascar]. Jayden, that East Timor crocodile film was just so beautiful and powerful. Have I mentioned everyone? And your favourite judge?

Margaret Pomeranz was definitely my favourite judge. And after I won, I went up to her, and I was just like, “Thank you, Margaret.” I didn’t realise how small she was. She was so lovely. I’ve literally started writing her a letter, with a pen.

World.title: Everyone has the wrong idea about my suburb. Our village is much more than you think
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I tell people where I live, it’s not unknown for residents in other parts of Sydney to say, “Oh, Double Bay”, in a tone of voice that suggests I’m surrounded by diamond-encrusted dowagers. And sure, this small suburb, five kilometres east of the CBD, is tucked between Darling Point and Point Piper, close to some of the richest people in Sydney and, indeed, Australia. But anyone who thinks Double Bay is just a smug little enclave supported solely by The Australian Financial Review Rich List is dead wrong. DB, as some locals call it, actually has a village vibe. Or double village vibe, since it’s bisected by the bellowing traffic of New South Head Road. On one side (known to some of us as the “dark side”) you have the big-name businesses: a decent Woolies, Dan Murphy’s, bakery, a really good public library, massive pet supplies shop and banks. There are also several establishments dedicated to the pursuit of beauty ... via surgery. Poodle walker in activewear crossing Guilfoyle Street, Double Bay. Oscar Colman Patrons outside the Royal Oak Hotel, at the corner of Bay Street and Knox Street. Oscar Colman Women pose for social media photographs on Cross Street. Oscar Colman The other side is where the harbour is. One of the nicest things you can do is take your flat white from the Bahia Cafe off Bay Street down to the park and the ferry, and watch the DB version of the passeggiata along the path that fringes the small beach. You’ll see mums with their small kids, joggers and people with dogs. Lots of dogs, ranging from hounds of the Baskervilles to various oodles and down to some that might make interesting hors d’oeuvres. On some days the ferry disgorges middle-aged men in ironed jeans and women wearing frilly dresses, all from the Circular Quay cruise ships – a 15-minute ride away – and bound for the fancy dress and homewares shops in Transvaal Avenue. Steyne Park nearby is the sports ground for the local primary school, as well as the place where the Ascham schoolgirls play touch football. You often see parents and coaches shouting encouragement to very small children kicking very large soccer balls. If you’re hell-bent on exercise yourself, it’s easy to walk into the CBD in about 50 minutes.



When I was growing up in Sydney’s northern suburbs, Double Bay was in the mysterious east, a part of the city my family and friends never visited, a posh place where rich people lived. I had no idea I would ever live in Double Bay myself, let alone for almost 30 years. (I moved here for love, not money.) When I arrived in 1997 the suburb felt much more stylishly European than it does now. It was a place of small shops stretching along New South Head Road and Knox Street like glittering beads on a necklace. They included Nellie Vida’s fashion boutique, the Mignon cake shop and Georges Restaurant, with its elegant and supercilious waiters; there were also the Swiss Deli, the Village Cinema, Lesley McKay’s excellent bookshop and 21 Espresso, famous for its matzo ball soup and borscht. DB has been the place of first settlement and the social centre for Sydney’s Jewish community since the 1930s: when I moved in, there were quite a few Jewish families living in our building. All that’s changed now. In the past 20 years the population of Double Bay has undergone a huge shift. It’s now a place of young men in expensive suits and gleaming loafers without socks, of long-haired women in expensive activewear queuing outside Baker Bleu in Guilfoyle Street, of Mercs and Porsches and occasionally Lamborghinis. There are also hordes of young children, many of whose parents endure driving to private schools in Rose Bay or Bellevue Hill rather than to the local primary school – a place they would know only when required to vote. Ca Phe Mai, a premium Vietnamese cafe and bar in the Kiaora Lane precinct. Oscar Colman Boutique Mode Sportif on Cross Street. Oscar Colman The Double Bay War Memorial featuring a bronze statue of an Anzac soldier stands in Steyne Park. Oscar Colman

World.title: ‘Inconvenient for the public’: ICAC witness has no memory of Catholic Schools NSW work
World.content:
ICAC’s Operation Rosny is investigating property developer Jean Nassif’s links to political powerbrokers, councils and Catholic schools. See all stories .

Lobbyist and one-time political staffer Jeremy Greenwood says he has no idea what work was done for Catholic Schools NSW despite his consultancy firm sending numerous invoices to the education body. Greenwood repeatedly told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Monday that he could not remember what work was carried out despite being shown near identical monthly invoices for $6600 for “digital proposal, strategic communications, and strategic counsel”. Jeremy Greenwood leaves the ICAC after providing evidence on Monday. Janie Barrett The commission heard that Greenwood’s consultancy firm Beckington, which he set up with fellow Liberal operative Christian Ellis, sent the invoices to Catholic Schools NSW, including one in July 2019 worth $16,000. That invoice was forwarded to Catholic Schools NSW’s boss Dallas McInerney’s Hotmail address, with a list of apparent services provided, including a digital proposal, a strategic communications proposal and a sign-on fee.



Greenwood’s name was on the invoice, but he said he could not remember any details about it. After pressing Greenwood several times, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked him: “Who can brief this commission, given your absence of memory, as to what work was actually done by way of digital proposal, strategic communications proposal, or strategic counsel?” Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, pictured delivering the opening address at the ICAC. Kate Geraghty Greenwood suggested she ask former Catholic Schools NSW staffer James Tudehope or Ellis. “Well conveniently Mr Tudehope is in New Zealand and Mr Ellis is in the United Kingdom,” Dwyer said.



Greenwood said that was inconvenient, to which Dwyer shot back: “Inconvenient to the public trying to work [out] why this money is being committed on a monthly basis.” Earlier in his evidence, Greenwood said that he had an interest in conservative causes, in particular abortion, but was not a member of the Reformers and later felt the right-wing Catholic group turned “toxic”. Greenwood appeared before the ICAC as it continues its probe into allegations of illegal political donations and links between fugitive developer Jean Nassif and Liberal operatives. He told the commission that he was interested in conservative social issues but less so in factional stoushes involving the Liberals and at no point considered himself a member of the Reformers despite being supportive of their work.



Greenwood was working for Nationals senator Matt Canavan when his friends Ellis and Robert Assaf started ramping up their recruitment efforts for the Catholic faction of the Liberals, he told the commission. While he was interested in the work of the Reformers, Greenwood said in 2018 he was “all about the Nationals” rather than Liberal Party matters. Loading “Most of the engagement I have with these guys would have been at a pub, or I’ve been dragged into a group chat,” Greenwood said. Greenwood said that while his boss Canavan spoke at a Reformers event, he mostly sat outside.



He would have been interested in policy talks organised by the Reformers, including one featuring former broadcaster Alan Jones, but was not involved in recruitment activities. Greenwood said he eventually began urging his friends to end their involvement with the factional group. He told the commission that he felt the Reformers “became so toxic” that he wanted his friends to stop. “I was supportive of their cause up until a point when it was negatively impacting me,” Greenwood said. He said the Reformers had started to cause him “a lot of grief professionally”.



At the start of his evidence, Greenwood was asked about friendships he had with other key figures linked to the Reformers, including the Perrottet brothers Dominic, Charles and Jean-Claude. Factional powerbroker Charles and Jean-Claude are persons of interest in this inquiry, but the former premier Dominic is not involved and nor is he accused of any wrongdoing. Greenwood also said that Ellis was one of his good friends and Ellis had been best man at his wedding. Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny ‘God granted us a victory’: The unlikely Liberal branch seized by the Reformers The commission heard that Greenwood visited Ellis in June in Britain, where Ellis had relocated in January and had “caught up” with him on four occasions. Dwyer told the commission in her opening statement that Ellis “has declined to give oral evidence to this public inquiry, during which he would be subject to cross-examination”.

World.title: Far-right nationalists take aim at Brisbane’s ‘Aussie’ posters
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Far-right nationalists take aim at Brisbane’s ‘Aussie’ posters Courtney Kruk August 10, 2026 — 4:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Far-right nationalists with links to anti-immigration rallies have defaced a street art poster campaign in Brisbane designed to challenge ideas of Australia’s national identity. It comes after one of the group claimed responsibility for a series of offensive posters plastered around Sydney and Melbourne earlier this year depicting Bondi shooter Naveed Akram. Self-proclaimed Australian nationalist and content creator Andre Mamet, who goes by the handle “Ausmaxx”, and Melbourne stockbroker Mitch Hobbs, aka “Sir Doug”, filmed themselves vandalising the posters in locations including South Brisbane’s Fish Lane and Norman Park over the weekend. The pair vandalised Adelaide artist Peter Drew’s distinctive poster series, replacing the “Aussie” label with “Indian”, “Chinese” and “not”.
