Courtney Kruk Federal Labor MP Renee Coffey shared video of her using a “step ladder, squeegee on a pole and my tallest son” to remove the words “Indian”, “Chinese”, and “not” which had been plastered over the distinctive “Aussie” label at Norman Park station in her seat of Griffith.



“When my son asked me where we were going, I said: ‘to fight racists’,” Coffey said. Adelaide-based artist Peter Drew launched the “Aussie” poster series in 2016 in response to what he saw as rising anti-immigration sentiment and xenophobia. It depicts Australians citizens who had been subject to the White Australia Policy. Peter Drew’s “Aussie” posters on Edward Street in Brisbane’s CBD. Courtney Kruk He revived the series earlier this year to mark its 10th anniversary, and in response to the March for Australia anti-immigration rallies that began last August. After visiting Sydney and Melbourne, Drew travelled to Brisbane at the end of July to erect 150 posters across inner-city suburbs and in Ipswich, where far-right politician Pauline Hanson ran a fish-and-chip shop before launching a political career.



He told this masthead he was not fazed by Mamet and Hobbs’ “latest brainwave”, adding that the point of the series was “to get under their skin”. Related Article Exclusive

Bondi shooting Posters of the Bondi shooter appeared around Melbourne. The culprit has now been unmasked “What we’ve got is a very small cohort of lost boys who are testing their ideology against reality, and every time it gets knocked back,” Drew said. “I like engaging with them and I don’t dislike them as people – it’s their ideas that I contend with. “When things like this happen … it keeps me going more than anything else.”



Coffey said she did not support illegal street art but was delighted when Drew’s work appeared in Brisbane. “Peter Drew’s iconic artwork represents an inclusive, warm, welcoming Australia that I believe in, and challenges narrow, exclusionary definitions pushed by our political opponents,” she said. Mitch Hobbs (left) and Andre Mamet (right) filmed themselves vandalising the works. Courtney Kruk “Racism has absolutely no place in our community, as evidenced by the number of locals who shouted out ‘thank you’ and passers-by who stopped to help us [on Sunday].” Mamet told this masthead: “Peter Drew’s art, despite being illegal graffiti, and as explained by him is used to deconstruct Australian identity, is celebrated and allowed.”



He did not elaborate further on the pair’s motivation to deface the works. Hobbs was also contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email Colin Kruger Updated August 10, 2026 — 4:38pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG’s chairman-elect Michael Ebeid has issued a grovelling apology to Labor senator Deborah O’Neill over his emails claiming her speech, which brought whistleblower allegations against the firm to light, contained “completely false” information. Ebeid, who has essentially been functioning as the chairman of the firm that is trying to recover from its top executives’ misuse of clients’ confidential audit documents, needs approval from KPMG partners to formally take up the role. That vote ends on Wednesday. KPMG’s incoming chairman Michael Ebeid issued a grovelling apology to Senator Deborah O’Neill. Getty Images Documents released by O’Neill’s parliamentary committee on Monday contained Ebeid’s personal apology for an email he sent early in the saga, which began this year, undermining the whistleblower’s claims. “What I wrote was wrong,” Ebeid told O’Neill in one document. “I described statements about the whistleblower’s allegations made by you to the Senate as false. I described the firm’s process as thorough. Events since have shown that neither was true, and that the concerns you raised on the whistleblower’s behalf have helped uncover serious wrongdoing and I can only thank you for that.”



Related Article Big four accountants KPMG directors flee as whistleblower scandal worsens He said he thought he was being helpful, based on his knowledge at the time. “However, with what I know now, my email was naive, embarrassing and wrong on every level,” Ebeid wrote. But the bigger issue for the embattled firm was the committee’s decision to release documents KPMG had battled to keep hidden under claims of legal professional privilege. The committee said it was in the public interest to release these documents ahead of another public grilling this Friday. The legal documents were the reports from two law firms, Allens and Ashurst, and relate to their work on the whistleblower complaints. KPMG had initially used the reports from the law firms to claim that the whistleblower’s complaints were unsubstantiated while refusing to release the actual documents publicly. A fresh investigation by Allens has led to a purge of KPMG’s most senior people as some of the most serious allegations have now been substantiated.



“The Ashurst and Allens processes were central to the claim that KPMG had undertaken comprehensive internal and external investigations prior to the speech given by Senator Deborah O’Neill on 24 March 2026,” the committee – chaired by O’Neill – said in a statement. It said the committee had found there was a “compelling public interest” in examining the results of the law firms’ investigations at its next hearing, allowing it to publish the previously legally privileged documents. Since May, the firm has lost its chief executive Andrew Yates, chairman Martin Sheppard, and sacked former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett after she lied about accessing sensitive board documents from client Lendlease and stored copies in her work locker. KPMG audit partner Kim Lawry also resigned from her senior roles this month after Westpac requested that she be removed from its audit “to ensure there is no distraction”. KPMG independent board member Patty Akopiantz quietly left the firm’s regional board last month, following former NSW premier Mike Baird’s exit in September, and fellow independent director Jane Hemstritch is expected to resign once replacements have been found. World.title: Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses Angus Delaney August 10, 2026 — 4:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state Coalition will seek to prohibit unions entering a person’s house and create occupational health and safety exemptions for employers as the Victorian government pushes ahead with its working-from-home laws. The opposition confirmed on Monday that it will not oppose Labor’s bill, but it will introduce seven proposed amendments to offer businesses greater protection after industry groups launched a last-ditch push to reverse legislation they say will send jobs and investment out of state. Premier Ben Carroll has been steadfast in his support of Labor’s working-from-home legislation. Louis Trerise Eight of the country’s largest business lobby groups joined forces on Monday, saying Labor’s plan to legislate the right to work from home two days a week when possible risked sending Victoria backwards at a time when its focus should be on turning around the economy, creating jobs and lifting living standards. Business Council of Australia executive director of advocacy Ben Wicks said the proposed legislation, which is set to pass the Victorian upper house this week, would increase the state’s unemployment rate of 5.1 per cent.



“It’s exactly the wrong time to be introducing a piece of legislation like this that we say costs jobs and costs investment,” Wicks said. “Our members tell us directly that this … will cost jobs and will cost investment.” Related Article Victorian Parliament Working from home laws set to extend to more workers, as Allan prepares legislation The group said companies already widely offer flexible arrangements, and the proposed laws are another layer of red tape that would see companies desert Victoria and expand their businesses interstate. “I’m concerned it’s the poison pill for jobs,” said Sally Curtain, chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. Tim Piper, the Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group, said businesses may even consider going offshore.



“I spoke to a member this morning who said to me, ‘working from home could also be working from the Philippines,’” he said. “You’ve got to remember that businesses have choices, whether it’s the rest of the country or whether it’s the rest of the world.” If the bill passes parliament as expected, it would come into effect on September 1 and be applicable to full-time employees, as well as part-time and regularly employed casuals on a pro rata basis. Employers would also be compelled to pay “reasonable costs” to enable their staff to work remotely. The Coalition has said it supports the right to work from home and will not oppose Labor’s bill, but it is seeking to introduce seven amendments to protect businesses. Australian Industry Group Victorian head Tim Piper said businesses may consider offshoring if the working-from-home changes pass. These include capping “reasonable costs” an employer must pay at $1000, limiting the right to employees who primarily work in Victoria and will continue to work from home in Victoria (unless mutually agreed to), and delaying an employee’s right to appeal a company’s decision until next year.



Other amendments are intended to prohibit the right of union entry into the home (similar to the conditions under which a union may access a workplace), excluding working from home when determining land tax liability, and protecting companies and directors from liability if employees are injured while working from home. The business groups said they felt there had been a lack of consultation on the legislation. Piper said they had not met directly with Premier Ben Carroll or his predecessor Jacinta Allan, but were expecting to meet Carroll this week. Since becoming premier a fortnight ago, Carroll has repeatedly said his government would stick to the promise to legislate the right to work from home, which was announced by Allan last year. Carroll has argued the move would save Victorians time and money, and said Labor had no plans to change the bill, but it would consider “sensible amendments” moved in the upper house.



“My door’s always open to the business community,” Carroll said on Monday morning. “We do know work from home works for families, but we also need to do everything we can to support our business community.” Related Article Victorian election Labor open to High Court challenge over work from home laws Members of the coalition of business groups have not ruled out launching or joining a potential High Court challenge against the legislation if it passes. Legal experts have cast doubt over the state government’s ability to legislate a right to work from home, as most workplace laws are under the jurisdiction of the federal government. “Certainly, I would expect a High Court challenge to occur with this legislation, keeping in mind we do not actually have a bill which has passed through the upper house yet, and time will tell how that will evolve over the coming months,” said Cath Evans, Victorian executive director of the Property Council of Australia. World.title: Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot Sam McClure August 10, 2026 — 4:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With 47 seconds remaining in the third quarter of Carlton and St Kilda’s season-opening AFLW match on Sunday, Channel Seven commentator Alistair Nicholson delivered a message to viewers that inadvertently captured one of the most significant challenges confronting the competition. “For Victorian viewers, you are going to Seven News. If you want to keep watching the footy, go to 7mate now.” St Kilda’s Tyanna Smith bursts away during the season opener against Carlton. AFL Photos via Getty Images Tyanna Smith had just burst through a centre bounce like Bailey Smith and booted a brilliant goal – her second – from outside 50 metres to put the Saints within 22 points. The football continued. Seven’s coverage on its primary Victorian channel did not.



Related Article AFL 2026 Carlton close on stunning AFL top 10 finish; Rowell dominant as Suns snap streak; Blues hold sway in AFLW opener There was nothing sinister about the decision. TV networks routinely move programming between channels, and Seven’s evening news remains among the most commercially important programs on its schedule. But the timing was striking. Four days later, there will be no men’s AFL match on Thursday night, with Melbourne and Hawthorn instead afforded clear air for their AFLW fixture. The contrast warrants examination.



Thursday night AFL has become one of the most valuable pieces of sporting content on Australian television, regularly attracting audiences of around one million across Seven’s platforms this season. This Thursday night’s AFLW game is expected to attract a fraction of that audience. So the decision to clear men’s footy from that timeslot to showcase the AFLW will cost hundreds of thousands of viewers. View post on X Within the space of four days, the industry will have provided two vastly different illustrations of where the AFLW currently sits. On Sunday, the broadcaster considered the product sufficiently expendable to move the final quarter from its primary channel.



On Thursday, the AFL will clear one of its most lucrative broadcast windows to provide the same competition with uncontested exposure. After a decade of AFLW, it is reasonable to ask whether this approach remains sustainable. Abbie McKay wins the ‘golden fist’ for her performance. Getty Images The creation of the AFLW has been among the most consequential developments in Australian sport this century. Its influence on female participation, pathways and the visibility of women in the game has been profound. Girls who once reached their early teenage years and discovered their football pathway effectively ended can now aspire to play the sport professionally. Clubs that existed for more than a century as overwhelmingly male institutions now have women wearing their jumpers at the elite level.



Those achievements are substantial and permanent. Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist But the success of female football as a participation movement and the commercial sustainability of an 18-team professional national competition are not necessarily the same proposition. Eleven seasons after its establishment, the AFLW should be sufficiently mature to withstand scrutiny of the latter. Professional sport is expensive.



Players must be paid. Football departments must be funded. Teams must travel around the country. Venues must be opened and staffed. Matches must be produced and broadcast to professional standards. The AFL and its broadcast partners are investing millions of dollars annually in a competition that remains a considerable distance from paying for itself. That investment was entirely understandable during AFLW’s establishment phase. New competitions require subsidies. Audiences take time to develop, sporting traditions are not manufactured overnight, and the AFL possessed both the financial capacity and strategic incentive to establish a national women’s competition. But an establishment phase cannot continue indefinitely.



The AFLW is now entering season 11. The question should no longer simply be how much the competition has grown, but how it eventually becomes commercially sustainable. That discussion becomes particularly relevant given the broader financial demands confronting the AFL. View post on X The league is preparing to establish a 19th licence in Tasmania, an undertaking that will require significant investment over many years. Expansion clubs GWS and Gold Coast continue to be heavily funded by the AFL. Clubs continue to seek greater distributions. Player payments continue to increase. The cost of operating football clubs continues to rise. The media industry underwriting much of that expenditure is simultaneously navigating one of the most difficult advertising markets in recent memory.



The AFLW game between Carlton and St Kilda rated 147,000 nationally, overlapping with the men’s West Coast-Collingwood match. The previous Sunday afternoon men’s game between Gold Coast and Melbourne rated 402,000. Related Article Opinion

AFLW The moment Daisy Pearce broke the ice inside the Australian camp Libby Birch AFL columnist Scheduling the women’s match as part of a double header with the Blues-Saints men’s clash meant there were more than 20,000 people watching at Marvel Stadium by midway through the last quarter. It would be absurd to expect AFLW to generate the same audiences and revenue as the AFL given the men’s competition has enjoyed more than a century to establish its cultural and commercial position. Nor does commercial sustainability necessarily require immediate profitability.



But there must be a credible trajectory towards an economic model in which the size and cost of the competition bears some relationship to the audience and revenue it generates. Perhaps that requires reconsidering how AFLW is scheduled. The instinct has often been to provide the competition with “clear air” — removing competing AFL matches and attempting to manufacture standalone marquee windows. Thursday night will provide another experiment in that philosophy. But there is an alternative argument.



Rather than seeking clear air for AFLW while the men’s season is on, perhaps the league would be better to persevere with fixtures that tap into the audience already watching Australian football. Double headers, such as Sunday’s Spud’s Game fixtures, integrated match days and fixtures positioned around major AFL games may provide AFLW with access to an audience far greater than it can presently attract on its own. The next stage of AFLW cannot simply be about expansion: more teams, more games, longer seasons, higher salaries and more premium broadcast windows. It must also be about demand. To extend the women’s season length to 14 home-and-away rounds, the league and the AFL Players’ Association agreed on key performance metrics: an average attendance of 6000 fans and 100,000 broadcast viewers per match. Those are ambitious targets across the season, but by staging select games in high-value timeslots, the league is giving W a chance to maximise its audience.



At some point, investment has to become a test of demand and Thursday night is exactly that. Related Article AFLW ‘We couldn’t get over that’: The AFLW norm baffling this Irish import How many people are watching? How many are attending? What are advertisers prepared to pay to reach that audience? What does each match cost to stage and broadcast? And what structure gives the competition the greatest chance to grow those numbers? Those questions should not be interpreted as an attack on women’s football. They are the questions asked of every professional sporting competition.



The AFLW has already transformed the pathway for women and girls who want to play Australian football and fundamentally altered the culture of the national game. Its second decade presents a different challenge. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers as she plans attack for parliament’s return
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers as she plans attack for parliament’s return Nick Newling August 10, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson has vowed to forge ahead with a legally questionable bill targeting foreign fighters and hit out at Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s oversight of migration policy, as the One Nation leader seeks to set the agenda for parliament’s return. Riding a wave of high poll results, Hanson on Monday fired off a series of social media posts laying out her plan for the coming fortnight and accusing Burke and Labor of orchestrating a secret plan to bring an additional million migrants into the country over the next four years. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has attacked Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke for the government’s handling of migration. Eamon Gallagher The party’s Protecting Australians from Foreign Terrorist Fighters Bill – its first complete policy proposal this term – will be introduced this week. However, her bill has been criticised by legal experts who say it will fail to withstand a High Court challenge. Hanson argues that the bill will strengthen powers to cancel or refuse passports and toughen bail laws for terrorism charges. A key pillar of the bill would create a new “foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order” that the minister could ask the Federal Court to impose. The existing exclusion order regime under the minister’s control would remain.



Burke recently said the bill “would last about 30 seconds in the High Court”, while constitutional law expert Anne Twomey told this masthead that the proposal appeared to be a delaying mechanism and would achieve little in its attempt to ban foreign fighters from returning. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was the target of Hanson’s ire on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Despite Twomey’s criticisms, Hanson on Monday claimed that the Sydney University professor saw it as “a good piece of legislation that is robust enough to withstand a challenge in the High Court”. Twomey was contacted for comment. Hours earlier, Hanson took to Facebook to accuse Burke of mismanaging Australia’s migration settings and lying to voters about attempts to pull back net overseas migration. The comments come after Burke abruptly delayed the announcement of the government’s migration overhaul package last week. “They already brought in 1.5 million in four years. That’s why your rent exploded, your pay went backwards, and your kids can’t buy a home. It’s why hospitals are turning away sick people,” Hanson wrote.



Hanson’s return to parliament comes after a falling out with Seven over her appearance on an episode of the show Spotlight, which filmed her spending time with British anti-Islam extremist Tommy Robinson. She was unapologetic about her interview with Robinson, a divisive figure whose appearance on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast prompted Nine, owner of this masthead, to part ways with its morning show host. Related Article Exclusive

Political expenses Empty five-star room: Hanson paid for $900-a-night hotel with party funds Hanson has claimed that Seven was originally supposed to pay for the trip but pulled out, forcing One Nation to carry the cost of a $900-a-night hotel room. She disputed reports in this masthead that the party paid for an empty room while she was on a side trip to Sicily, partially funded by her mining-billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart, to attend a Dolce & Gabbana fashion show. Burke’s address to the National Press Club was delayed after cabinet ministers raised questions about political backlash and unresolved financial costs. The minister is expected to provide more detail in coming days on the plan to slash net overseas migration intake to its budget forecast of 225,000 a year.



Labor is weighing up whether to rework the country’s skilled migration program, place stricter rules on working holidaymakers and family reunion visas, and slash working rights for people who overstay their visas. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce doubled down on Hanson’s comments on Monday, telling News24, formerly Sky News: “You meet [migrants] when you’re trying to drive a car to work. That’s why you can’t get anywhere.” Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Assistant Foreign Affairs Minister Matt Thistlethwaite came to Burke’s defence on Monday, claiming the figures cited by Hanson were not correct. “Those numbers that Pauline Hanson refers to are net overseas migration numbers, which includes Australian citizens who are living overseas and returning home. Is Pauline Hanson saying that Australians living overseas do not have the right to return home?” Thistlethwaite asked during a News24 appearance.



“The better figure is permanent migration. That we’ve set at 185,000 for the last couple of years, and we’ve met that figure. That figure is based a lot on what employers tell us they need.” Net overseas migration – long-term arrivals into the country minus departures – peaked under Labor in September 2023 as borders reopened after the COVID pandemic, but has consistently fallen since then. Figures in the May budget showed Labor anticipated the net overseas migration rate to be 295,000 in the last financial year. World.title: ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Elliot Constable was named winner of the ABC’s rebooted reality series Race Around the World. The competition, which sent six young filmmakers – Constable, Jayden O’Neill, Kate McGuinness, Lucinda Price, Mikaela Zuiderduyn and William He – around the world to each film 10 videos in 100 days, was caught up in controversy towards the end, when billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart threatened legal action against the public broadcaster over a film that featured commentary about her. The film, by Kate McGuinness, was also reported to the ABC Ombudsman, but the complaint was thrown out. ABC boss Hugh Marks also issued an apology about the offending episode, saying the content “has fallen short of community expectations”. Constable spoke to national TV editor Louise Rugendyke about his experiences on the race, the controversy and which film he watched to relax. Race Around the World winner Elliot Constable (middle) with (from left) judge Danny Philippou, former winner Olivia Rousett, host Zan Rowe, judge Margaret Pomeranz and judge and former contestant John Safran. Elliot Constable in Nepal for episode six of Race Around the World and his film The Ghurka Detox. Congratulations Elliot! You have been back in the country for about 10 days now, do you finally feel like you have landed on earth? That’s just wild that it’s been two weeks already. It’s so overwhelming. I’ve been receiving so many lovely messages. I don’t think it’s fully sunk in yet because we filmed the [final] episode about a week ago [and it was broadcast last night], so I’ve just been sitting around, sleeping on my couch.



That final episode must have been very overwhelming, because you had only just landed back in the country from Brazil, you were face-to-face with the judges, and then you beat Kate by only one point. Related Article ★★★★

Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks My film went first, and I was like, “OK, that was well received” and then when I saw Kate’s film, that was maybe one of my favourite films of the entire season. And when [judge] Margaret [Pomeranz] said, “Elliot” [to announce the winner], it was quite surreal. I would have been happy if anyone else had won it as well. Obviously, I’m stoked that I won. But I truly was surrounded by incredible filmmakers, talented artists, lovely individuals. There was a comment online like, “Why didn’t you write a speech?” Not that I didn’t believe I was going to win or anything, but the whole thing was this kind of dream, really. I spoke to you before you left and you seemed quite overwhelmed about the task ahead of you. When did you feel like you hit your stride? Elliot Constable in Norway in episode four of Race Around the World. I always felt like I could do it, that’s why I applied for the show. I tried to do it years ago when I started this whole [filmmaking] thing out in South America, [where I would] make little films and try and sell them back to Australia. I didn’t realise how crazy or how intense the experience would be. I think [we were up to filming] episode five when it started going to air, which added another layer of intensity, because then you had the Australian public watching your films and commenting. So we were in a bit of a bubble, and then it was just like, “Whoa”. But obviously the first film [about a woman in Moldova trying to return to Kyiv for cancer treatment] was received really well. I got a lot of points. That was when I was like, “OK, maybe I do want to win this.” What was the most challenging part?



Related Article ★★★

Review Ted Lasso goes beyond extra time with its fourth season, and we pay the penalty It just didn’t stop. It was very hard to switch off because you put everything into a story, you’re editing every night, you’re filming day and night. And I think, maybe, one or two films I edited before the deadline, whereas every other film, it was just to the deadline. I was exporting [files] a few minutes before it was due because you just want it to be perfect. And then you submit it, and the next day you’re presenting your film to Australia, and then they tell you where you’re going, and two hours later, you’re on a flight. So you pack up your hotel room, or wherever the hell you’re staying, and then you’re on a flight, and you immediately go back to, “OK, what am I going to do there?” So it was just not switching off. I don’t know how many flights I got. I watched one movie in the entire three or four months. When I was on the plane, I was either sleeping or studying. I struggled even speaking to friends and family. It’s hard to explain what’s going on, and you’re always up against it. I went from California to the North Pole. I think it took 40 hours to get there, so the jet lag, my body just started to [go], “All right, here we go again.” That was the challenge, just surviving: “Have I eaten today? What is the time? Am I in California now?” Elliot Constable in episode two, in South Africa for his film about wildlife poaching, Guardians of the Wild. What was the movie you watched? Marty Supreme. I love those directors [Josh Safdie, who used to work with his brother Benny]. Before this show, I would love flights, I love plane food, sitting there and watching the latest Hollywood movie with a glass of wine and butter chicken or whatever, but it was just non-stop. How did you cope with the public feedback? As you said, it wasn’t until you were up to filming episode five that you were able to see what the public thought of your work.



I read the feedback. I probably had the better end of the stick, but then it started to get more negative. One of my favourite comments was, “Hell is Lucinda filming something and Elliot sound mixing it.” I gave her a call and we had a good laugh about that. So there is some funny feedback, then it starts to get a little bit nastier. And the girls were treated far worse than me. But there is good feedback as well, and stuff that you’re like, “Oh yeah, fair.” Filmmaker Kate McGuinness in her controversial Race Around the World film. ABC What was the discussion among the contestants when the backlash began over Kate’s film? We were in contact all the time. I looked at a lot of the feedback, but you try and disconnect yourself a little bit from that. So I can’t really comment on that specifically, I was just trying to put one foot in front of the other. I found it really hard when there was negative feedback and hate on my colleagues, my friends. Is she OK? Yeah, yeah, she’s OK. You said the girls suffered a bit more with negative feedback. That really says everything about being a woman on television, doesn’t it?



Well, I mean the feedback inherently on [online comment forum] Reddit is just sexist. They got a lot more hate than the guys, so I think that says everything. But we all supported each other, and most of us stayed off those comments. Race Around the World’s new contestants (from left) Lucinda, Mikaela, Jayden, Elliot, Kate and William. Do you think the ABC should have apologised for Kate’s video? That’s far above my pay grade. I’m not even sure what the situation is now, to be honest. Which film – that wasn’t one of yours – was your favourite?

Far out. That’s 60 films. The last episode was spectacular. I thought Kate’s film [about the dad in China] was just brilliant. Kate’s Utah film [about data centres] is one of my favourites, like top three, and Mikaela’s film [in Mongolia] was incredible. Lucinda’s last film [about ageing in Los Angeles] was incredible. I loved William’s bull-riding film [in Madagascar]. Jayden, that East Timor crocodile film was just so beautiful and powerful. Have I mentioned everyone? And your favourite judge?

Margaret Pomeranz was definitely my favourite judge. And after I won, I went up to her, and I was just like, “Thank you, Margaret.” I didn’t realise how small she was. She was so lovely. I’ve literally started writing her a letter, with a pen.

World.title: Everyone has the wrong idea about my suburb. Our village is much more than you think
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I tell people where I live, it’s not unknown for residents in other parts of Sydney to say, “Oh, Double Bay”, in a tone of voice that suggests I’m surrounded by diamond-encrusted dowagers. And sure, this small suburb, five kilometres east of the CBD, is tucked between Darling Point and Point Piper, close to some of the richest people in Sydney and, indeed, Australia. But anyone who thinks Double Bay is just a smug little enclave supported solely by The Australian Financial Review Rich List is dead wrong. DB, as some locals call it, actually has a village vibe. Or double village vibe, since it’s bisected by the bellowing traffic of New South Head Road. On one side (known to some of us as the “dark side”) you have the big-name businesses: a decent Woolies, Dan Murphy’s, bakery, a really good public library, massive pet supplies shop and banks. There are also several establishments dedicated to the pursuit of beauty ... via surgery. Poodle walker in activewear crossing Guilfoyle Street, Double Bay. Oscar Colman Patrons outside the Royal Oak Hotel, at the corner of Bay Street and Knox Street. Oscar Colman Women pose for social media photographs on Cross Street. Oscar Colman The other side is where the harbour is. One of the nicest things you can do is take your flat white from the Bahia Cafe off Bay Street down to the park and the ferry, and watch the DB version of the passeggiata along the path that fringes the small beach. You’ll see mums with their small kids, joggers and people with dogs. Lots of dogs, ranging from hounds of the Baskervilles to various oodles and down to some that might make interesting hors d’oeuvres. On some days the ferry disgorges middle-aged men in ironed jeans and women wearing frilly dresses, all from the Circular Quay cruise ships – a 15-minute ride away – and bound for the fancy dress and homewares shops in Transvaal Avenue. Steyne Park nearby is the sports ground for the local primary school, as well as the place where the Ascham schoolgirls play touch football. You often see parents and coaches shouting encouragement to very small children kicking very large soccer balls. If you’re hell-bent on exercise yourself, it’s easy to walk into the CBD in about 50 minutes.



When I was growing up in Sydney’s northern suburbs, Double Bay was in the mysterious east, a part of the city my family and friends never visited, a posh place where rich people lived. I had no idea I would ever live in Double Bay myself, let alone for almost 30 years. (I moved here for love, not money.) When I arrived in 1997 the suburb felt much more stylishly European than it does now. It was a place of small shops stretching along New South Head Road and Knox Street like glittering beads on a necklace. They included Nellie Vida’s fashion boutique, the Mignon cake shop and Georges Restaurant, with its elegant and supercilious waiters; there were also the Swiss Deli, the Village Cinema, Lesley McKay’s excellent bookshop and 21 Espresso, famous for its matzo ball soup and borscht. DB has been the place of first settlement and the social centre for Sydney’s Jewish community since the 1930s: when I moved in, there were quite a few Jewish families living in our building. All that’s changed now. In the past 20 years the population of Double Bay has undergone a huge shift. It’s now a place of young men in expensive suits and gleaming loafers without socks, of long-haired women in expensive activewear queuing outside Baker Bleu in Guilfoyle Street, of Mercs and Porsches and occasionally Lamborghinis. There are also hordes of young children, many of whose parents endure driving to private schools in Rose Bay or Bellevue Hill rather than to the local primary school – a place they would know only when required to vote. Ca Phe Mai, a premium Vietnamese cafe and bar in the Kiaora Lane precinct. Oscar Colman Boutique Mode Sportif on Cross Street. Oscar Colman The Double Bay War Memorial featuring a bronze statue of an Anzac soldier stands in Steyne Park. Oscar Colman

World.title: ‘Inconvenient for the public’: ICAC witness has no memory of Catholic Schools NSW work
World.content:
ICAC’s Operation Rosny is investigating property developer Jean Nassif’s links to political powerbrokers, councils and Catholic schools. See all stories .

Lobbyist and one-time political staffer Jeremy Greenwood says he has no idea what work was done for Catholic Schools NSW despite his consultancy firm sending numerous invoices to the education body. Greenwood repeatedly told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Monday that he could not remember what work was carried out despite being shown near identical monthly invoices for $6600 for “digital proposal, strategic communications, and strategic counsel”. Jeremy Greenwood leaves the ICAC after providing evidence on Monday. Janie Barrett The commission heard that Greenwood’s consultancy firm Beckington, which he set up with fellow Liberal operative Christian Ellis, sent the invoices to Catholic Schools NSW, including one in July 2019 worth $16,000. That invoice was forwarded to Catholic Schools NSW’s boss Dallas McInerney’s Hotmail address, with a list of apparent services provided, including a digital proposal, a strategic communications proposal and a sign-on fee.



Greenwood’s name was on the invoice, but he said he could not remember any details about it. After pressing Greenwood several times, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked him: “Who can brief this commission, given your absence of memory, as to what work was actually done by way of digital proposal, strategic communications proposal, or strategic counsel?” Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, pictured delivering the opening address at the ICAC. Kate Geraghty Greenwood suggested she ask former Catholic Schools NSW staffer James Tudehope or Ellis. “Well conveniently Mr Tudehope is in New Zealand and Mr Ellis is in the United Kingdom,” Dwyer said.



Greenwood said that was inconvenient, to which Dwyer shot back: “Inconvenient to the public trying to work [out] why this money is being committed on a monthly basis.” Earlier in his evidence, Greenwood said that he had an interest in conservative causes, in particular abortion, but was not a member of the Reformers and later felt the right-wing Catholic group turned “toxic”. Greenwood appeared before the ICAC as it continues its probe into allegations of illegal political donations and links between fugitive developer Jean Nassif and Liberal operatives. He told the commission that he was interested in conservative social issues but less so in factional stoushes involving the Liberals and at no point considered himself a member of the Reformers despite being supportive of their work.



Greenwood was working for Nationals senator Matt Canavan when his friends Ellis and Robert Assaf started ramping up their recruitment efforts for the Catholic faction of the Liberals, he told the commission. While he was interested in the work of the Reformers, Greenwood said in 2018 he was “all about the Nationals” rather than Liberal Party matters. Loading “Most of the engagement I have with these guys would have been at a pub, or I’ve been dragged into a group chat,” Greenwood said. Greenwood said that while his boss Canavan spoke at a Reformers event, he mostly sat outside.



He would have been interested in policy talks organised by the Reformers, including one featuring former broadcaster Alan Jones, but was not involved in recruitment activities. Greenwood said he eventually began urging his friends to end their involvement with the factional group. He told the commission that he felt the Reformers “became so toxic” that he wanted his friends to stop. “I was supportive of their cause up until a point when it was negatively impacting me,” Greenwood said. He said the Reformers had started to cause him “a lot of grief professionally”.



At the start of his evidence, Greenwood was asked about friendships he had with other key figures linked to the Reformers, including the Perrottet brothers Dominic, Charles and Jean-Claude. Factional powerbroker Charles and Jean-Claude are persons of interest in this inquiry, but the former premier Dominic is not involved and nor is he accused of any wrongdoing. Greenwood also said that Ellis was one of his good friends and Ellis had been best man at his wedding. Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny ‘God granted us a victory’: The unlikely Liberal branch seized by the Reformers The commission heard that Greenwood visited Ellis in June in Britain, where Ellis had relocated in January and had “caught up” with him on four occasions. Dwyer told the commission in her opening statement that Ellis “has declined to give oral evidence to this public inquiry, during which he would be subject to cross-examination”.

World.title: Far-right nationalists take aim at Brisbane’s ‘Aussie’ posters
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Far-right nationalists take aim at Brisbane’s ‘Aussie’ posters Courtney Kruk August 10, 2026 — 4:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Far-right nationalists with links to anti-immigration rallies have defaced a street art poster campaign in Brisbane designed to challenge ideas of Australia’s national identity. It comes after one of the group claimed responsibility for a series of offensive posters plastered around Sydney and Melbourne earlier this year depicting Bondi shooter Naveed Akram. Self-proclaimed Australian nationalist and content creator Andre Mamet, who goes by the handle “Ausmaxx”, and Melbourne stockbroker Mitch Hobbs, aka “Sir Doug”, filmed themselves vandalising the posters in locations including South Brisbane’s Fish Lane and Norman Park over the weekend. The pair vandalised Adelaide artist Peter Drew’s distinctive poster series, replacing the “Aussie” label with “Indian”, “Chinese” and “not”. Courtney Kruk Federal Labor MP Renee Coffey shared video of her using a “step ladder, squeegee on a pole and my tallest son” to remove the words “Indian”, “Chinese”, and “not” which had been plastered over the distinctive “Aussie” label at Norman Park station in her seat of Griffith.



“When my son asked me where we were going, I said: ‘to fight racists’,” Coffey said. Adelaide-based artist Peter Drew launched the “Aussie” poster series in 2016 in response to what he saw as rising anti-immigration sentiment and xenophobia. It depicts Australians citizens who had been subject to the White Australia Policy. Peter Drew’s “Aussie” posters on Edward Street in Brisbane’s CBD. Courtney Kruk He revived the series earlier this year to mark its 10th anniversary, and in response to the March for Australia anti-immigration rallies that began last August. After visiting Sydney and Melbourne, Drew travelled to Brisbane at the end of July to erect 150 posters across inner-city suburbs and in Ipswich, where far-right politician Pauline Hanson ran a fish-and-chip shop before launching a political career.



He told this masthead he was not fazed by Mamet and Hobbs’ “latest brainwave”, adding that the point of the series was “to get under their skin”. Related Article Exclusive

Bondi shooting Posters of the Bondi shooter appeared around Melbourne. The culprit has now been unmasked “What we’ve got is a very small cohort of lost boys who are testing their ideology against reality, and every time it gets knocked back,” Drew said. “I like engaging with them and I don’t dislike them as people – it’s their ideas that I contend with. “When things like this happen … it keeps me going more than anything else.”



Coffey said she did not support illegal street art but was delighted when Drew’s work appeared in Brisbane. “Peter Drew’s iconic artwork represents an inclusive, warm, welcoming Australia that I believe in, and challenges narrow, exclusionary definitions pushed by our political opponents,” she said. Mitch Hobbs (left) and Andre Mamet (right) filmed themselves vandalising the works. Courtney Kruk “Racism has absolutely no place in our community, as evidenced by the number of locals who shouted out ‘thank you’ and passers-by who stopped to help us [on Sunday].” Mamet told this masthead: “Peter Drew’s art, despite being illegal graffiti, and as explained by him is used to deconstruct Australian identity, is celebrated and allowed.”



He did not elaborate further on the pair’s motivation to deface the works. Hobbs was also contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email Colin Kruger Updated August 10, 2026 — 4:38pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG’s chairman-elect Michael Ebeid has issued a grovelling apology to Labor senator Deborah O’Neill over his emails claiming her speech, which brought whistleblower allegations against the firm to light, contained “completely false” information. Ebeid, who has essentially been functioning as the chairman of the firm that is trying to recover from its top executives’ misuse of clients’ confidential audit documents, needs approval from KPMG partners to formally take up the role. That vote ends on Wednesday. KPMG’s incoming chairman Michael Ebeid issued a grovelling apology to Senator Deborah O’Neill. Getty Images Documents released by O’Neill’s parliamentary committee on Monday contained Ebeid’s personal apology for an email he sent early in the saga, which began this year, undermining the whistleblower’s claims. “What I wrote was wrong,” Ebeid told O’Neill in one document. “I described statements about the whistleblower’s allegations made by you to the Senate as false. I described the firm’s process as thorough. Events since have shown that neither was true, and that the concerns you raised on the whistleblower’s behalf have helped uncover serious wrongdoing and I can only thank you for that.”



Related Article Big four accountants KPMG directors flee as whistleblower scandal worsens He said he thought he was being helpful, based on his knowledge at the time. “However, with what I know now, my email was naive, embarrassing and wrong on every level,” Ebeid wrote. But the bigger issue for the embattled firm was the committee’s decision to release documents KPMG had battled to keep hidden under claims of legal professional privilege. The committee said it was in the public interest to release these documents ahead of another public grilling this Friday. The legal documents were the reports from two law firms, Allens and Ashurst, and relate to their work on the whistleblower complaints. KPMG had initially used the reports from the law firms to claim that the whistleblower’s complaints were unsubstantiated while refusing to release the actual documents publicly. A fresh investigation by Allens has led to a purge of KPMG’s most senior people as some of the most serious allegations have now been substantiated.



“The Ashurst and Allens processes were central to the claim that KPMG had undertaken comprehensive internal and external investigations prior to the speech given by Senator Deborah O’Neill on 24 March 2026,” the committee – chaired by O’Neill – said in a statement. It said the committee had found there was a “compelling public interest” in examining the results of the law firms’ investigations at its next hearing, allowing it to publish the previously legally privileged documents. Since May, the firm has lost its chief executive Andrew Yates, chairman Martin Sheppard, and sacked former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett after she lied about accessing sensitive board documents from client Lendlease and stored copies in her work locker. KPMG audit partner Kim Lawry also resigned from her senior roles this month after Westpac requested that she be removed from its audit “to ensure there is no distraction”. KPMG independent board member Patty Akopiantz quietly left the firm’s regional board last month, following former NSW premier Mike Baird’s exit in September, and fellow independent director Jane Hemstritch is expected to resign once replacements have been found. World.title: Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses Angus Delaney August 10, 2026 — 4:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state Coalition will seek to prohibit unions entering a person’s house and create occupational health and safety exemptions for employers as the Victorian government pushes ahead with its working-from-home laws. The opposition confirmed on Monday that it will not oppose Labor’s bill, but it will introduce seven proposed amendments to offer businesses greater protection after industry groups launched a last-ditch push to reverse legislation they say will send jobs and investment out of state. Premier Ben Carroll has been steadfast in his support of Labor’s working-from-home legislation. Louis Trerise Eight of the country’s largest business lobby groups joined forces on Monday, saying Labor’s plan to legislate the right to work from home two days a week when possible risked sending Victoria backwards at a time when its focus should be on turning around the economy, creating jobs and lifting living standards. Business Council of Australia executive director of advocacy Ben Wicks said the proposed legislation, which is set to pass the Victorian upper house this week, would increase the state’s unemployment rate of 5.1 per cent.



“It’s exactly the wrong time to be introducing a piece of legislation like this that we say costs jobs and costs investment,” Wicks said. “Our members tell us directly that this … will cost jobs and will cost investment.” Related Article Victorian Parliament Working from home laws set to extend to more workers, as Allan prepares legislation The group said companies already widely offer flexible arrangements, and the proposed laws are another layer of red tape that would see companies desert Victoria and expand their businesses interstate. “I’m concerned it’s the poison pill for jobs,” said Sally Curtain, chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. Tim Piper, the Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group, said businesses may even consider going offshore.



“I spoke to a member this morning who said to me, ‘working from home could also be working from the Philippines,’” he said. “You’ve got to remember that businesses have choices, whether it’s the rest of the country or whether it’s the rest of the world.” If the bill passes parliament as expected, it would come into effect on September 1 and be applicable to full-time employees, as well as part-time and regularly employed casuals on a pro rata basis. Employers would also be compelled to pay “reasonable costs” to enable their staff to work remotely. The Coalition has said it supports the right to work from home and will not oppose Labor’s bill, but it is seeking to introduce seven amendments to protect businesses. Australian Industry Group Victorian head Tim Piper said businesses may consider offshoring if the working-from-home changes pass. These include capping “reasonable costs” an employer must pay at $1000, limiting the right to employees who primarily work in Victoria and will continue to work from home in Victoria (unless mutually agreed to), and delaying an employee’s right to appeal a company’s decision until next year.



Other amendments are intended to prohibit the right of union entry into the home (similar to the conditions under which a union may access a workplace), excluding working from home when determining land tax liability, and protecting companies and directors from liability if employees are injured while working from home. The business groups said they felt there had been a lack of consultation on the legislation. Piper said they had not met directly with Premier Ben Carroll or his predecessor Jacinta Allan, but were expecting to meet Carroll this week. Since becoming premier a fortnight ago, Carroll has repeatedly said his government would stick to the promise to legislate the right to work from home, which was announced by Allan last year. Carroll has argued the move would save Victorians time and money, and said Labor had no plans to change the bill, but it would consider “sensible amendments” moved in the upper house.



“My door’s always open to the business community,” Carroll said on Monday morning. “We do know work from home works for families, but we also need to do everything we can to support our business community.” Related Article Victorian election Labor open to High Court challenge over work from home laws Members of the coalition of business groups have not ruled out launching or joining a potential High Court challenge against the legislation if it passes. Legal experts have cast doubt over the state government’s ability to legislate a right to work from home, as most workplace laws are under the jurisdiction of the federal government. “Certainly, I would expect a High Court challenge to occur with this legislation, keeping in mind we do not actually have a bill which has passed through the upper house yet, and time will tell how that will evolve over the coming months,” said Cath Evans, Victorian executive director of the Property Council of Australia. World.title: Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot Sam McClure August 10, 2026 — 4:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With 47 seconds remaining in the third quarter of Carlton and St Kilda’s season-opening AFLW match on Sunday, Channel Seven commentator Alistair Nicholson delivered a message to viewers that inadvertently captured one of the most significant challenges confronting the competition. “For Victorian viewers, you are going to Seven News. If you want to keep watching the footy, go to 7mate now.” St Kilda’s Tyanna Smith bursts away during the season opener against Carlton. AFL Photos via Getty Images Tyanna Smith had just burst through a centre bounce like Bailey Smith and booted a brilliant goal – her second – from outside 50 metres to put the Saints within 22 points. The football continued. Seven’s coverage on its primary Victorian channel did not.



Related Article AFL 2026 Carlton close on stunning AFL top 10 finish; Rowell dominant as Suns snap streak; Blues hold sway in AFLW opener There was nothing sinister about the decision. TV networks routinely move programming between channels, and Seven’s evening news remains among the most commercially important programs on its schedule. But the timing was striking. Four days later, there will be no men’s AFL match on Thursday night, with Melbourne and Hawthorn instead afforded clear air for their AFLW fixture. The contrast warrants examination.



Thursday night AFL has become one of the most valuable pieces of sporting content on Australian television, regularly attracting audiences of around one million across Seven’s platforms this season. This Thursday night’s AFLW game is expected to attract a fraction of that audience. So the decision to clear men’s footy from that timeslot to showcase the AFLW will cost hundreds of thousands of viewers. View post on X Within the space of four days, the industry will have provided two vastly different illustrations of where the AFLW currently sits. On Sunday, the broadcaster considered the product sufficiently expendable to move the final quarter from its primary channel.



On Thursday, the AFL will clear one of its most lucrative broadcast windows to provide the same competition with uncontested exposure. After a decade of AFLW, it is reasonable to ask whether this approach remains sustainable. Abbie McKay wins the ‘golden fist’ for her performance. Getty Images The creation of the AFLW has been among the most consequential developments in Australian sport this century. Its influence on female participation, pathways and the visibility of women in the game has been profound. Girls who once reached their early teenage years and discovered their football pathway effectively ended can now aspire to play the sport professionally. Clubs that existed for more than a century as overwhelmingly male institutions now have women wearing their jumpers at the elite level.



Those achievements are substantial and permanent. Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist But the success of female football as a participation movement and the commercial sustainability of an 18-team professional national competition are not necessarily the same proposition. Eleven seasons after its establishment, the AFLW should be sufficiently mature to withstand scrutiny of the latter. Professional sport is expensive.



Players must be paid. Football departments must be funded. Teams must travel around the country. Venues must be opened and staffed. Matches must be produced and broadcast to professional standards. The AFL and its broadcast partners are investing millions of dollars annually in a competition that remains a considerable distance from paying for itself. That investment was entirely understandable during AFLW’s establishment phase. New competitions require subsidies. Audiences take time to develop, sporting traditions are not manufactured overnight, and the AFL possessed both the financial capacity and strategic incentive to establish a national women’s competition. But an establishment phase cannot continue indefinitely.



The AFLW is now entering season 11. The question should no longer simply be how much the competition has grown, but how it eventually becomes commercially sustainable. That discussion becomes particularly relevant given the broader financial demands confronting the AFL. View post on X The league is preparing to establish a 19th licence in Tasmania, an undertaking that will require significant investment over many years. Expansion clubs GWS and Gold Coast continue to be heavily funded by the AFL. Clubs continue to seek greater distributions. Player payments continue to increase. The cost of operating football clubs continues to rise. The media industry underwriting much of that expenditure is simultaneously navigating one of the most difficult advertising markets in recent memory.



The AFLW game between Carlton and St Kilda rated 147,000 nationally, overlapping with the men’s West Coast-Collingwood match. The previous Sunday afternoon men’s game between Gold Coast and Melbourne rated 402,000. Related Article Opinion

AFLW The moment Daisy Pearce broke the ice inside the Australian camp Libby Birch AFL columnist Scheduling the women’s match as part of a double header with the Blues-Saints men’s clash meant there were more than 20,000 people watching at Marvel Stadium by midway through the last quarter. It would be absurd to expect AFLW to generate the same audiences and revenue as the AFL given the men’s competition has enjoyed more than a century to establish its cultural and commercial position. Nor does commercial sustainability necessarily require immediate profitability.



But there must be a credible trajectory towards an economic model in which the size and cost of the competition bears some relationship to the audience and revenue it generates. Perhaps that requires reconsidering how AFLW is scheduled. The instinct has often been to provide the competition with “clear air” — removing competing AFL matches and attempting to manufacture standalone marquee windows. Thursday night will provide another experiment in that philosophy. But there is an alternative argument.



Rather than seeking clear air for AFLW while the men’s season is on, perhaps the league would be better to persevere with fixtures that tap into the audience already watching Australian football. Double headers, such as Sunday’s Spud’s Game fixtures, integrated match days and fixtures positioned around major AFL games may provide AFLW with access to an audience far greater than it can presently attract on its own. The next stage of AFLW cannot simply be about expansion: more teams, more games, longer seasons, higher salaries and more premium broadcast windows. It must also be about demand. To extend the women’s season length to 14 home-and-away rounds, the league and the AFL Players’ Association agreed on key performance metrics: an average attendance of 6000 fans and 100,000 broadcast viewers per match. Those are ambitious targets across the season, but by staging select games in high-value timeslots, the league is giving W a chance to maximise its audience.



At some point, investment has to become a test of demand and Thursday night is exactly that. Related Article AFLW ‘We couldn’t get over that’: The AFLW norm baffling this Irish import How many people are watching? How many are attending? What are advertisers prepared to pay to reach that audience? What does each match cost to stage and broadcast? And what structure gives the competition the greatest chance to grow those numbers? Those questions should not be interpreted as an attack on women’s football. They are the questions asked of every professional sporting competition.



The AFLW has already transformed the pathway for women and girls who want to play Australian football and fundamentally altered the culture of the national game. Its second decade presents a different challenge. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers as she plans attack for parliament’s return
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers as she plans attack for parliament’s return Nick Newling August 10, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson has vowed to forge ahead with a legally questionable bill targeting foreign fighters and hit out at Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s oversight of migration policy, as the One Nation leader seeks to set the agenda for parliament’s return. Riding a wave of high poll results, Hanson on Monday fired off a series of social media posts laying out her plan for the coming fortnight and accusing Burke and Labor of orchestrating a secret plan to bring an additional million migrants into the country over the next four years. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has attacked Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke for the government’s handling of migration. Eamon Gallagher The party’s Protecting Australians from Foreign Terrorist Fighters Bill – its first complete policy proposal this term – will be introduced this week. However, her bill has been criticised by legal experts who say it will fail to withstand a High Court challenge. Hanson argues that the bill will strengthen powers to cancel or refuse passports and toughen bail laws for terrorism charges. A key pillar of the bill would create a new “foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order” that the minister could ask the Federal Court to impose. The existing exclusion order regime under the minister’s control would remain.



Burke recently said the bill “would last about 30 seconds in the High Court”, while constitutional law expert Anne Twomey told this masthead that the proposal appeared to be a delaying mechanism and would achieve little in its attempt to ban foreign fighters from returning. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was the target of Hanson’s ire on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Despite Twomey’s criticisms, Hanson on Monday claimed that the Sydney University professor saw it as “a good piece of legislation that is robust enough to withstand a challenge in the High Court”. Twomey was contacted for comment. Hours earlier, Hanson took to Facebook to accuse Burke of mismanaging Australia’s migration settings and lying to voters about attempts to pull back net overseas migration. The comments come after Burke abruptly delayed the announcement of the government’s migration overhaul package last week. “They already brought in 1.5 million in four years. That’s why your rent exploded, your pay went backwards, and your kids can’t buy a home. It’s why hospitals are turning away sick people,” Hanson wrote.



Hanson’s return to parliament comes after a falling out with Seven over her appearance on an episode of the show Spotlight, which filmed her spending time with British anti-Islam extremist Tommy Robinson. She was unapologetic about her interview with Robinson, a divisive figure whose appearance on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast prompted Nine, owner of this masthead, to part ways with its morning show host. Related Article Exclusive

Political expenses Empty five-star room: Hanson paid for $900-a-night hotel with party funds Hanson has claimed that Seven was originally supposed to pay for the trip but pulled out, forcing One Nation to carry the cost of a $900-a-night hotel room. She disputed reports in this masthead that the party paid for an empty room while she was on a side trip to Sicily, partially funded by her mining-billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart, to attend a Dolce & Gabbana fashion show. Burke’s address to the National Press Club was delayed after cabinet ministers raised questions about political backlash and unresolved financial costs. The minister is expected to provide more detail in coming days on the plan to slash net overseas migration intake to its budget forecast of 225,000 a year.



Labor is weighing up whether to rework the country’s skilled migration program, place stricter rules on working holidaymakers and family reunion visas, and slash working rights for people who overstay their visas. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce doubled down on Hanson’s comments on Monday, telling News24, formerly Sky News: “You meet [migrants] when you’re trying to drive a car to work. That’s why you can’t get anywhere.” Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Assistant Foreign Affairs Minister Matt Thistlethwaite came to Burke’s defence on Monday, claiming the figures cited by Hanson were not correct. “Those numbers that Pauline Hanson refers to are net overseas migration numbers, which includes Australian citizens who are living overseas and returning home. Is Pauline Hanson saying that Australians living overseas do not have the right to return home?” Thistlethwaite asked during a News24 appearance.



“The better figure is permanent migration. That we’ve set at 185,000 for the last couple of years, and we’ve met that figure. That figure is based a lot on what employers tell us they need.” Net overseas migration – long-term arrivals into the country minus departures – peaked under Labor in September 2023 as borders reopened after the COVID pandemic, but has consistently fallen since then. Figures in the May budget showed Labor anticipated the net overseas migration rate to be 295,000 in the last financial year.
